catalogTitle: Spiritual Coins are Created by our Desire to Give שקלים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Jew's heartfelt desire to give the half-shekel creates spiritual coins, because deep in every Jewish heart lies a point no sin can reach, and he shows this point in Yom Kippur, Purim and the haftarah of King Yehoash.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Moshe Rabbeinu comes each year at Parshas Shekalim to lift up the Jewish people. He brings the Rema MiPano's question: how does the angel Michael offer korbanos in the heavenly Beis HaMikdash, when korbanos must come from each year's new shekalim? The Pri Tzaddik answers with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who filled a valley with gold coins by his word: a Jew's yearning to give, when he hears Parshas Shekalim, creates spiritual coins. The Rav ties Shekalim to the tip of the yud and to the hidden point in the heart described by the Rambam, the inner Holy of Holies that surfaces on Yom Kippur and Purim. He then shows that Yehoash, who killed Zechariah, is the haftarah's hero of the shekalim, proving that no sin reaches that point. He closes with a Gemara about Rabbah bar bar Chanah: more is demanded of a person on a higher level.

en: According to the Pri Tzaddik, the yearning of each Jew to give the shekel, aroused when Parshas Shekalim is read, creates spiritual coins from which the heavenly korbanos are bought.
Through the Rambam's ruling on a coerced consent, the Rav explains that every Jew, even a rasha, has a hidden point in his heart that wants to do Hashem's will.
Since man is a small world, every Jew has an inner Holy of Holies, which comes into contact on Yom Kippur and, even more, on Purim.

Yehoash, who sinned against the Holy of Holies by killing Zechariah on Yom Kippur, is the one who strengthened the mitzvah of the shekalim, showing that no sin reaches the point that Shekalim touches.
Yom Kippur and Purim both come through a lottery, which has no reason, because they come from the root point where tzaddik and rasha are the same.
From the Gemara of Rabbah bar bar Chanah the Rav learns that for a person on a higher level, what is middas chassidus for others is the din.

title.en: Moshe's yearly lift and the heavenly korbanos

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Moshe Rabbeinu comes each year at Parshas Shekalim to lift up every Jew. He then brings the Rema MiPano: the angel Michael offers korbanos in the heavenly Beis HaMikdash, and since korbanos must be bought from each year's new shekalim, the question is where the money comes from.

title.en: The Pri Tzaddik: coins created by desire

summary.en: The Rav brings the Pri Tzaddik's answer through the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who turned a valley into gold coins by his word. A Jew too has the power of speech, so when he hears Parshas Shekalim and yearns to give, spiritual coins are created, and from them the heavenly korbanos are brought.

title.en: The tip of the yud and the hidden will

summary.en: The Rav links the four parshiyos to the four letters of Hashem's Name, with Shekalim as the yud and its tiny tip that is above the Name. He then brings the Rambam on a man forced until he says 'I want': deep in every Jew's heart is a hidden point that wants Hashem's will, even in a rasha.

title.en: The inner Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur and Purim

summary.en: Since man is a small world, every Jew has a Holy of Holies inside him, which he touches on Yom Kippur, and Purim is a Yom Kippur that goes even higher. The Rav explains the Jews' rescue in the Purim story and the merit of the shekalim that preceded Haman's shekalim through this point, where all Jews are equal.

title.en: The haftarah: Yehoash and Zechariah

summary.en: The Rav tells the story behind the haftarah: Yehoash was hidden as an infant in the Holy of Holies from Asalyah and crowned at seven by Yehoyada. After Yehoyada's death Yehoash had Yehoyada's son Zechariah, a kohen and navi, killed in the Beis HaMikdash on Yom Kippur.

title.en: World, year and soul: why Yehoash fits Shekalim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was made in three matching dimensions, place, time and soul, each with a Holy of Holies, so killing Zechariah on Yom Kippur near the Kodesh HaKodashim violated all three. Yet Yehoash is the one who strengthened the mitzvah of the shekalim, and the Rav says no one fits the haftarah better, because Shekalim shows a point in the heart, the tip of the yud, that no sin reaches.

title.en: Two lotteries: Yom Kippur and Purim

summary.en: Following the Tanya, the Rav notes that both Yom Kippur and Purim come through a lottery. The two identical goats, Yaakov and Esav, are separated only by lot; the Chasam Sofer's round dance of the tzaddikim shows all are equally close to the center; and a lottery win has no reason, because it comes from the root point. He concludes that Yehoash proves no sin reaches that point.

title.en: On the sedra: more is asked of the great

summary.en: The Rav adds a word on the sedra with the Gemara of Rabbah bar bar Chanah, whose workers broke his wine barrel, and asks why Rav called it the din. He explains that the higher a person's level, the more is required of him, and illustrates it with a story of a brilliant student of Rebbe Reb Bunim of Peshischa who mocked a Zohar.

catalogTitle: צירוף חודש ניסן - “ישמחו השמים ותגל הארץ” - חודש מלא חסד (פירושים על הגדה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Nissan, whose letter-combination of Hashem's Name comes from "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz", is a month of chesed and renewal in which Hashem's kingship is revealed, and that the mitzvos of Pesach night, above all eating matzah and saying the Haggadah, plant emunah and draw down salvation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the renewal of Nissan: nature sprouts and sings because Hashem knocks on every Jew's heart, as in "pischi li" of Shir HaShirim. Through Vayikra's small aleph and the calendar he shows that Nissan reveals the love hidden in Adar. Pesach means opening, and matzah is the key that opens the heart. Nissan's letter-combination comes from "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz", followed by "Hashem malach": Nissan completed creation with the birth of Klal Yisrael and is the time of Hashem's kingship and of a judgment in chesed. The two central mitzvos are removing chametz, which is the yetzer hara and Amalek's doubt, and eating matzah, the food of emunah. Emunah brings true freedom and joy. Saying the Haggadah draws down the salvations of the Exodus, and the shiur ends with the final redemption hinted in the last day of Pesach.

en: Nissan brings renewal to the world: the sprouting and singing of nature reflect Hashem's love and kindness toward Klal Yisrael at this time.
The letter-combination of Hashem's Name for Nissan comes from "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz": the joy above is revealed on earth, leading to "Hashem malach".
Nissan is a time of kingship and of judgment in chesed, judged by Hashem Himself, in contrast to the judgment with din in Tishrei.
The two central mitzvos of Nissan are removing chametz, which stands for the yetzer hara and the doubts of Amalek, and eating matzah, which is emunah.
Emunah brings true freedom and joy: one who relies on Hashem depends on nothing else.
Saying the Haggadah is not only a remembrance: it draws down the salvations of the Exodus again for Klal Yisrael.

matzah as the food of emunah

title.en: Nissan's renewal and Hashem's knock

summary.en: The Rav opens with Shabbos HaChodesh and the renewal of Nissan, when nature sprouts and sings. He brings "kol dodi dofek" and "pischi li" from Shir HaShirim: Hashem knocks on every Jew, His head full of the dew of blessing, and asks him to open up.

title.en: Vayikra's small aleph: Nissan reveals Adar

summary.en: The Rav explains that Vayikra, read in Nissan, is a word of love, written with a small aleph. Adar is a month of hiddenness when the aleph seems missing; through the calendar sign at-bash he shows that Nissan reveals what was hidden in Adar, that it was a call of love all along.

title.en: Pesach as opening; matzah as the key

summary.en: The Rav explains that Pesach is a time of opening, and that the Targum's word for matzah means opening; matzah is the key that opens the heart. Like two pianos tuned to the same key, Jews connect to Nissan's chesed by doing chesed, which is why Pesach begins with giving to the poor.

title.en: The letter-combination "Yismechu hashamayim"

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that Nissan's combination of Hashem's Name is the first letters of "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz": the angels' joy above is revealed below in nature and in Jews' song. The verse continues "Hashem malach", and he introduces the dispute whether the world was created in Nissan or Tishrei.

title.en: Nissan completes creation; Hashem's kingship

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was created in Tishrei in deed but in Nissan in thought, since Klal Yisrael, the purpose of creation, became a nation at the Exodus; this is why the first of the Ten Commandments mentions the Exodus. Nissan, the new year for kings, is when Hashem's kingship is revealed, while the nations were given Tishrei.

title.en: Kingship and a judgment of chesed

summary.en: The Rav describes Nissan as the time when kingship is decided above and below, and when Hashem Himself will take over the kingship, which is why the redemption is tied to Nissan. He explains that the judgment of Nissan is greater than that of Tishrei but comes through chesed, as the straight order of the letters in "aviv" hints, in contrast to the reversed letters of Tishrei.

title.en: The Chozeh's notes and the two mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav tells, from the Bnei Yissaschar, how the Chozeh of Lublin wrote down in the first days of Nissan all that would happen in the year, and connects it to the verse about setting up the Mishkan on the first of the first month. He then explains that every mitzvah is a symbolic act that arouses above, and that all of Nissan revolves around two mitzvos.

title.en: Chametz, Amalek and the war against doubt

summary.en: The Rav asks why chametz has stringencies no other prohibition has, and answers from the Zohar that chametz is the yetzer hara. The main war with Amalek is on Erev Pesach; Amalek is doubt in emunah, rooted in bad middos such as pride, and today it spreads as heresy. Chametz must be removed before emunah can enter, a war that runs from Purim to Pesach.

title.en: Searching the heart; matzah is emunah

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Lechovitcher sent a messenger to tell his chassidim to search the holes and cracks, and they davened Maariv for hours with great cries. He explains that one searches the heart as far as one can, then nullifies the rest and asks Hashem to remove it, and that matzah, the food of emunah, does this.

title.en: Matzah as a capsule; the freedom of emunah

summary.en: The Rav compares matzah to a capsule that lets the body swallow emunah, and explains why the preparations for Pesach are so great. He brings the Satmar Rav that this whole night is matzah, and the Arizal that matzah equals three times Hashem's Name with its filling. Pesach night's freedom, he says, is the freedom of one who relies on his Father in heaven.

title.en: Leaning on Hashem: joy versus sadness

summary.en: From the Midrash on "vayasev" the Rav explains reclining as leaning on Hashem. Simcha comes from being able to lean, while atzvus is the feeling of being abandoned, and idols are called atzabim. Avraham, the first believer, has his day on Pesach, and the emunah of Pesach grows from the first day to the last, which hints at techiyas hameisim.

title.en: Karpas, the Chasam Sofer and living with a question

summary.en: The Rav explains that karpas is done so the child asks, and tells how the Chasam Sofer let his son walk around with a question on emunah for days before answering, to teach that one can live with a question and still believe. In Egypt Jews nearly fell into the fiftieth gate of impurity; today that gate is heresy, and the main test before Moshiach is emunah.

title.en: The rasha, and the Haggadah as drawing emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the rasha denies the principles of emunah, yet today, since we have the Torah, even he can be rescued. The purpose of the Haggadah is to draw down emunah by speaking about it, and Pesach night is the time a father can plant emunah in his child. He brings the Targum Yonasan that on Pesach night the angels sing and the storehouses of dew open.

title.en: Haggadah from "gid"; the night that is day

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haggadah comes from the word for a vein, which carries life, and from the word for mazal that flows down: saying it draws down. The night of the Exodus shone like a summer day, and the sages in Bnei Brak drew that light down until they did not know it was morning. From this he explains why Pesach night cannot be the source for mentioning the Exodus at night.

title.en: Drawing salvation: matzos, the Ropshitzer and the plagues

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Haggadah draws down the miracles of the Exodus again. He tells how the Ropshitzer, during the war between Napoleon and Russia, threw matzos into the oven on Erev Pesach to affect the war, and that Avraham prepared for his war by baking matzos. Each plague recalled draws salvation for Jews, and later generations expounded more plagues because more salvation is needed.

title.en: Rabbi Eliezer's four and Rabbi Akiva's five

summary.en: The Rav asks why Rabbi Eliezer counted four plagues in each plague and Rabbi Akiva five. Through the Gemara in Menachos about Moshe watching Rabbi Akiva expound the crowns of the letters, he explains that Rabbi Eliezer, linked to Moshe's soul, drew from the four letters of Hashem's Name, while Rabbi Akiva drew from the crown above them.

title.en: The last day of Pesach and the final song

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the haftarah of Beshalach, Devorah's song after a salvation that lasted forty years, with the haftarah of Pesach, David's song that ends with the eternal salvation of Moshiach. A new feminine song gives birth to further salvations, while the final one is masculine. He ends with the last day of Pesach, Moshiach's light and the hope that this be the last Pesach in exile.

catalogTitle: הלכות והתעוררות באפיית מצה בקדושה ובזריזות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that matzah, the 'food of emunah', binds a Jew to Hashem as chametz cuts him off, and urges that it be baked with zerizus, kedushah and every hiddur, with tefillah for success.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the joy with which Jews bake matzah and with 'ushmartem es hamatzos': zerizus is the very core of this mitzvah, and from it Chazal learn zerizus for all mitzvos. Matzah is the Zohar's 'food of emunah'; Pesach is the head of the festivals, tied to Avraham Avinu, the head of emunah, and the night of telling over yetzias Mitzrayim, the root of the whole Torah. Since eating matzah is almost the only eating-mitzvah left in galus, it must be done with every hiddur. In spring, when everything sprouts, the Seder night opens the blessings of Torah and yiras Shamayim. He then turns to practical concerns in today's bakeries: hired workers, clean hands and clothes, talking and spitting, eating chametz during breaks, sleeves, nails, cold water, and saying 'l'shem matzas mitzvah' aloud. He praises chaburos of ehrliche Yidden who bake with mikvah and kedushah, tells stories of tzaddikim's sensitivity, explains through the Radbaz that chametz is the yetzer hara, and closes with a story showing that one must also pray for a kosher Pesach.

en: From 'ushmartem es hamatzos' the Rav teaches that zerizus is part of the essence of baking matzah, and from it Chazal learn zerizus for every mitzvah.
Matzah is the 'food of emunah'; the matzah one sees is only a capsule, and inside it is emunah, the root of all the mitzvos.
Since matzah is almost the only mitzvah of eating left in galus, it must be baked with every hiddur and great effort.
Matzah must be baked lishmah by Yidden who care about it; matzah baked by hired workers without mesorah, or by machine, lacks this.
Chametz is the yetzer hara that cuts a Jew off from Hashem, while kosher matzah binds him to Hashem.
Beyond all the care, one must pray and give tzedakah to merit kosher matzah and a kosher Pesach.

title.en: Zerizus and the food of emunah

summary.en: The Rav opens with the joy of baking matzah and the custom of drawing the water with joy, then teaches from 'ushmartem es hamatzos' that zerizus is the core of this mitzvah. Matzah is the Zohar's 'food of emunah', like a capsule holding medicine, and Pesach, head of the festivals, is tied to Avraham Avinu, head of emunah.

title.en: Avraham's matzos and Pesach as the festival of emunah

summary.en: The Rav shows that Avraham Avinu baked matzos and that all his successes came on Pesach, because Pesach instills emunah through the telling of yetzias Mitzrayim over the matzah. Emunah is the first of the Ten Commandments and the root of all mitzvos, so matzah teaches about all the mitzvos.

title.en: The last eating-mitzvah and the blessings of Nissan

summary.en: The Rav cites a sefer that protests careless matzah baking: in galus matzah is almost the only mitzvah of eating left, so it needs every hiddur. In spring, when all of nature sprouts, the Seder night opens the blessings of Torah, halachah and yiras Shamayim, and he urges a matzah with all hiddurim rather than relying on generic brands.

title.en: A hard mitzvah: zechus, tefillah and lishmah

summary.en: The Rav says matzah is a hard mitzvah to fulfil properly and one needs a zechus, tefillah and tzedakah to merit good matzah. He describes market matzah baked by hired workers without mesorah, the need for clean hands every eighteen minutes, and stresses that matzah must be baked lishmah by Yidden who care.

title.en: The oven worker, clean clothes and talking

summary.en: The Rav tells of a visit to a bakery where the oven worker was the company's regular employee, which troubled him. He brings from the poskim that one should brush off clothes after eating before baking, and warns that talking while baking can lead to spitting a crumb of chametz onto the matzah.

title.en: Breaks, sleeves, nails and cold water

summary.en: The Rav asks that those who stay to the end of the baking not eat chametz during the break, but rather Pesach matzah or egg matzah, mentioning briefly that the poskim disagreed about such matzos. He then discusses sleeves rubbing old dough onto new matzos, cutting nails, washing in cold water, and blood from the hands, which makes dough chametz at once.

title.en: Keeping cool and the power of speech

summary.en: The Rav mentions the Chasam Sofer's marble tables and urges keeping everything as cold as possible, not keeping rolling pins near the oven, and not banging the sticks, which makes cracks that hold dough. He then explains the great power of a Jew's speech, as with hekdesh, and therefore one should say aloud 'l'shem matzas mitzvah' when baking.

title.en: Saying lishmah, again and again

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that a house built aloud for avodah zarah is struck with tzaraas, and the Bnei Yissaschar that the generation of the dispersion repeated 'havah' to strengthen their intent; so too one should say 'l'shem mitzvah' many times. He explains why machine matzos are not used at the Seder, praises the bochurim's baking, and notes that galus has weakened certain mitzvos, but Hashem accepts what Yidden do.

title.en: Chaburos, mikvah and the sense of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav welcomes chaburos of ehrliche Yidden who bake their own matzos, and mentions the practice of going to mikvah before baking. He tells of a talmid of the Lechovitcher who would not eat meat because the shochet had not gone to mikvah, and of Rav Avraham of Slonim who sensed that plates were not toveled, and brings the Mishnah in Chagigah on levels of purity.

title.en: Matzah binds, chametz cuts off

summary.en: The Rav says one should avoid idle talk and leitzanus while baking, since matzah absorbs what is said over it. Matzah must be guarded from thieves, the forces of the Satan; chametz cuts a Jew off from Hashem and matzah binds him. He brings the Radbaz, who explains the great strictness of chametz in that chametz is the yetzer hara.

title.en: Chumros of Pesach and the need for tefillah

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Vizhnitzer Rebbe's fervor at bedikas chametz, says one must not mock those with chumros on Pesach, citing the Bnei Yissaschar, and tells a story from the Satmar Rav of a tzaddik who found wheat in his soup despite all his care and was answered from Heaven that he had not prayed. He closes asking that people give tzedakah and pray before baking, with a brachah for a kosher and joyous Pesach.

catalogTitle: ראש כל מועדות נשאת פסח; כנגד אברהם אבינו - חסד ואמונה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Pesach, the head of all the festivals, is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, and therefore the Yom Tov of chesed, renewal and above all emunah, which a Jew takes in by eating matzah, the food of faith.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the three festivals corresponding to the three Avos: Pesach, the head of the festivals, belongs to Avraham, the root of Klal Yisrael. Only Pesach and milah carry kares for neglect, and kares shows that these mitzvos bind a Jew to Avraham and to his people. He then shows that Nissan is the month of chesed and the right side, while Tishrei is din, and that every Nissan the world is renewed: nature rises as if from the dead, and a Jew too must rise and renew his service. Avraham's quality is emunah, inherited by every Jew; at the Exodus the ten plagues revealed that Hashem created and runs the world. A story of souls sent down again and again leads to the lesson of complete trust in hashgacha pratis without saying 'would have'. Matzah, above time and place, is the food of emunah. He ends with preparing for Pesach through prayer, with stories, and with a tefillah for the final redemption.

en: Pesach is the head of the festivals because it corresponds to Avraham Avinu, the first point of Klal Yisrael, and it binds a Jew to his root.
The punishment of kares for neglecting Pesach and milah shows that these mitzvos are a bond, connecting a Jew to Avraham and to Klal Yisrael.
Nissan is a time of renewal in heaven that reaches down into nature, and a Jew is meant to renew himself spiritually and rise from his spiritual death.
Avraham's quality is emunah, inherited by every Jew, and the Exodus, seen by millions, is the foundation of the faith that is passed from generation to generation.
Emunah means trusting that everything comes from Hashem's personal providence, so a Jew should never say 'it would have been better'.
Matzah is the food of emunah: unlike chametz, which needs time and takes up space, it stands above time and place, as emunah does.

title.en: Pesach, head of the festivals, and Avraham

summary.en: The Rav explains that the three festivals correspond to the three Avos, with Pesach against Avraham, the root of the Avos and of Klal Yisrael, which makes it the head of the festivals. Shavuos and Sukkos have a higher holiness, but Pesach is the beginning and binds a Jew to his root.

title.en: Kares as a bond; Avraham's Pesach

summary.en: The Rav asks why only Pesach and milah carry kares, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim that kares shows the mitzvah is a bond, connecting a Jew to Avraham and to the nation. He then lists events of Avraham's life that took place on Pesach: the covenant, the milah, the matzah he baked and the war with the four kings.

title.en: Nissan, the month of chesed and the right side

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham is the attribute of chesed and the right side, which a Jew always puts first, and that Nissan is the month of the right side, whose name follows the alphabet in order, while Tishrei reverses it and is the month of din. With this he explains how the world was created in Tishrei in thought but in Nissan in deed.

title.en: Nissan renewal and techiyas hameisim

summary.en: The Rav explains that every festival repeats what happened originally, so every Nissan the world and the bond of Klal Yisrael are renewed. Nature in spring rises as if from the dead, the haftarah of Yechezkel's dry bones is read on Pesach, and a Jew must ask himself whether he too will rise and serve Hashem with life; even repainting the house and new clothes for Pesach express this renewal.

title.en: Avraham's emunah and the Exodus

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham's quality is emunah, which every Jew inherits, so Avraham's festival plants emunah. At the Exodus Hashem showed through the ten plagues, which correspond to the ten utterances of creation, that He created the world and runs it; this was seen by millions, as the Rambam writes, and is passed down from parent to child.

title.en: Seder night, the time to plant emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings that the first of the Ten Commandments is emunah, rooted in the Exodus, and the Ohev Yisrael that the Seder night, when matzah and maror lie before us, is the time to tell the children about the Exodus and plant emunah in them. In the last generations, as the Gemara says of Chavakuk, everything rests on emunah alone.

title.en: The souls' complaint and 'would have'

summary.en: The Rav tells a story told by a disciple of the Ba'al Shem Tov: souls that kept failing and coming back complained until they reached Hashem, who advised them to rely on emunah alone, on one condition, never to say 'would have'. He illustrates with a brother who moved the alarm clock and a wife whose late breakfast cost a deal, and explains that 'would have' denies hashgacha pratis.

title.en: Emunah, the test of our time

summary.en: The Rav calls emunah the soul of a Jew, the Avraham within him, and connects it with the blessing of Magen Avraham. He brings the Chofetz Chaim's words that there would be no more dybbuks, since now the test is to believe without seeing, and compares the questions of our generation to Avraham's test at the Akeidah.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that matzah is the food of faith, with an inner power like a vitamin or a pill. Everything in this world happens in time and place, while emunah is above both; chametz needs time and rises to take up space, but matzah does not. Bread is holy, three times the Name Havayah, but matzah equals three times the Name with its full spelling.

title.en: Praying for emunah; chametz and the yetzer hara

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew must ask Hashem for complete emunah, which is the essence of his soul and for which even sinners gave their lives. He calls for preparing for Pesach in body and spirit, explaining with the Radvaz and the Zohar that the special strictness about chametz is because chametz is the yetzer hara, and ends with learning, davening and tzedakah before Pesach.

title.en: The tzaddik and the grain of wheat

summary.en: The Rav tells a story he heard from the Klausenburger Rav about a tzaddik who worked with great effort for a kosher Pesach and found a grain of wheat in his soup at the Seder. Asking in a dream, he was told that he had forgotten to pray to Hashem, and was shown how a bird dropped the grain down the chimney.

title.en: Salvation through the mitzvos of Pesach

summary.en: The Rav says that without healthy emunah learning and davening are lacking, and that through the mitzvos of Pesach great salvations can be drawn down, which is why the Haggadah counts the plagues. He tells of the Ropshitzer's matzos against the Russians and Avraham's matzos against the four kings, urges davening and learning with life, tells of the Sanzer Rav's joy after the Seder, and closes with a prayer for the final Pesach in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: The Lesson of the מגילה: Find 'ה Peeking Through the Cracks of Your life. Explanation of פורים קטן

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that Purim and its Megillah train a Jew to find Hashem hidden behind nature, rulers and events, peeking out through the cracks, and explains Purim Katan of a leap year.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the greatness of Purim, compared with Yom Kippur, and explains Purim Katan: in a leap year the moon has fallen far behind the sun, so in the first Adar we are too weak to keep Purim, and Hashem has the Megillah read in heaven; the second reading, in the second Adar, accomplishes more. He then explains Amalek through three readings of 'karcha': cooling a Jew's fervor, making him impure, and teaching that everything is chance. This is the 'double hiding' of 'haster astir', which is why Hashem's name seems absent from the Megillah and hides in the word 'hamelech', whose gematria equals the incomplete 'kes Kah'. Through the Bnei Yissaschar's parable he shows that a miracle inside nature is greater still. The Megillah trains the eye to find Hashem through the cracks, in history, in the news and behind every costume. He closes with Adar as the month of laughter at the world, Yaakov's complaint, Mordechai, and David's response to Shimi.

en: In a leap year the first Adar is too far from the 'sun' of Hashem for us to keep Purim, so Hashem has the Megillah read in heaven, and the second reading in the second Adar accomplishes more.
Amalek 'cooled off' the Jews; life always pulses up and down, and the war against Amalek is to hold on through the cold periods until Hashem warms a person again.
Amalek and Haman stand for the belief that everything is chance ('mikreh'), which is the double concealment of 'haster astir' that marks the Megillah and the time before Moshiach.
Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah in the word 'hamelech', because His name and throne are incomplete ('kes Kah') while Amalek exists.
Adar is the season of miracles cloaked in nature, and reading the Megillah is an exercise in finding Hashem behind that cloak.
After Purim one should be able to read the news and all of history between the lines and see Hashem directing everything; the whole world is a Megillah.
Nothing happens without Hashem, so one may not blame a person for what happens to him, as seen from Yaakov's complaint and from David's response to Shimi.

title.en: The greatness of Purim

summary.en: The Rav introduces Purim Katan this Shabbos and says Purim is greater than any Yom Tov: Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim', and in the future Yom Kippur will rise to Purim's level. Purim is 'masked', different from how it appears, like a child in costume.

title.en: Purim Katan and the second reading

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Megillah says 'hasheinis' in the feminine if it refers to the second month, and explains with the moon falling behind the sun: in the first Adar we are too weak to keep Purim, so Hashem has the Megillah read in heaven, as Michael offers on the altar above, and the second reading is greater.

title.en: Amalek cools off: the pulse of life

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek represents the Satan and that 'asher karcha' means he cooled the Jews off. All life pulses up and down like a heartbeat or a pause in music, and the war against Amalek is to hold on through the cold until Hashem sends warmth again.

title.en: Karcha as impurity and as chance

summary.en: The Rav brings two more readings of 'karcha': Amalek made the Jews impure, and Amalek teaches that things happen by chance ('mikreh'), denying Hashem's individual providence. He brings the Midrash calling Haman 'son of Korcha' and notes that Amalek equals 'safek', doubt, in gematria.

title.en: Haster astir: the double hiding

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Esther is hinted in 'haster astir' and the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of a father who hides from his child, and then hides that he is hiding. This double concealment was the setting of the Megillah and, he says, is the state of most of Klal Yisrael before Moshiach, caused by Haman's philosophy of chance.

title.en: Hashem's name hidden in 'hamelech'

summary.en: The Rav notes that Hashem's name is absent from the Megillah alone among the 24 books, because its setting is hester panim, and brings the Midrash on 'evel gadol', a mourning that grew as the decreed day approached. Yet, per the Midrash, every 'hamelech' in the Megillah refers to Hashem.

title.en: Kes Kah, the puppet king and the gematria of hamelech

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi on 'ki yad al kes Kah': Hashem's name and throne are incomplete until Amalek is erased, so His rule is concealed and we credit events to rulers. Achashverosh was a marionette moved by strings from above; 'hamelech' equals 'kes Kah' and Haman in gematria (95), and 'machi Amalek' equals 'kisei Havayah'.

title.en: Hidden miracles every day

summary.en: The Rav says there are no open miracles in the Megillah, unlike Nisan, yet every person has hidden miracles daily, as said in Modim; the body is far more complex than a car and keeps working. In Adar the same miracles are cloaked in nature, and the Megillah story could have been reported in the newspapers.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar's parable: a miracle in nature

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying patient for whom the one doctor and the one medicine arrive just in time, showing that someone directs events without breaking nature, which is an even greater miracle. Adar is the season of such natural miracles, and 'Megillas Esther' means revealing the hidden.

title.en: Peeking through the cracks

summary.en: The Rav compares reading the Megillah to a surgeon reading an x-ray and brings 'mashgiach min hachalonos, metzitz min hacharakim': Hashem watches through the cracks. He retracts his earlier statement: Hashem's name is in the Megillah, hidden in the initial and final letters of key phrases, as in 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom'.

title.en: The whole world is a Megillah

summary.en: The Rav says that after Purim one should read the newspaper between the lines and see Hashem behind the world's leaders, and points to Eretz Yisrael always being in the headlines. The whole world is a Megillah to be revealed, and the Purim costumes teach to look beneath every disguise.

title.en: Adar, the month of laughter

summary.en: The Rav brings Sefer Yetzirah, which assigns each month an organ and activity: Adar's is laughter. The plague of locusts fell in Adar, where Hashem says He 'made sport' of Egypt. In Adar one laughs at the passing material world, as the Kotzker said the whole world is not worth a sigh, because Hashem directs everything.

title.en: Yaakov's complaint and Mordechai the 'troublemaker'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov once forgot himself and blamed his sons, while Hashem was making Yosef king. He then retells the nine years of the Megillah: Mordechai opposed going to Achashverosh's feast and refused to bow to Haman, and was blamed as a troublemaker, but in the end it was clear he was right all along.

title.en: David, Shimi and the lesson of the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav explains that people blamed David for not killing Shimi, Mordechai's ancestor; in truth, because David saw that Hashem told Shimi to curse, Mordechai was born to teach hashgachah pratis and write the Megillah. He concludes that the same Achashverosh brought mourning and joy: all are puppets, and nothing happens without Hashem.

catalogTitle: יו"ט של יובל; שיר השירים; והשתוקקות לגאולה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Pesach as the level of yovel and the fiftieth gate, above the seven of Shabbos, and from it explains why Hillel alone knew that the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos, why David found the place of the Mikdash, and why Shlomo and Moshiach carry the light of the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's comment that the word 'im' by the omer and by yovel means an obligation, and with the Gemara's story of Hillel, who alone knew that the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos and was made Nasi. He sets beside it Doeg's envy of David for finding the place of the Mikdash. Using Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of world, year and soul, he explains that above the seven days of creation stands the level of 'pele', the fiftieth: yovel in time, the Mikdash in place, and the king in the soul. Pesach is the fiftieth gate, so it overrides Shabbos, which is only seven. David is Shabbos and Shlomo, his inner self, is yovel; Hillel is a gilgul of Shlomo, which is why he knew the halacha. The Rav ends with Shir HaShirim's closing plea, the hard galus of Yishmael, and a call to daven on Pesach with emunah for the redemption.

en: Above the seven of Shabbos and shmitah stands the fiftieth, yovel, which is 'pele', beyond measure and understanding; Shavuos and Matan Torah, the Mikdash and Pesach all belong to it.
The place of the Mikdash is not named in the Torah because it is above 'place'; it must be sought, and only David, the 'reishis' and king of the soul, could find it.
Pesach is the fiftieth gate, which is why the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos, which is only the level of seven.
David is the seventh, Shabbos, while his inner depth, revealed in his son Shlomo who built the Mikdash, is yovel; Shlomo's era is a model of the days of Moshiach.
Hillel knew that Pesach overrides Shabbos because he is a gilgul of Shlomo, from the root of yovel, and not only because he had learned it from Shemaya and Avtalyon.
The Rav says the days of Pesach are days of geulah and a time to daven, with emunah in Hashem alone, for the final redemption.

candidateTopics: Pesach as yovel and the fiftieth gate

title.en: 'Im' by the omer and by yovel

summary.en: During the days of the omer the Rav cites Rashi that 've'im takriv' by the omer means an obligation, proven from 've'im yihyeh hayovel', and asks why the Torah uses 'im' by yovel. He then begins the Gemara's account of an Erev Pesach that fell on Shabbos, when the Bnei Beseira did not know whether the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos.

title.en: Hillel becomes Nasi

summary.en: The Rav tells how Hillel ruled that Pesach overrides Shabbos, how the Bnei Beseira stepped down and made him Nasi, how he rebuked them and then forgot the law of carrying the knife until he saw what the people did. He brings the Rema MiPano that the kingship of Torah stayed with Hillel's family because he descends from David.

title.en: Doeg's envy and the three dimensions

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Zevachim that David and Shmuel determined the place of the Mikdash, and that Doeg, a greater scholar, envied David for it, which he likens to the Bnei Beseira and Hillel. He then brings Sefer Yetzirah that the world exists in place, time and soul, each with its 'king' and beginning, called 'pele'.

title.en: Above the seven: yovel and the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seven days of creation and the middos from chesed to malchus have something above them: after shmitah comes yovel, after seven weeks of sefirah comes the fiftieth day, Shavuos and Matan Torah, 'bimshoch hayovel'. A slave whom the seventh year cannot free goes free at yovel, and Moshe added the fiftieth day because it is above reckoning.

title.en: The Mikdash, a place above place

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Beis HaMikdash is the place of yovel and 'pele': the Sanhedrin goes up there for a matter that is 'yipalei', and the Aron took up no space. Therefore the Torah gives no directions to the place of the Mikdash, only 'lishichno tidreshu', which he links by gematria to 'reishis'.

title.en: David, king of the soul, finds the Mikdash

summary.en: The Rav explains that the king is the 'pele' of the soul: even Shmuel did not know which son of Yishai was the king, just as the place of the Mikdash must be sought. Only David, the soul of Adam HaRishon and the 'reishis', could find the place, which answers Doeg's envy.

title.en: Pesach, the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Rav explains that Nissan is the head of time and Pesach comes from the fiftieth gate, which Jews receive as a gift on the Seder night and then work toward through sefirah. He brings the Maharal on why Haman fell on the first day of the omer, and explains that Pesach is yovel and therefore overrides Shabbos.

title.en: David is Shabbos, Shlomo is yovel

summary.en: The Rav links Rosh Chodesh Nissan to the Kodesh HaKodashim and to 'kinas beischa'. He brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that a father's inner self is revealed in his son: David is the seventh, Shabbos, and his inner depth, yovel, came out in Shlomo, who built the Mikdash and whose reign the Rambam's picture of Moshiach resembles.

title.en: Hillel, Shlomo, and the fiftieth Exodus

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that Moshiach must come from Shlomo, and the Rema MiPano that Hillel is a gilgul of Shlomo. He asks why the Seder expounds 'Arami oved avi' and answers that the fiftieth mention of the Exodus, belonging to the days of Moshiach, is there; therefore Pesach overrides Shabbos, and the Bnei Beseira could not know it.

title.en: Hillel's ruling from the root of his soul

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Seder night is a time of asking without knowing, and that Hillel's ruling revealed the fiftieth gate because he is Shlomo, so the kingdom was set in his hand. Hillel credited Shemaya and Avtalyon out of humility, so Heaven made him forget the knife, revealing that his knowledge came from his soul's root. This also explains 'im' by the omer and yovel.

title.en: Shir HaShirim's last plea and Har HaMoriah

summary.en: The Rav says the days of Pesach are days of geulah, when a Jew must long for redemption. Shlomo ends Shir HaShirim with 'berach dodi', a plea that Hashem flee the galus with His people to Har HaMoriah. Yet today Yishmael holds that place, and he brings the Chasam Sofer that korbanos cannot be offered because Yishmael will not let a Jew go up.

title.en: The galus of Yishmael, 'pere adam'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam's Igeres Teiman that no galus is harder than that of Yishmael, from 'oyah li' in Tehillim, and that Yishmael hates peace. He brings Rav Chaim Vital that 'bekum aleinu adam' refers to Yishmael, the 'pere adam', and the Chofetz Chaim's warning that a Yishmaeli remains a 'pere adam' whatever he becomes.

title.en: 'Adam velo melech'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the same passuk refers to Haman, 'adam velo melech', and the Bnei Yissaschar that the seven nations parallel the seven middos and the Girgashi, as malchus, accepted Hashem's kingship and left. Achashverosh as a king had a spark of malchus, Haman did not; Yishmael too has only princes and no king, which makes his galus so hard.

title.en: Only Hashem can help: davening on Pesach

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yishmael is the impure side of yesod, a Friday that never reaches Shabbos, and that only Hashem can save from him, not politics or the military. Pesach, a time of revealed Shechinah, is the time to daven with emunah in Hashem and in tzaddikim for the redemption and for 'berach dodi'.

catalogTitle: א יום טוב פון אמונה דרשה לילדי תפארת יונה

oneLiner.en: Speaking to children, the Rav explains that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first believer, and that its matzah and its 'great wealth' are emunah in Hashem.

abstract.en: Addressing children, the Rav opens by calling Pesach the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu: Avraham was the first Jew, Pesach is the first Yom Tov of the year, and Avraham is the one figure in the Torah of whom it is written that he ate matzos. He was also the first of whom the Torah says that he believed in Hashem. Since matzah is called the food of emunah, eating it with joy plants emunah in a Jew for the whole year. The Rav describes that emunah: Hashem stands over a person and sees and knows everything he does, says and thinks, so how could he sin; Hashem can do everything, so one may rely on Him and not worry. He then shows how Avraham's own life ran on Pesach, and how the 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is, for every Jew, emunah. He closes with the coming Pesach of the future, when Moshiach will say he came because of the children who learned, davened and kept away from aveiros.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu: he was the first Jew, Pesach is the first Yom Tov, and he is the one tzaddik in the Torah of whom it says he ate matzos.
Matzah is the food of emunah; eating it with joy gives a Jew emunah for the whole year.
Emunah means believing that Hashem stands over a person and sees everything he does, says and thinks, which keeps him from sin.
Since Hashem can do everything, a Jew can rely on Him and need not worry about what he needs.
The 'great wealth' with which Jews leave Pesach is emunah, the greatest treasure a Jew owns.
In the future redemption Moshiach will say that he came because of the children who learned Torah, davened and kept away from aveiros.

title.en: Pesach, matzah and Avraham's emunah

summary.en: The Rav tells the children that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first Jew and the first in the Torah who believed in Hashem and ate matzos. Since matzah is the food of emunah, eating it with joy gives emunah for the whole year.

title.en: Hashem stands over us; the true great wealth

summary.en: The Rav explains that emunah means knowing Hashem sees everything and can do everything, so one keeps from sin and relies on Him. He shows how Avraham's life ran on Pesach and that the 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is, for every Jew, emunah.

title.en: The great Pesach of the future

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the future Pesach when Hashem will gather Jews from every land, ties it to the haftarah of the dry bones, and says Moshiach will credit the children who learned, davened and avoided aveiros. He closes by urging joy and emunah through the rest of Pesach.

catalogTitle: The Love of Hashem to Even the Lowest Jew

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows from Amalek, Haman and the silver hooks of the Mishkan that Hashem never forgets even the most distant Jew, and that Purim is the Yom Tov of the rejected.

abstract.en: The Rav asks how Amalek dared attack Klal Yisrael under the Clouds of Glory, and answers that he attacked only those of Shevet Dan whom the clouds spat out for carrying an idol. Because Amalek struck these sinners, Hashem's war with Amalek lasts for all generations, which shows how He loves even a fallen Jew. Haman repeated the mistake: he saw the Jews' sins in Achashverosh's time and thought Hashem no longer cared for them. The Rav then explains that the silver of the 1,775 shekels became the hooks of the pillars, which protrude outside the Mishkan and stand for the rejected Jews; Moshe forgot them, and the soul of Rabbi Akiva, the 'heel', reminded him. Haman paid no counterweight for these Jews, and his decree turned back on him. Purim is therefore the comfort of the simplest Jew. Adar, the end of the golus, and Adar Sheni outside the twelve combinations, call for teshuvah, and a ben Torah's teshuvah lifts all of Klal Yisrael.

en: Amalek could attack only the Jews of Shevet Dan whom the Clouds of Glory had rejected because of their idol, and Hashem's war with Amalek for all generations comes from his attacking these fallen Jews.
Haman made the same mistake as Amalek: seeing the Jews' sins in Achashverosh's time, he thought Hashem would no longer protect them.
The silver of the 1,775 shekels went to the hooks of the pillars, which protrude outside the Mishkan, and these represent Jews who seem rejected and forgotten.
Haman thought the rejected Jews needed no counterweight to their shekalim, but Hashem had not forgotten them, and the decree turned back on Haman and Amalek.
Purim is the comfort and hope of the simplest and most distant Jew, since it shows that no Jew is ever written off by Hashem.
Before Moshiach every Jew will do teshuvah; even a small teshuvah is a start, and Adar, the end of the golus, is a time for it.
Klal Yisrael is like one rope: when a ben Torah raises himself through teshuvah and Torah, the bottom of the rope rises as well.

title.en: Whom Amalek was able to attack

summary.en: The Rav asks how Amalek dared attack the Jews under the Clouds of Glory, and explains that he struck only those of Shevet Dan whom the clouds spat out for carrying the idol of Michah. Hashem's war with Amalek for all generations shows how much He loves even a Jew who has fallen.

title.en: Haman repeats Amalek's mistake

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the Jews of Haman's time were liable for bowing to the image and enjoying Achashverosh's feast, and explains that Haman, like his grandfather Amalek, thought this left them unprotected. He then describes the camp of Dan at the edge of the Machaneh, and how the Mishkan's camps parallel the Beis HaMikdash, the Azarah and Yerushalayim.

title.en: The hooks outside the Mishkan and Rabbi Akiva

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew's half-shekel became the silver sockets of the Mishkan, but some silver went to the hooks that protrude outside the curtains, representing Jews who seem rejected and forgotten. Moshe Rabbeinu forgot what that silver was used for, and the soul of Rabbi Akiva, the 'heel' of Klal Yisrael and the head of Torah she'baal peh in golus, reminded him.

title.en: Haman's shekalim and the joy of the simple Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haman offered his silver only against the Jews whose silver went to the sockets, thinking the rejected ones needed no counterweight; but Hashem remembered them, and the decree turned back on Haman so that Amalek's memory is erased. Therefore Purim is the Yom Tov of the simplest Jew, who feels at home on it.

title.en: Every Jew will do teshuvah before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara and the Rambam that before Moshiach all Jews will do teshuvah, and if not, a ruler like Haman will force them to. He explains from Hashiveinu in Shemoneh Esrei that a small teshuvah is a first step, and describes today's 'drizzle' of teshuvah that will become a storm when Moshiach comes and the rejected are readmitted.

title.en: Adar Sheni and the ben Torah's teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Adar is the end of the golus and a month of teshuvah, and that Adar Sheni stands outside the twelve combinations of the Shem Havayah, like the Jews outside the camp, yet Purim is for them too. He closes with the Chofetz Chaim's words that one ben Torah's bittul Torah affects a distant Jew, and that Klal Yisrael is like one rope, so a ben Torah's teshuvah lifts everyone.

catalogTitle: בליל הסדר זוכים לגילוי שכינה כל אחד לפי מדריגתו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Pesach, the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, is the foundation of all the moadim because it plants emunah, and that at the Seder each Jew, according to his level, receives emunah and a measure of gilui Shechinah, and through telling the makkos draws salvation for Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the three regalim as the inheritance of the three Avos: Pesach is Avraham's yom tov of chesed and emunah. The Seder exists to plant emunah, and each person, by his level, receives some gilui Shechinah, as shown by a story of the Seer of Lublin. Mitzrayim was the kelipah of denial, so emunah, the root of all mitzvos, comes before Shavuos. Since the moadim are the lifeblood of Klal Yisrael, Pesach is the head of them all, and only Pesach-related mitzvos carry kareis. Matzah is the food of emunah that becomes part of one's flesh. A tzaddik is measured by his emunah. The makkos rose from water to the heavens to answer Pharaoh, and they mirror the ten utterances of creation in reverse. Telling them again brings them about again, so the Rav urges saying the Haggadah with fire, closing with a simple Jew whose sincere bracha annulled a decree.

en: Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, inherited from Avraham Avinu, and the Seder is meant to plant emunah in every Jew.
At the Seder each Jew, according to his level, merits some revelation of the Shechinah.
Pesach is the head and foundation of the moadim; although Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, only the Pesach-related mitzvos carry kareis.
Matzah is the food of emunah: Hashem placed the emunah of that night into a food so that it becomes part of a Jew's flesh and blood.
Whatever happened at Yetzias Mitzrayim happens again each year, and telling the makkos at the Seder draws blows upon the enemies of Israel and healing for the Jews.

title.en: Pesach, emunah and gilui Shechinah at the Seder

summary.en: The Rav links the three regalim to the three Avos, Pesach being Avraham's yom tov of chesed and emunah. The Seder is meant to plant emunah, and each person receives some gilui Shechinah by his level, as shown by the Seer of Lublin lifting his tallis at 'u-ve-mora gadol'.

title.en: Mitzrayim as denial; emunah before mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Mitzrayim was the kelipah of denial, as Pharaoh said 'I do not know Hashem', so leaving it means knowing Hashem. Through the dispute of the Ramban with the Rambam he shows that emunah is the foundation of the mitzvos, which is why Pesach precedes Shavuos and is called the head of all the moadim.

title.en: The moadim depend on Jews in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that sanctifying the month can only happen in Eretz Yisrael, and that Hillel's fixed calendar works only because Jews living there, even simple farmers, keep it. He cites the Rambam that it is Hashem's kindness that Jews never ceased from the land, since without the moadim Klal Yisrael could not live.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Rav says Pesach heads the moadim because Avraham, who gave his life for emunah, heads the Avos. The great clarity of emunah at makkas bechoros was placed by Hashem into the matzah so it would be absorbed into flesh and blood; every yom tov has such a food.

title.en: Why only Pesach carries kareis

summary.en: The Rav ranks the regalim: Pesach is Avraham's level, Shavuos higher, Sukkos higher still. Yet only Pesach's mitzvos (chametz, the korban Pesach, and milah which holds it back) carry kareis, showing that Pesach, the foundation, binds a Jew to Hashem most deeply.

title.en: Telling the story; a Jew is measured by emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that through telling Yetzias Mitzrayim to the children emunah is absorbed. He cites the Chasam Sofer, who lengthened the telling and barely had time to eat before midnight, and discusses the deadline of chatzos. A tzaddik's tefillin are greater than a simple Jew's only through greater emunah.

title.en: The makkos as an answer to Pharaoh

summary.en: The Rav explains the makkos as Hashem's answer to Pharaoh's denial. The three groups each open with a passuk about knowing Hashem at a different level, and the makkos rise from water through earth, fire, air and the luminaries up to the souls of the firstborn, showing Hashem rules from bottom to top.

title.en: Makkos, the ten utterances, and retelling

summary.en: The Rav says Yetzias Mitzrayim recurs every year. The ten makkos reveal the ten utterances of creation in reverse order, and lead to the Ten Commandments. Retelling makes it happen again, as with the son of Reb Yechezkel of Kuzmir, whose retelling of his father's miracle healed another sick man.

title.en: Saying the Haggadah with fire for salvation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Haggadah multiplies the makkos because saying them draws more blows on the enemies and more healing for Israel, according to one's fervor, and he urges saying it with fire in the danger now facing Eretz Yisrael. He explains spilling wine from the cup and closes with the Ropshitzer and Rimanover, who saw a simple Jew's sincere bracha annul a decree.

catalogTitle: צד א: הנחיצות שהמצות יאפו ע"י יר"ש

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the holiness of matzah, like that of a sefer Torah, comes from Hashem through a messenger acting lishmah, and so the matzos should be baked by G-d-fearing people with kavanah and joy.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chesed L'Avraham: in the thirty days before Pesach, Hashem takes the Jews out of the klipah of Mitzrayim a thirtieth each day, and one must prepare for it through daily remembrance of yetzias Mitzrayim and accepting the yoke of Heaven. He brings the Ohr HaChaim that in Egypt the Jews sank to the forty-ninth gate of impurity, while before Moshiach they will reach the fiftieth, from which only the power of Torah can bring them out; this is how he reads the rasha of the Haggadah. He explains that Pesach, whose penalty is kares, is the foundation that binds a Jew to Hashem, the time of emunah, and matzah is its food. Then, from the sofer who is only Hashem's messenger, he shows that holiness depends on intent lishmah, and urges baking matzos oneself, with kavanah and joy, and eating such matzos all Pesach, since the same holy names are in them as in Egypt.

en: In the thirty days before Pesach Hashem takes the Jews out of the klipah of Mitzrayim little by little, and one must prepare to be taken out.
Before Moshiach the Jews will fall into the fiftieth gate of impurity, and with the power of Torah they can be brought out of it.
Pesach, whose penalty for chametz is kares, is the foundation of the Yamim Tovim and binds a Jew to Hashem; it is the time of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah.
A sofer who writes lishmah is Hashem's messenger; the holiness comes from Hashem, which is why the sofer may not sit on one bench with the sefer Torah he wrote.
Matzos baked lishmah with kavanah, dveikus and joy by G-d-fearing people are not the same as matzos baked without kavanah, even if one fulfils the obligation with those.
The same holy names that were in the matzah the Jews ate in Egypt are in the matzah today, so one can say 'ha lachma anya'.

candidateTopics: the four sons of the Haggadah
hiddur in tefillin, mezuzos and tzitzis

title.en: Thirty days of leaving Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chesed L'Avraham that from Purim, thirty days before Pesach, Hashem takes the Jews out of the klipah of Mitzrayim a little each day, and explains Mitzrayim as 'meitzar yam', what holds back the fifty gates of understanding. He says one must prepare through the daily remembrance of yetzias Mitzrayim and accepting the yoke of Heaven, asking Hashem to bend the yetzer to His service.

title.en: The forty-nine gates and the fiftieth

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim that the Jews fell to the forty-ninth gate of impurity in Egypt, explaining 'avadim hayinu' as bondage to the klipah, and that before Moshiach they will fall into the fiftieth gate, from which Torah can bring them out. He reads the rasha of the Haggadah as one in the fiftieth gate of heresy, whom the Torah still tries to pull out, and notes that yetzias Mitzrayim is mentioned fifty times in the Torah, against the fifty gates.

title.en: Pesach as the foundation of emunah

summary.en: The Rav answers, in the name of his rebbe, why the Torah mentions yetzias Mitzrayim more than fifty times: only fifty are in praise. He then explains with the Chiddushei HaRim that Pesach, whose penalty is kares, is the foundation that binds a Jew to Hashem, the time of emunah, recommends Shomer Emunim to those who feel weak in emunah, and calls matzah the food of emunah, like a vitamin a doctor prescribes.

title.en: The sofer as Hashem's messenger

summary.en: The Rav asks why a sofer may not sit on one bench with the sefer Torah he wrote, and answers that writing lishmah makes him Hashem's messenger, so the holiness comes from Hashem. The same holds for tefillin, mezuzos and tzitzis, so one should seek out a G-d-fearing sofer and spend money on it, and he describes how in Skver the tzitzis are made by hand by carefully chosen people, since a machine cannot have intent.

title.en: Baking matzos lishmah oneself

summary.en: The Rav urges going to bake matzos oneself, since the holiness of the matzah comes from the kavanah, and describes baking with joy and repeating 'lishmah'. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on the generation of the tower, contrasts a bochur who bakes after davening and mikveh with workers who bake while chatting, and explains that those who permit machine matzos rely on Rishonim who require only guarding lishmah, which is not a hiddur.

title.en: Hiddur matzos all Pesach and 'ha lachma anya'

summary.en: The Rav explains that, following the Chasam Sofer and others, eating matzah all of Pesach is a mitzvah, compares it to the sukkah, and so recommends eating the chaburah's matzos the whole Yom Tov. He explains 'ha lachma anya': the same holy names are in today's matzah as in Egypt, the physical matzah being only an envelope, and closes by urging preparation and kavanah in the thirty days.

catalogTitle: צד ב: מעלות פסח כמו מעלת ימי הבחרות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Pesach and Nissan are the beginning of the bond with Hashem and must be guarded with every stringency, and that a person's years as a bachur are his own Nissan.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the stringencies of Pesach: chametz is forbidden even in the smallest amount, and the Ba'al HaTanya writes that on Pesach one should be stringent even for a single opinion among the Rishonim. The reason is that Pesach is a beginning, when Jews left Egypt and became a nation, and a beginning must be firm. The physical world shows the same: growth begins in Nissan, as the blessing on blossoming trees shows. In a person's life, his years as a bachur are his Nissan. Then Hashem gives unearned gifts, a light in learning and davening, as a chassan sends gifts at the start of a bond, and as the night of the Seder brings a great light. So a bachur must guard himself like Pesach, since an hour then is worth years later. The Rav brings the Avnei Nezer on the worth of Nissan, and the Imrei Emes crying out a passuk for the hearts of the bachurim, and closes with a brachah.

en: Pesach carries special stringencies because it is a beginning, and a beginning must be firm and entirely good.
Nissan is the beginning of growth both in the physical world and in Jewish history, when Jews became a nation.
In a person's life, the years as a bachur are his Nissan, the time when he forms himself and his future image.
Hashem gives unearned gifts at the beginning of the bond, as a chassan sends gifts, and as the Seder night brings a great light.
A bachur must guard himself with every stringency, as a Jew does on Pesach, because a moment in those years is worth years later.

title.en: Why Pesach has so many stringencies

summary.en: The Rav describes how the Yamim Tovim ascend from Pesach, and the special stringencies of Pesach, citing the Ba'al HaTanya that one should be stringent even for a single opinion. He explains that Pesach is the beginning, when Jews became a nation, and a beginning must be firm.

title.en: Nissan as the start of growth and of the bond

summary.en: The Rav shows that growth begins in Nissan, as the blessing on blossoming trees shows, and that Nissan is a time without full completeness, like a bachur. He explains the unearned gifts of that time by a chassan sending gifts at the start of a bond, bringing a teshuvah about a broken shidduch, and the great light of the Seder night.

title.en: The years of bachurus are Nissan

summary.en: The Rav applies the idea to a bachur, who must guard himself like Pesach since then he forms his future. He brings a letter that an hour in those years is worth years, the Avnei Nezer on the worth of time in Nissan, and the Imrei Emes crying out a passuk for the bachurim's hearts, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: The Hidden נס of the מגילה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows children that the Megillah is full of hidden miracles, cloaked in nature like the month of Adar, and that Purim trains a person to find Hashem behind everything that happens.

abstract.en: Speaking to boys, the Rav says Purim is not a costume holiday but the foundation of emunah. Yet before the Megillah we bless Hashem for making miracles, and walking through the story he finds none: unlike the plagues and the splitting of the Sea, everything could have been read in a newspaper. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying man for whom an unexpected doctor and an unexpected medicine arrive at the same moment, and adds his own image of a watch that reassembles itself when shaken. Then he explains two kinds of miracles: those that break nature, like the manna, and nature itself, which only habit hides. Nisan is the month of open miracles; Adar, from 'aderes', a cloak, is the month of cloaked ones. The Megillah's perfect timing, and events in our own day, show Hashem's hand. Purim, he concludes, trains a person to find Hashem in his own life.

en: Purim is not a Jewish Halloween but, the Rav says, the foundation of emunah in the Ribono shel Olam.
Read on the surface, the Megillah has no open miracle: every event is natural, unlike the plagues and the splitting of the Sea.
There are two kinds of miracles: those where Hashem changes nature, and those hidden inside nature, which people take for granted only because they are used to them.
Nisan is the month of open miracles, while Adar, related to 'aderes', a cloak, is the month of miracles cloaked in nature.
In golus Hashem hides in nature, but the Megillah shows His hand through perfect timing: each event happened exactly when it was needed.
Purim teaches how to read the Megillah, history and current events, and to find Hashem hiding in one's own life, as in a game of hide-and-seek.

title.en: Searching the Megillah for miracles

summary.en: The Rav tells the boys that Purim is not a Jewish Halloween but the foundation of emunah, and notes that before the Megillah we bless Hashem for making miracles. He then walks through the whole story, contrasts it with the plagues and the splitting of the Sea, and finds no miracle at all: everything could have been read in a newspaper.

title.en: The doctor, the medicine and the watch

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a man with two hours to live, whose only cure is a medicine six months away that only a distant doctor can give, until both the doctor and the medicine unexpectedly arrive at the door. He asks whether that is not a miracle, and adds a parable of a watch taken apart and put in a can, which reassembles itself when shaken.

title.en: Two kinds of miracles: Nisan and Adar

summary.en: The Rav explains two kinds of miracles: the manna, which breaks nature, and wheat growing from the ground, which is no less a miracle but is taken for granted; he brings the Chasam Sofer's picture of the generation born in the desert who saw bread grow from the ground as a wonder. Nisan is named for the open miracles of the Exodus, while Adar, from 'aderes sei'ar', a cloak, is the month of cloaked miracles.

title.en: Hidden miracles in the Megillah and today

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the open miracles of the Beis HaMikdash with golus, where Hashem is shrouded in nature, and goes back through the Megillah showing how each event came exactly when it was needed. He tells of the Iraqi Scud missiles, where only one man was killed, a man the Steipler had cursed, and brings the Midrash that 'the King' in the Megillah refers to the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Purim as hide-and-seek with Hashem

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Purim teaches how to read the Megillah, history and current events, calling it a game of hide-and-seek in which Hashem says 'find Me'. The costumed visitor at the seudah shows that all the world's rulers are only cloaked, and the same Hashem who made the plagues and the manna makes miracles today. He tells the boys to train themselves to look for Hashem in everything that happens and to know He takes care of them.

catalogTitle: צד א: פסח - יו"ט של עשיית המצוות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Pesach, the head of all the festivals and the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, is the time of emunah, which a Jew draws into himself through the mitzvos of the yom tov and above all through matzah baked with heart, while the events of the day call for preparing seriously for Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that each Pesach and each Shabbos is greater than the one before: the generations are lower, but because they are so low they can raise sparks the earlier generations could not reach, and bodies become ever more refined. That is why mitzvos, done with the body, are in this respect greater than Torah. Nissan is full of physical preparation, and Pesach, the yom tov of Avraham, is the root of the festivals. Turning to the war of the day, he relates traditions of tzaddikim about the nations being dragged into war before Moshiach and urges serious preparation, so as not to spoil the moment. He then shows, through the two reasons given for Shabbos, that yetzias Mitzrayim reveals the ten sayings of creation and is the root of emunah. Every Jew inherits emunah from Avraham; Pesach and matzah, the food of faith, bring it into the open, so the matzah should be baked by sincere Jews with heart, not mechanically.

en: Each Pesach and Shabbos is greater than the last, because the low generations before Moshiach can raise sparks from a place the earlier generations never reached.
The soul needs no repair; it came down to refine the body, which is why mitzvos, done with the body, are in this respect greater than Torah study.
Pesach is the head of all the festivals and the yom tov of Avraham Avinu; through it a Jew binds himself to the root, to emunah.
Yetzias Mitzrayim revealed openly the ten powers of creation that no one saw, and so it is the root of emunah.
Every Jew has emunah by inheritance from Avraham; Torah, mitzvos and Pesach bring the hidden faith into the open.
Matzah is the food of faith; it should be baked by sincere Jews with heart and joy, and a mitzvah should not be done mechanically.
