matzah as the food of faith
ikvesa d'meshicha and the war before Moshiach
mitzvos with the body versus torah

title.en: Lower generations, greater refinement

summary.en: The Rav says each Pesach and Shabbos is greater than the last: the late generations are so low that they can raise sparks from the fiftieth gate, and bodies grow more refined. Since the soul came down only to refine the body, he explains with the Tanya why mitzvos are in this respect greater than Torah.

title.en: Pesach, head of the festivals

summary.en: Nissan is full of physical preparation, and Pesach is the head of all the festivals. The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim that the kares of Pesach shows it binds a Jew to the root, and explains that Pesach is Avraham's yom tov, just as the blessing is Magen Avraham, while Magen David belongs to the time of Moshiach.

title.en: Not a time for jokes: the war before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav says joking has become a klipah in Chassidus, and that this is a serious time: the Midrash says war between kingdoms heralds Moshiach. He relates a tradition passed down from Reb Mottele of Slonim that before Moshiach the nations will be dragged into war against their will, and applies it to the war in Iraq.

title.en: Tzaddikim foresee; preparing seriously

summary.en: The Rav explains why the tradition was meant to be passed on: to strengthen Jews when they would be frightened. He tells of the Stoliner Rebbe's prediction about Russia and of the Bluzhever Rav, who turned pale at a joke that Moshiach had come because he was not yet ready, and calls for approaching this Pesach very seriously.

title.en: From Purim to erev Pesach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the war on Amalek begins on Purim and ends on erev Pesach, and the Avnei Nezer on why the main Purim seudah is held at night, noting that the war began on Purim night. He warns not to spoil the moment, and introduces the series of talks he will build on the Nesivos Shalom until Pesach.

title.en: Creation and the Exodus: one testimony

summary.en: The Rav asks how the two reasons for Shabbos in the two Luchos, creation and yetzias Mitzrayim, belong together. With the Chiddushei HaRim and the Arizal he shows that the ten plagues mirror the ten sayings of creation in reverse, so the Exodus revealed what was hidden at creation and is the root of emunah; Pesach is the yom tov of emunah.

title.en: Inherited faith and the food of faith

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew, even a sinner, believes by inheritance from Avraham, and that there is no true Jewish heretic, only a coating. Torah, mitzvos and Pesach bring this faith into the open, and matzah, called the food of faith in the Zohar, carries holy names into the body.

title.en: Simplicity, not mechanical kavanos

summary.en: The Rav brings Rebbe Reb Elimelech and Rav Tzadok that one should serve Hashem simply and not with calculated kavanos, which make a mitzvah mechanical, as with a shofar blower watching the second hand. He describes a matzah bakery he saw and says matzah should be baked by sincere Jews with kavanah and joy.

title.en: Matzah as a sign; emunah the foundation

summary.en: The Rav brings Tosafos that matzah is the sign of Pesach in place of tefillin, and the view that eating matzah all of Pesach is a mitzvah, compared to sukkah. He closes that emunah is a Jew's dearest possession and the foundation of all mitzvos, and that Pesach, the root of the festivals, deserves more care than any other yom tov.

catalogTitle: צד ב: דצ"ך עד"ש באח"ב בגימטרי' ישמעאלים (עניני דיומא במלחמה באירק)

oneLiner.en: During the war in Iraq before Pesach, the Rav calls for tefillah for the Jewish soldiers, explains that today's Arabs of Iraq are Bavel and Yishmael, and shows that Rabbi Yehuda's simanim d'tzach adash b'achav equal 'Yishmaelim' in gematria.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a phone call from an army chaplain: over a thousand Jewish soldiers are now in Iraq as the battle for Baghdad begins, and he calls on everyone to daven for them and for the geulah. Iraq is Bavel, by the rivers Pras and Chidekel where the Jews sat and wept, and its Arabs, who identify with Bavel, carry the din of Bavel. He brings Dovid Hamelech's blessing on whoever repays Bavel and the duty to pray for the welfare of the kingdom, especially America, a kingdom of kindness. The Yishmaelim began galus Mitzrayim by selling Yosef; therefore at the Seder one pours wine at d'tzach adash b'achav, which equals Yishmaelim, drawing judgment on them. He contrasts Edom and Yishmael, then teaches that any Jew may have his hour, as the boy's whistle in the Ba'al Shem Tov's story showed, and stresses the power of the first twelve days of Nissan and of minhag Yisrael, before closing with Pesach preparation.

en: The Rav says one is obligated to daven for the Jewish soldiers fighting in Iraq, and that the war should bring the geulah.
The Arabs of Iraq identify with Bavel and therefore have the din of Bavel, just as those who present themselves as a nation receive its din.
There is a mitzvah to pray for the welfare of the government one lives under, especially America, which has never persecuted or expelled Jews.
Rabbi Yehuda's simanim d'tzach adash b'achav equal 'Yishmaelim' in gematria; pouring wine there draws judgment on the Yishmaelim, who began galus Mitzrayim.
Every Jew has his hour, when a single heartfelt tefillah or moment of teshuvah can accomplish more than the greatest tzaddik of the generation.
The first twelve days of Nissan, when the Nesiim are read, have the power to subdue the twelve princes of Yishmael, and a minhag Yisrael can be stronger than a halachah.

candidateTopics: galus Mitzrayim and the sale of Yosef

title.en: Jewish soldiers in Iraq and the call to daven

summary.en: The Rav tells of a call from an army chaplain who reported over a thousand Jewish soldiers in Iraq as the battle for Baghdad begins. He explains why the enemy's name is not mentioned, citing the Bnei Yissaschar, and says one is obligated to daven for the soldiers and for the geulah the war should bring.

title.en: By the rivers of Bavel

summary.en: The Rav points out that the war is taking place by the rivers Pras and Chidekel, the rivers of Bavel. He describes the Babylonian ruler who saw himself as a new Nevuchadnetzar and fired missiles at Eretz Yisrael, and recalls the Jews who sat by these rivers in galus and refused to play the songs of Zion.

title.en: The Arabs as Bavel; praying for America

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Arabs of Iraq identify with Bavel and so have its din, bringing Rashi on the king of Arad and a Midrash that the Babylonians will be revived to receive their punishment. He cites Dovid Hamelech's blessing on whoever repays Bavel, and the mitzvah to pray for the government, especially America, a kingdom of kindness.

title.en: Yishmael began galus Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that galus Mitzrayim began with the sale of Yosef to the Yishmaelim, citing Targum Yonasan. He brings from the Chofetz Chaim that the angels above speak of a person as Jews speak of him below, so arousing merit on Jews and judgment on the wicked has effect in Heaven.

title.en: D'tzach adash b'achav equals Yishmaelim

summary.en: The Rav asks why Rabbi Yehuda's simanim are recited at the Seder, explains that wine has the power to draw kindness to Jews and judgment to their enemies, and reveals that d'tzach adash b'achav equals Yishmaelim in gematria. He contrasts Edom, from whom converts come, with Yishmael, from whom none come, and links the two to se'or and chametz.

title.en: Every Jew has his hour

summary.en: The Rav teaches that no one knows how much his learning and davening can accomplish, bringing the Mishnah that every person has his hour and the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of the simple boy whose whistle on Yom Kippur annulled a decree. He adds Rashi's 'when the fox has its hour' and the Gemara that a person should see the world as half meritorious and half guilty.

title.en: The twelve days of Nissan and the power of minhag

summary.en: The Rav describes the days of Nissan as a time when the world is renewed, and brings Targum Yonasan that the twelve Nesiim's offerings subdue the twelve princes of Yishmael. Though reading the Nesiim in Nissan is only a minhag, he explains that minhag Yisrael carries the prophecy of Klal Yisrael, citing the Kuzari and the minhag of Hallel on Rosh Chodesh.

title.en: Removing the world's chametz; Rosh Chodesh Nissan

summary.en: The Rav explains why Yishmael's name may be mentioned though it is forbidden to name a rasha, since it is written in the Torah. He describes the pre-Pesach cleaning as burning the world's chametz, Yishmael and Amalek, urges learning in every free moment, and closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov on Rosh Chodesh Nissan as the Rosh Hashanah for kings and wishes for Pesach in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: דרוש בענין: מעשה ברבי אליעזר וכו' ובני בניו של המן שלמדו תורה בבני ברק

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how Timna's desire to cling to the family of Avraham survived, hidden and untouched, through Amalek and Haman until it produced Haman's descendants who learned Torah in Bnei Brak, and how the Tannaim of the Haggadah came there to repair them.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Sfas Emes on the Tannaim in Bnei Brak who lost track of time, and with the question why Amalek was only weakened. He then takes up the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak, though no convert may be accepted from Amalek. The answer lies in Timna: her desire to join the family of Avraham was a real bond, and since she came to Elifaz only as a pilegesh, her line passed through Amalek like an insulated wire without becoming Amalek. Haman's joy at Esther's feast freed that spark, which became Rav Shmuel bar Shilas. Shaul's sparing of Agag and Moshe's lowered hands left a remnant for Purim. The people of Bnei Brak struggled with the morning Krias Shema, a flaw from Zeresh, and the Tannaim, sharing their flaw by missing the matzah, repaired them. He closes with Birkas Hachama on erev Pesach and the power of a Jew's desire.

en: Timna's desire to cling to the family of Avraham was a sign of a real bond, and a good desire is never lost.
Because Timna began as a pilegesh, with no true bond, her line only passed through Amalek, so the ban on accepting converts from Amalek did not apply to Haman's descendants who came from her.
Amalek was deliberately not wiped out, by Moshe's lowered hands and by Shaul sparing Agag, so that Purim and Haman's righteous descendants could come about.
The Tannaim came to Bnei Brak to repair Haman's descendants, who could not properly say the morning Krias Shema.
The Rav says one must daven to have a desire for Torah, tefillah and mitzvos, since Pesach is the time of desire.

candidateTopics: Haggadah: the Tannaim in Bnei Brak
Timna and the descendants of Haman
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas and teachers of children
Purim and the feast of Esther

title.en: Bnei Brak, Amalek and Haman's descendants

summary.en: The Rav cites the Sfas Emes that the Tannaim lost track of time, asks why Amalek was only weakened, and brings Menashe's mockery of the verse about Timna. He then cites the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak and asks how, when no convert may be accepted from Amalek.

title.en: Timna's desire and what a pilegesh is

summary.en: Citing the Rambam that every verse is equally from Heaven, the Rav explains that Timna had a desire for kedushah, that desire means clinging, and that a desire shows a real connection. A pilegesh, though, has no true bond, and as the beginning of a thing holds all of it, her tie to Elifaz stayed separate, like an insulated wire.

title.en: Timna's line passes through Amalek

summary.en: The Rav explains that from Timna came Amalek and Haman, and from Haman's descendants Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, the model teacher of children. Since Timna's line only passed through Amalek, the oath against converts from Amalek does not apply; he adds the Gilgulei Neshamos that Timna was reincarnated in Bilaam's donkey.

title.en: Haman's joy at Esther's feast

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kedushas Levi and Tiferes Shlomo, who ask how Haman could feel joy, and answer that the holy feast of Esther gave him vitality, from which his righteous descendants could come. The Rav adds that this freed the spark of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, compares it to Agag fathering a child the night Shaul spared him, and notes that the feast was a Pesach meal.

title.en: Zeresh saved, and Haman's war on the moadim

summary.en: The Rav explains why Zeresh escaped: the spark destined for Haman's descendants passed through her. He reads 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' as holding Hashem's Name and the words 'they learned Torah in Bnei Brak', and explains that Haman hated the Yamim Tovim and the schoolchildren that sustain Klal Yisrael, while Timna, as Bilaam's donkey, spoke in favor of the three festivals.

title.en: Blessing Haman on Purim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one must drink on Purim until he cannot tell 'blessed Mordechai' from 'cursed Haman', and the Arizal that a blessing said on Haman by mistake goes only to the spark of holiness in him. The same holds for Zeresh, from whom came Shilas, the mother of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas.

title.en: Why Agag and Amalek were left alive

summary.en: The Rav asks why Shmuel never rebuked Shaul for sparing Agag, and brings the Ruzhiner: by leaving Agag, from whom Haman came, Shaul brought Purim to the world. This also explains why Moshe lowered his hands and Amalek was only weakened, so that a remnant would stay until Moshiach ben Yosef; Haman fought the moadim and the schoolchildren, the two things that come from Timna.

title.en: Bnei Brak's struggle with Krias Shema

summary.en: The Rav explains that the people of Bnei Brak, descendants of Haman, struggled with the morning Krias Shema, as many people today complain they cannot concentrate on it. This was a flaw from Zeresh, who sought to stop Mordechai's morning Krias Shema, and a gentile's flaw passes to his descendants even after conversion; Amalek also had a hold on the tribe of Dan, in whose land Bnei Brak lay, so the sages came from the Galil to help them.

title.en: Why the Tannaim missed the matzah

summary.en: Returning to the Sfas Emes, the Rav asks how Hashem let the great Tannaim miss eating matzah on Pesach night, and explains that the telling of the Exodus takes a Jew out of all his troubles, which made the night right for helping the people of Bnei Brak. He then develops that at a great success something must be given to the Sitra Achra, like the se'ir la'azazel, mayim acharonim and kaparos, and suggests that the fast on Pesach in Esther's time was such an appeasement for the Purim miracle.

title.en: The Tannaim repair Haman's descendants

summary.en: The Rav brings from the Ba'al Shem Tov that a tzaddik can only lift a sinner if he has some share in the sin, and explains that the Tannaim, by not eating matzah as the Jews could not in Haman's time, gained that share and freed Haman's descendants to say Krias Shema. He returns to the Rambam that the verse about Timna equals Shema Yisrael, and concludes with the power of a Jew's desire.

title.en: Birkas Hachama: the sun belongs to Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav turns to the year's Birkas Hachama, approached with great desire. He explains that Hashem gave the sun, nature, to Esav and the moon to Yaakov, yet in truth everything belongs to Yisrael, and only in this world does Esav seem to hold nature, as Yerushalayim is written without a yud during the exile.

title.en: The sun's return, erev Pesach, and desire

summary.en: The Rav explains that when the sun returns to its first point, as before the sin, it is revealed that the world was made for Yisrael, and Birkas Hachama comforts the sun that it will return to Yaakov. A Birkas Hachama on erev Pesach is greater, since the war against Amalek, Shaul's war with Agag and that of Moshiach ben Yosef, is erev Pesach. He closes that Pesach is desire, that Timna's desire survived until Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, and with a tefillah for the coming of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: A Remembrance for the Forgotten Jew (Connection to פרשת פקודי)

oneLiner.en: Through the extra silver of the half-shekel that Moshe Rabbeinu forgot and that became the hooks outside the Mishkan, the Rav shows that Hashem never rejects even the most distant Jew, and that Purim, especially in a year of Adar Sheni, belongs to the forgotten Jews of our generation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Maggid's test of the Ba'al HaTanya as ba'al koreh: every sedra speaks to its week, and the Adar parshiyos tell of Purim. The silver of the half-shekel of 600,000 Jews made exactly the hundred adanim, which carry Hashem's name; the silver of the extra 3,550 Moshe forgot, until Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him it became the hooks outside the holiness. Every Jew is a letter of the Torah, and those at the end, like the tribe of Dan cast out of the camp, are the ones Amalek attacks, wrongly thinking Hashem rejected them. The thirteenth month and the Megillah lack Hashem's name; Adar Sheni is the Purim of the forgotten Jew, and Haman repeated Amalek's error. Our generation lives in a double hiding, and Purim grows greater for it. The Rav ends by rebuking indifference to Jews in trouble and urging tefillah in the double Adar.

en: The half-shekel of exactly 600,000 Jews made the hundred adanim, whose name contains Hashem's name, while the silver of the extra 3,550 became the hooks that stood outside the holiness of the Mishkan.
Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, and none is rejected by Hashem: Amalek attacked the outcasts of the tribe of Dan thinking Hashem had cast them off, and Purim refutes him.
The thirteenth month has no combination of Hashem's four-letter name and the Megillah has no mention of His name; Adar Sheni is therefore the Purim of the Jews in whom Hashem is not seen.
Our generation lives in a double hiding: not only is Hashem hidden, but most Jews do not even know that He is hiding, and the test of the time is to believe that He is there and runs everything.
Purim grows greater with each generation, because the further the Jews fall, the more Purim, the festival of the rejected, belongs to them.

The Rav says that the blame for the lack of salvation lies not with Jews who know nothing but with those raised in Torah, who must not stay indifferent to their brothers' troubles and should use the double Adar for tefillah.

title.en: The Maggid tests the Ba'al HaTanya

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Maggid of Mezritch chose the young Ba'al HaTanya as ba'al koreh after he knew how each sedra, each aliyah and each person called up relates to the week. From this he turns to the Adar parshiyos, which tell of Purim and of the decree against the Jews.

title.en: The adanim and the forgotten silver

summary.en: The Rav describes the hundred silver adanim made from the half-shekel of 600,000 Jews. Since the census counted 603,550, there was extra silver; at the accounting Moshe Rabbeinu forgot what he did with it, until, the Midrash says, Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him that he made the hooks for the pillars of the courtyard.

title.en: Every Jew a letter of the Torah

summary.en: The Rav asks why Moshe forgot and why Rabbi Akiva had to remind him. He describes the camp of four groupings around the Mishkan, and explains that the 600,000 root souls match 600,000 letters of the Torah, so each Jew is a letter whose absence would spoil the Sefer Torah; the five Chumashim mirror the camp.

title.en: Dan outside the camp and Amalek

summary.en: The Rav explains that part of the tribe of Dan, always a source of trouble and placed last in the camp, was cast out from under the clouds of glory, and Amalek attacked them thinking Hashem had rejected them. He says Hashem rejects no Jew, not even the worst, and that Purim is the refutation of Amalek's claim to the Jew on the fringe.

title.en: Adar Sheni and the hooks outside

summary.en: The Rav explains that the thirteenth month has none of the twelve combinations of Hashem's name, like the Megillah, and Adar Sheni is the Purim of Jews in whom Hashem is not seen. The adanim carry Hashem's name, while the forgotten Jews' silver became hooks outside the holiness; yet a vav joins, so even they stay connected to the camp.

title.en: The last eight pesukim and forgetting

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara on who wrote the last eight pesukim of the Torah, Yehoshua or Moshe with tears, and calls them the forgotten pesukim, since Moshe's death and the broken luchos brought forgetting. The souls at the end of the Torah went through forgetting, so Moshe forgot them, and Rabbi Akiva, from a root without forgetting, reminded him.

title.en: Yehoshua against Amalek

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek attacks the souls at the end of the Torah, so Yehoshua, not Moshe, fights Amalek and writes the last pesukim. He brings that only Rachel's children can stand against Esav, as Yosef and Binyamin were not part of the brothers' sale, and that Moshiach ben Yosef will fight Amalek last.

title.en: Haman's shekalim and his mistake

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that in a leap year the Megillah is read in the second Adar, to join redemption to redemption. He then discusses Haman's ten thousand talents against the half-shekel, and shows that Haman paid only for the 600,000, not the 3,550 extra Jews, repeating Amalek's mistake that some Jews are rejected.

title.en: Our generation and the double hiding

summary.en: The Rav applies this to the last generation before Moshiach, the rejected thirteenth month of history, when masses of Jews do not know what Shema Yisrael means; Purim grows greater for them. Through the Gemara on Esther and a parable of a father hidden from his son, he explains the double hiding of today and the test to believe that Hashem is there.

title.en: A call to wake up and daven

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the months when tefillos are accepted, of the promises about this year, and of the yahrzeit of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech, telling how the Belzer Rav waited at the window for Moshiach the year before the war. He says the blame lies with Jews raised in Torah, rebukes indifference to Jews in trouble, and urges using the double Adar for tefillah.

catalogTitle: ביאור מצות פדיון פטר חמור: לב טוב' אמונה' ופשטות

oneLiner.en: Through the mitzvah of redeeming the firstborn donkey, the Rav shows that the klipah of Mitzrayim is a begrudging eye, that the donkey's holiness is its simplicity, and that the generation before Moshiach brings the geulah through simple emunah and a good heart toward others.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the two mitzvos of the firstborn donkey, redemption and breaking its neck, and asks for whom the second was given at all. He then asks why the verse about borrowing from the Egyptians appears inside Moshe's warning of makas bechoros. Using Rashi's two reasons for the mitzvah and the Arizal's teaching that Egypt's root is tzaras ayin, a begrudging eye, he explains that makas bechoros broke that root, so the Egyptians could now give with good will. The donkey that carried the wealth with a good eye earned redemption; a stingy owner is sent a donkey that must be destroyed, purifying his own trait. With the Maharal he explains the donkey's virtue as simplicity, like matzah, and its flaw as laziness, absent in the special donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach. Our simple generation's task is emunah peshutah, together with goodwill toward every Jew, which will bring Moshiach on his donkey.

en: According to the Arizal, the root klipah of Mitzrayim is tzaras ayin: an inability to give to or begrudge good to anyone else.
Makas bechoros struck the root of Egypt and broke its tzaras ayin, which is why the borrowing from the Egyptians, given with chen, belongs inside the warning of that plague.
A man's soul extends into his possessions, so a stingy owner's trait enters his firstborn donkey, and breaking its neck weakens the trait in him.
Following the Maharal, the donkey's virtue is simplicity, a spiritual virtue like that of matzah and the Kohen Gadol's white garments, while its flaw is laziness.
The generation before Moshiach has no great attainments; its particular mitzvah is simple emunah, and that emunah gives strength to Moshiach's donkey to come.
Pesach, the Yom Tov of emunah and of chesed, is the time to break the klipah of Mitzrayim by begrudging no one, including other Chassidim and other Rebbes.

title.en: Two mitzvos of the firstborn donkey

summary.en: After thanking the Stoliner chevra, the Rav recalls the morning's reading of Kadesh li kol bechor and the two mitzvos of the firstborn donkey, redemption and breaking its neck. He asks for whom the mitzvah of breaking the neck was given, since an honest Jew redeems and one who disobeys would not break the neck either.

title.en: Borrowing inside the warning of makas bechoros

summary.en: The Rav goes through the verses of Moshe's last warning to Pharaoh, which Rashi says was said while still standing before him, and notes that the command to borrow from the Egyptians and the chen they were given are inserted in the middle. He asks why this appears twice and what borrowing has to do with makas bechoros.

title.en: Rashi's two reasons and Egypt's begrudging eye

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's two reasons why only the donkey among impure animals has this mitzvah: Egypt is compared to donkeys, and the donkeys helped carry out the wealth. He suggests one reason fits redemption and the other breaking the neck, then brings the Arizal that Egypt's root is tzaras ayin, as the Gemara says even the nations' kindness is for themselves.

title.en: Matzah, free fish, and the broken root of Egypt

summary.en: The Rav brings that the Egyptians fed the Jews matzah so they would eat little, and the Midrash on the fish eaten 'for free', both showing Egypt could not give. He explains that makas bechoros broke Egypt's angel and root, so its tzaras ayin was nullified and the Egyptians gave with chen, a free gift; this is why the borrowing is part of the warning.

title.en: The soul extends into one's possessions

summary.en: The Rav explains that the donkey, though linked to Egypt, helped with a good eye and so earned redemption. From the Pri Tzaddik he brings that a person's soul extends into his property, illustrated by Rebbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey that would not eat untithed food; a stingy owner's trait enters his donkey, and destroying it weakens the klipah, like Moshe grinding the egel.

title.en: Seeing the kedushah in one's produce

summary.en: Returning to his opening question, the Rav brings from the Divrei Yisrael, in the name of Rebbi Yechezkel of Kuzmir, that in Temple times a Jew could see in his field how much of the produce held the kedushah of terumah, a fortieth, a fiftieth or a sixtieth. In the same way a good-eyed Jew sees holiness in his firstborn donkey and redeems it, while a stingy one is sent a donkey carrying Egypt's klipah, and breaking its neck purifies his heart, like burning chametz.

title.en: The donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Moshe rode the special donkey created at twilight, the same one Avraham took to the Akeidah and on which Moshiach will come. He asks why the donkey alone of the impure animals has kedushah and answers with the Maharal: the donkey is chomer, utterly simple, and simplicity, with nothing mixed in, is a spiritual virtue close to Hashem, while the horse's pride and beauty is only a physical one.

title.en: Matzah, white garments and simple Jews

summary.en: Continuing the Maharal, the Rav explains that matzah is holy because it is simple flour and water without the added work of time, and that the Kohen Gadol entered the Kodesh HaKodashim in plain white garments. He tells how the Ruzhiner refused a communal leader's offer to keep simple Jews out of the town shul, saying his forebears were all simple Jews.

title.en: Simplicity with zrizus, not laziness

summary.en: The Rav asks why the simple donkey is nonetheless impure and answers that it is also lazy, while matzah is simplicity joined with zrizus. Using the Gemara that one running on Erev Shabbos is exempt, he explains that the donkey created at twilight on Erev Shabbos was made in haste, so the donkey of Avraham, of Moshe at the Exodus and of Moshiach has the virtue of matzah, and every donkey shares some kedushah through its kind.

title.en: A simple generation and its mitzvah of emunah

summary.en: The Rav describes our generation as simple, without the Yom Kippur and Yamim Noraim of earlier generations. From the Gemara and the Tanya he brings that each person and each generation has its own mitzvah, and that the mitzvah of the generation before Moshiach is emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments, which is above understanding; even those who saw the miracles at the sea still had emunah in what lay beyond their grasp.

title.en: Simple emunah brings Moshiach's donkey

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the redemption comes in the merit of emunah and explains that the simpler the emunah, the more strength it gives Moshiach to come on his simple donkey, like the emunah of our grandmothers. He shows the same at the Akeidah: Avraham's levels and feeling were taken from him, and he went on the donkey with simple emunah.

title.en: Temimus: every Jew and his own Rebbe

summary.en: The Rav says the simple Jew who serves Hashem without politics brings Moshiach, and that a donkey, unlike a horse, never rebels against its master. Every Jew is bound to his own Rebbe or Rosh Yeshiva, but disparaging another is not temimus; he brings the Sanzer Rav on this and the Chasam Sofer's letter that Moshiach could have come in the generation of Rebbi Yaakov Emden and Rebbi Yonasan, but did not because disciples disparaged the gedolim.

title.en: Pesach: emunah, chesed and fargin

summary.en: The Rav calls Pesach the Yom Tov of simple emunah and of chesed, a time to break the klipah of Mitzrayim by rejoicing in another Jew's virtues, and brings that matzah, the food of emunah, brings emunah when eaten all of Pesach. He ends with a brachah for a speedy geulah; dedications and an announcement follow.

catalogTitle: א - שבע קולות של שירה הם כנגד השבע ספירות. השביעית (מלכות) כנגד שבת. ב - ביזת הים - להוציא כח הנעלם שבתוכנו.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the twelve paths of Kerias Yam Suf and the twelve tones of song mark an exile still divided, while the future redemption will have only the seven tones of joy that come together in Shabbos, and he urges saying the daily Shirah with joy to bring salvation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mechilta: had the Jews at the sea said 'Hashem melech' instead of 'Hashem yimloch', there would have been no further exile. He asks why the sea split into twelve paths while the future sea will split into seven streams. Through Yosef, whose name points to the future redemption, he explains that the Exodus was only half a redemption, a Yachatz, and the sea split then only in Yosef's merit. He then turns to song: a niggun is a heavenly match of tones, its seven tones parallel the seven days, the seven shepherds and Shabbos, while twelve stands for division. On the piano, seven white keys of chesed and five black keys of din make twelve, the tones of exile; in the future only the seven will remain. He closes with Sefer Chareidim's six easy segulos, above all saying the Shirah daily with joy, which draws salvation for the Jews of Eretz Yisroel.

en: The Exodus and the splitting of the sea were only half of the redemption, a Yachatz; the rest of the debt of exile still has to be completed in the long galus.
The sea split for Yosef's merit, because his self-sacrifice went beyond nature, yet it stays bound to its original condition, which will be fulfilled in the days of Moshiach.
A niggun is a heavenly match of tones that fit one another, as incomprehensible as a shidduch, which is why song belongs at a wedding.
The seven tones of song parallel the seven days of creation, the seven shepherds and the seven 'kol Hashem', and Shabbos, the seventh, completes them, so Shabbos is the day of song.
Twelve, the tribes, the weekday brachos and the seven white with five black keys, is division and exile; seven, Shabbos, Yerushalayim and David, is unity and redemption.
In the future there will be only the seven tones of joy, song without weeping, and then 'Hashem melech' will be said.
Saying the Shirah daily with joy and intent is an easy segulah for atonement and draws miracles and salvation for all of Klal Yisroel.

niggun as a match of tones
Yosef and Yehuda and the two Moshiachs
exile as division, redemption as unity

title.en: Why 'yimloch' and not 'melech'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mechilta that had the Jews said 'Hashem melech' there would have been no more exile, and asks why they did not. He contrasts the twelve paths of the sea with the seven streams of the future and asks why the sea returned 'to its first condition' after the miracle.

title.en: Yosef and the redemption split in two

summary.en: Yosef's name alone points to the future redemption. The Rav brings the Chida that 190 years of exile remained owed, so the redemption was split like Yachatz; the sea did not want to split before its time, but split for the merit of Yosef's coffin and his self-sacrifice beyond nature.

title.en: Song as a heavenly match of tones

summary.en: Before Shvi'i shel Pesach the Rav discusses kinds of song: poetry whose lines rhyme, and niggun, tones that fit one another wondrously, unlike a cat walking on a piano. Like a shidduch, which only Hashem makes, this cannot be explained; he brings the Gra that most secrets of the Torah depend on the wisdom of music.

title.en: Seven tones and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tikkunei Zohar that a heavenly palace opens only through niggun, and explains that song has seven tones completed by Shabbos, the day of song. He tells of the Baal HaTanya answering the scholars of Shklov with a niggun, and links the seven tones to the seven days, the seven shepherds ending with David, the seven 'kol Hashem' of Havu laShem and the Beis HaMikdash harp.

title.en: Yaakov's niggun to unite Yosef and Yehuda

summary.en: Song at a wedding fits because a wedding is a match. The Rav explains that Yaakov sent a niggun of Eretz Yisroel with 'mizimras ha'aretz' to awaken the union of Yosef and Yehuda, the two Moshiachs, whose rift born of jealousy, like the moon's, is the root of exile.

title.en: Noise without harmony; seven shepherds and twelve princes

summary.en: Tones with no connection to each other, like the music of the gentile world that Jews copy, arouse lowly desires, a union Hashem did not decree. The Rav contrasts the seven shepherds, who belong to every Jew and unite in Shabbos, with the twelve tribal princes, each only for his own tribe, a state of separation.

title.en: Shabbos and Yerushalayim unite the tribes

summary.en: The twelve middle brachos of Shemoneh Esreh belong to the weekdays; on Shabbos one bracha gathers all Jews, like Yerushalayim, which was not divided among the tribes. The Rav ties Shabbos, Yerushalayim, David and malchus together and explains that after the seven psalms of Kabbalas Shabbos one can sing.

title.en: White and black keys: chesed and din

summary.en: On the piano seven white keys bring out joy and five black half-keys bring out sadness, like shevarim. The Rav explains white as chesed and black as din, and that joining them makes tiferes, the beauty of a niggun, and twelve tones. He brings the Mechilta reading 'bakosharos' as weeping and song.

title.en: Twelve tones of exile, seven of redemption

summary.en: Since Kerias Yam Suf was only half the redemption, it was still weeping with song, twelve tones like the twelve tribes before uniting under David. In the future there will be only the seven white tones of joy, the seven streams, gematria shirah; therefore at the sea they said 'yimloch', and in the future 'Hashem melech' will be said.

title.en: Shvi'i shel Pesach, the Shabbos of Pesach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Likkutei Torah that Shvi'i shel Pesach is the Shabbos of Pesach, its greatest day, and the Sfas Emes that the open spaces of the Shirah show the heart opening. The haftorah is David's song, and Acharon shel Pesach's haftorah is of Moshiach; chassidim stressed saying the daily Shirah with joy.

title.en: Sefer Chareidim's easy segulos for atonement

summary.en: Like costly medicines next to free healing herbs in the field, Sefer Chareidim lists six easy segulos that bring atonement without fasts and hardship. The Rav goes through five: answering Amen yehei shmei rabba with all one's strength, keeping Shabbos properly, letting slights pass, hisbodedus, and listening eagerly to a sage's words of aggadah.

title.en: The sixth segulah: the daily Shirah

summary.en: The sixth segulah is saying the Shirah daily with joy. The Rav brings the Yalkut and the Zohar: one who says it daily with intent merits to say it in the future, Moshiach is found in it, and Knesses Yisroel is crowned with the crown prepared for Moshiach. Pesach is emunah, and the Shirah draws great miracles.

title.en: Daily miracles and the Jews of Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Jews of Eretz Yisroel, surrounded by enemies, need salvation beyond nature, and daily miracles go unnoticed. The Rav brings the Ramban at the end of Bo and the Yaavetz that Jewish survival in exile is a greater miracle than the sea, and explains that the Shirah, which mentions the inhabitants of Peleshes, draws that salvation.

title.en: The real battle is in the beis medrash

summary.en: The war of Yishmael in Eretz Yisroel is a war against Hashem, as the attacks on the Jews of Meah Shearim show. The Rav says the battle is fought in every shul and beis medrash, and every Jew is a soldier with Torah, tefillah and the daily Shirah said with joy.

title.en: Yom tov is redemption, not commemoration

summary.en: Jewish festivals are not commemorations of past events like a national holiday; every Pesach redemption comes down to the world, and each care with chametz nullifies the sitra achra. The Rav closes with a brachah for salvation and for singing the new song of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: יום של התגלות עלמא דאתכסייא של כל יהודי אפילו של דתן ואבירם (ובענין גודל פגם המחלוקת)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that at the splitting of the sea the hidden world (alma d'iskasya) was revealed, so that even Dasan and Aviram, the worst of quarrelers, were awakened and had the sea split again for them, and that machlokes is the great obstacle before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi and Targum Yonasan: Pharaoh spoke about Dasan and Aviram, who stayed in Egypt, and the Be'er Mayim Chaim brings a Chazal that the sea split a second time for them. To explain what changed, he contrasts the revealed world with the hidden world, alma d'iskasya, which was revealed at the sea. He illustrates the hidden world with shidduchim, which even a bas kol cannot grasp, and with Leah, whose tears tore her from Esav's root. The splitting on Shvi'i shel Pesach was only partial; the second one, in Acharon shel Pesach's haftarah, will reach even those left behind. He reconciles the Ibn Ezra and Ramban on the Shirah, brings the Rama MiFano that Eliyahu's two bulls were Dasan and Aviram, and concludes that today's machlokes is the Satan's work on the erev Shabbos before Moshiach, from which every Jew must run.

en: Dasan and Aviram stayed in Egypt, and according to a Chazal brought by the Be'er Mayim Chaim the sea split a second time for them.
At the splitting of the sea, on Shvi'i shel Pesach, the hidden world (alma d'iskasya) was revealed, as the Baal HaTanya says in Torah Ohr.
Acharon shel Pesach's haftarah speaks of a second, greater splitting of the sea in the days of Moshiach, which will be a path even for those who were left behind.
Every Jew, even the worst, has a hidden point of love for Hashem that can never be ruined, and it is revealed on the last days of Pesach.
Machlokes tears a Jew away from Hashem's oneness, and the Rav says that whoever fears Heaven must resolve to have no part in any machlokes.
The machlokes of today comes because it is the erev Shabbos before Moshiach, when the Satan works to keep the light of Shabbos and peace from entering.

title.en: Dasan and Aviram stayed in Egypt

summary.en: The Rav opens with the reading of Shvi'i shel Pesach: Rashi and Targum Yonasan explain that Pharaoh spoke of those who stayed in Egypt, Dasan and Aviram, and the Be'er Mayim Chaim brings a Chazal that the sea split a second time for them. He asks what changed in them at the sea, and also raises the dispute of the Ibn Ezra and the Ramban whether 'ki va sus Paroh' is part of the Shirah.

title.en: The bas kol and the hidden world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Megillah that when Yonasan ben Uziel translated the Prophets a bas kol asked who revealed its secrets, and he had to stand up and say it was he; he asks why the bas kol did not know. He introduces the revealed and hidden worlds, and the Baal HaTanya's teaching that at the splitting of the sea the hidden was uncovered, as the covering sea turned into dry land.

title.en: Shidduchim come from the hidden world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tzemach Tzedek that the root of a shidduch is so high it cannot descend into the physical world until a shadchan's untruth brings it down, and tells how the Divrei Chaim paid every shadchan even when the match did not go through. He explains that a bas kol is lower than prophecy and unclear, so it cannot grasp a hidden zivug and announces wrong matches until the right one; this is why it did not know who Yonasan ben Uziel was.

title.en: Leah's tears and Esav's hidden spark

summary.en: From the Heichal HaBrachah the Rav explains that Esav, 'admoni' like David, carried a high spark of holiness from the hidden world. Leah too is of the hidden world while Rachel is of the revealed, so Leah was fit for Esav; with her tears she tore herself from Esav's root into Yaakov's and changed her mazal, a revelation of the hidden world like the splitting of the sea.

title.en: The second splitting of the sea

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Shvi'i shel Pesach, when the sea split, with Acharon shel Pesach, whose haftarah from Yeshayahu speaks of a second splitting still hidden, 'yosif Hashem shenis yado'. Then high souls now buried deep in the mud will have their tikkun; the sea did not want to split the first time because the Jews were not yet ready, but in the future all Jews will pass through, those not ready tearing themselves from their root of evil with tears.

title.en: Yosef's coffin and the sea's refusal

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Jews kept their holiness in Egypt in Yosef's merit, apart from Shlomis bas Divri, and that the sea split when it saw Yosef's coffin, since Yosef had split his own 'sea', the yetzer hara. He asks why Hashem then had to rebuke the sea, and answers with the Be'er Mayim Chaim's Chazal: the rebuke was for the second splitting, for Dasan and Aviram, who had no share in Yosef's holiness.

title.en: Do Dasan and Aviram have a share in Olam Haba?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah in Sanhedrin and the Braisa of the 'doreshei reshumos' who hold that even those listed have a share, proven from 'morid Sheol vaya'al'. The Ohr HaChaim says that even Korach's company has a share, but not Dasan and Aviram, who have no tikkun; the Tiferes Shlomo protests that every Jew will reach his tikkun and shows that 'morid Sheol vaya'al' equals Dasan and Aviram in gematria.

title.en: A path for those who were left behind

summary.en: The Rav explains that Acharon shel Pesach's haftarah, 'vehaysa mesilah lish'ar amo', promises a path for those who stayed in Egypt. The exodus came before its time, from the forty-nine gates of impurity, but when Moshiach comes, through the power of the Torah, even those in the fiftieth gate will come out, as hinted in the Haggadah's answer to the rasha. He shows that Dasan and Aviram's whole career was machlokes, from 'nitzim' to 'nitzavim'.

title.en: The first splitting was only a sign

summary.en: The Rav shows that the haftarah of Acharon shel Pesach hints at Dasan and Aviram, and brings the Midrash that at the sea the Jews did not say 'Hashem melech', because the exodus came early and the exile had to complete it. With the Ramban's rule that the events of the fathers are a sign for the children, he concludes that the splitting on Shvi'i shel Pesach is a sign of the true one still to come, when even the worst Jew will reach his tikkun.

title.en: Machlokes, and the Shirah of Dasan and Aviram

summary.en: The Rav says there is no damage like machlokes, which is the world of separation of the sitra achra, opposed to Hashem's oneness; Yerushalayim was destroyed because of it, and Dasan and Aviram were souls of separation. He then answers the opening question: the second 'uvnei Yisrael halchu bayabasha' refers to Dasan and Aviram crossing after the miracle ended, so the Ibn Ezra is right that it is part of a Shirah and the Ramban is right that it is not part of the Shirah of all Israel.

title.en: Eliyahu's two bulls and the tikkun at Ne'ilah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rama MiFano that the two bulls Eliyahu brought on Har HaCarmel were Dasan and Aviram, and the Midrash that the bull meant for Ba'al refused until told that a kiddush Hashem would come through it too. He explains that achdus is the unity of Hashem, that Yom Kippur is the day of achdus, and that the two bulls reach their tikkun at Ne'ilah, when Jews cry out 'Hashem hu haElokim'.

title.en: The hidden point revealed at the sea

summary.en: The Rav explains why Moshe mentions Dasan and Aviram and not Korach: Korach had a tikkun, while for Dasan and Aviram Hashem's wonder was the second splitting, and 'asah' means 'tikken'. He then answers the opening question: the plagues did not move them, but when the hidden world was revealed at the sea their hidden point awoke, they did teshuvah and ran to the sea. He calls to use Shvi'i and Acharon shel Pesach, when the hidden love in every Jew is revealed and even the last Jew can be raised.

title.en: Today's machlokes on the erev Shabbos of history

summary.en: The Rav says that the machlokes among Jews today is the Satan's plan, since Moshiach will bring achdus, and that souls with sparks of Dasan and Aviram are among us. He says every Jew with fear of Heaven must resolve to have no part in any machlokes and to run from it, and that fighting between chassidus groups is a distortion of the Ba'al Shem Tov's way. He brings the Gemara in Gittin of the two men whom the Satan set quarreling every erev Shabbos until Rabbi Meir made peace, and explains that today is the erev Shabbos before Moshiach.

title.en: Shalom is Hashem's name

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that 'ki tov' is missing on the second day of creation because machlokes was created then, and explains that shalom is the name of Hashem and of Yerushalayim and is the test of whether a thing is desired by Hashem. He closes with the Baal HaTanya that Shvi'i shel Pesach is the Shabbos of Pesach, calls to work for shalom, and blesses that all Jews merit it together.

catalogTitle: The Eternal נסים of מגילת אסתר

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the miracles of the Megillah are hidden inside nature, just as Hashem's name is hidden in it, and that reading the Megillah trains a Jew to find Hashem behind world events and his own daily life.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the joy of Adar and asks how we can make the bracha 'she'asa nisim' over a Megillah that reads like an ordinary court story, with no split sea and no mention of Hashem's name. He answers that Nisan, the first month, is the month of revealed miracles, while Adar, the last, means a cloak: its miracles are covered by nature. Nature itself is a miracle, as bread from the ground would be to someone raised on the mann. Through a parable of a dying patient saved by a medicine and a doctor arriving just in time, he shows that the Megillah's nes is a jigsaw puzzle of natural events, and that current events, from the Gulf War onward, are a Megillah being written now. 'HaMelech' means Hashem, rulers are marionettes, and His name hides in the words. Reading the Megillah teaches a Jew to read the world and his own life.

en: The Megillah tells a seemingly natural story with no open miracle and no mention of Hashem's name, yet we make the bracha 'she'asa nisim' over it.
Nisan is the month of revealed miracles; Adar, the month furthest from it, means a cloak, and its miracles are hidden in nature.
Nature itself is a miracle made by the same Hashem who makes open miracles; we fail to see it only because we are used to it.
The nes of the Megillah is a jigsaw puzzle of many small natural events, each one needed, put together by Hashem.
In the Megillah 'HaMelech' alludes to Hashem, and in the same way world leaders are marionettes moved by strings from above.
Hashem's name is in the Megillah, hidden in the first and last letters of words, and one has to look for it.
The Megillah is a drill in reading the world: one who learns to read it can find Hashem in current events and in his own life.

candidateTopics: Hashem's name hidden in the Megillah

title.en: A Megillah without open miracles

summary.en: The Rav opens with the joy of Adar and the great kedusha of Megillas Esther, written with ruach hakodesh. He points out that Hashem's name never appears in it and that it reads like a plain court story, and asks how we can then make the bracha 'she'asa nisim'.

title.en: Nisan and Adar: revealed and cloaked miracles

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Nisan, the first month and the month of revealed miracles, with Adar, the last month, whose name means a cloak, as in 'aderes se'ar'. He explains that nature is itself a miracle, using the example of a child raised on the mann who first sees bread grow from the ground.

title.en: Parable of the patient and the medicine

summary.en: The Rav tells a parable of a dying patient whose only cure is a medicine from China and a doctor from America, both months away, who both arrive just in time. Nothing supernatural happened, yet anyone sees there was a plan, and this, he says, is the kind of nes in the Megillah.

title.en: The jigsaw puzzle of the Megillah and of today

summary.en: The Rav shows how every detail of the Megillah, from Vashti's removal to Mordechai understanding Bigsan and Teresh and the king's sleepless night, is a screw in one machine. He applies this to current events such as the Gulf War and the fall of Russia, and explains that court gossip a yeshiva boy rightly ignores was, in Achashverosh's time, the unfolding of a nes.

title.en: Why Hashem's name is missing; 'HaMelech'

summary.en: The Rav gives a simple reason why Hashem's name is absent from the Megillah and brings the Midrash that 'HaMelech' alludes to Hashem, comparing it to a believer reading about the president in the newspaper. He brings the passuk that the hearts of kings are in Hashem's hand and Rashi that Amalek conceals Hashem's name and throne.

title.en: Rulers as marionettes

summary.en: The Rav describes a marionette show whose thin strings the audience cannot see. Achashverosh's sudden change from Haman's side to Esther's shows that he was a marionette, and the Rav applies the same to the leaders of his day, who turn this way and that as Hashem pulls the strings.

title.en: Hashem's hidden name in the Megillah and in history

summary.en: The Rav explains why some ba'alei kriah read 'Yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom' in one breath: the Arizal explains that its first letters spell Hashem's name, which appears at turning points of the story, sometimes backwards in final letters. Likewise Hashem's hand is hidden in history, where the empires that oppressed the Jews are gone and the Jews live on.

title.en: Learning to read the Megillah and the world

summary.en: The Rav explains the bracha 'al mikra Megillah' as learning to read, like a doctor reading an x-ray, and calls the Megillah a drill in finding Hashem in newspapers and history books. With the masked collector at the Purim seudah and a late lunch at home, he concludes that the world is masked, Hashem directs every detail, and one who learns this fears no one.

catalogTitle: בימי ספירה צריכים לעשות תשובה על שורש העבירות - המדות (שייכות לפרשת קדושים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the days of Sefirah, as the beginning and root of the year, are the time to do teshuvah on the root of sin, the middos, and that this is the meaning of 'kedoshim tihyu'.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'kedoshim tihyu' and contrasts Chanoch, who separated himself and became an angel, with Avraham, who went down to the people. He then asks why there are three seasons of teshuvah: Sefirah, Shovavim, and Elul-Tishrei. Using the dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nissan, he explains Nissan as the birth and chesed of creation and Tishrei as its full growth and din. A long thread follows on the first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh Nissan at the dedication of the Mishkan, which was burned because that day had no lessening of the moon, and on Nadav and Avihu, who sensed the days of Moshiach. Then he turns to his main point: Nissan and Sefirah are the time to repair the roots, the middos, from which sins grow, while Tishrei is for deeds and Shovavim for removing stains. He reads 'kedoshim tihyu' with the Ramban as sanctifying what is permitted, and urges everyone, by his own measure, to grow with nature during the remaining weeks.

en: The days of Sefirah are a season of teshuvah, one of three in the year together with Shovavim and Elul-Tishrei.
Nissan is the beginning and birth of creation, ruled by chesed; Tishrei is creation fully grown, ruled by din, matching the views of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer.
The first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh, at the dedication of the Mishkan, was not eaten because on that day the moon was not diminished, and this is the best sign for all generations.
Every sin grows from a bad midda; whoever repents only for the sin and not for the midda falls back into the same sin.
In Nissan and Sefirah one repairs the middos, the root; in Tishrei the deeds, the fruit; and in Shovavim one removes the stains left after teshuvah.
'Kedoshim tihyu' means, as the Ramban explains, to sanctify oneself in what is permitted and not be a glutton within the Torah's permission, and it was said to all of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Kedoshim tihyu: Chanoch and Avraham

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'kedoshim tihyu' and contrasts Chanoch, who withdrew and became an angel, with Avraham, who went down to people; holiness must not contradict closeness to others, which is why the parsha was said in public. He then brings the Chasam Sofer that Nadav and Avihu were reincarnated in Pinchas, who is Eliyahu, as a repair for their strange fire.

title.en: Three seasons of teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the days of Sefirah are days of tikkun and teshuvah, and that there are three such seasons: Sefirah, Shovavim and Elul-Tishrei. He asks how they differ, and begins with Nissan as the head of the months, bringing the Maharal that a beginning lasts for its first quarter.

title.en: Nissan's growth and the burned se'ir

summary.en: The Rav describes Nissan, Iyar and Sivan as the season of birth and growth in nature and in Klal Yisroel. He then asks why the first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh, offered on the day the Mishkan was set up, was burned and not eaten, when a beginning should be a good sign, and raises the question of how Nadav and Avihu could rule before Moshe and enter after drinking wine.

title.en: Tishrei and Nissan: din and chesed

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nissan, and explains that both are true: Nissan is the birth of creation in chesed, Tishrei its maturity in din. Each Tanna follows his own approach, and according to Rabbi Eliezer the beginning of the world is hinted in Bereishis, while the true beginning of the world is from its middle, Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The middle of the Torah and Rosh Chodesh

summary.en: According to Rabbi Yehoshua, the beginning of creation is hinted in the middle of the Torah, at the words 'darosh darash' about the se'ir of the chatas. The Rav connects Bereishis and 'se'ir' to the six hundred thousand souls of Klal Yisroel, and explains that the se'ir of Rosh Chodesh is an atonement for the lessening of the moon, which is Klal Yisroel in galus.

title.en: The day the Mishkan was set up

summary.en: Rosh Chodesh Nissan is the root of all roots, and the day the Mishkan was set up was, as the Gemara in Megillah says, like the day of creation, a taste of the days of Moshiach. On that day the moon was whole and needed no atonement, so not eating the se'ir was the best possible sign, and this is why it is hinted in the middle of the Torah.

title.en: Nadav and Avihu sensed the days of Moshiach

summary.en: Nadav and Avihu became the soul of Eliyahu, the herald of the redemption, and are 'after death'. The Rav describes the days of Moshiach, when, as Yirmiyahu says, no one will need to teach another, and explains that Nadav and Avihu felt this so strongly on that day that they lost themselves; their entering after drinking wine shows their greatness, not their smallness.

title.en: Wine, Eliyahu and kevius

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Berachos that whether one may make a meal of wine will be decided when Eliyahu comes, the Midrash about the first vineyard planted, where wine turns a man into a sheep, a lion, a monkey and a pig, and the Gemara that wine's end is blood, explaining with gematria that a little wine holds Hashem's Name and too much leaves only 'dam'. Eliyahu is the holy side of the mazal of Ma'adim; Nadav and Avihu, sensing the time of Eliyahu when wine can no longer harm, entered after drinking.

title.en: Fifty-one days and Pesach Sheni

summary.en: The Rav shows that the Sefirah period, like Elul-Tishrei, has fifty-one days, hinted in the two 'na' of 'Ana Hashem' in Hallel, and that its thirtieth day, Pesach Sheni, parallels Rosh Hashanah as a day of tikkun. Mishael and Eltzafan, who became impure from Nadav and Avihu, merited the parsha of Pesach Sheni, showing that impurity of death can be repaired.

title.en: The middos are the root of sin

summary.en: The Rav explains that Sefirah is the time to repair the middos, bringing Rabbi Chaim Vital that the middos are the root of all mitzvos and worse than sins, and the Be'er Mayim Chaim. He shows how lashon hara grows from arrogance, machlokes from the need to win, as with Yeravam ben Nevat, and eating forbidden food from desire, and says that people repeat sins because they did teshuvah on the sin and not on the midda.

title.en: Using each midda for good

summary.en: The Rav goes through the middos: chesed through tzedakah, favors and learning with others; gevurah against the yetzer hara, even in permitted things; tiferes in knowing one's own great worth, so that every mitzvah, like counting the Omer, is precious; netzach in fighting for Yiddishkeit and not to defeat another; and hod in bowing down and praising Hashem.

title.en: Root, fruit and stains

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: Nissan, when everything sprouts, is for repairing the root, the middos; Tishrei, the time of harvest, is for teshuvah on deeds; and Shovavim is a 'laundry season' for removing the stains that remain after teshuvah, as Rabbeinu Yonah writes. He adds that through Nadav and Avihu's self-sacrifice Aharon merited entering the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur.

title.en: The Rambam's Sefer Kedushah in the Sefirah parshiyos

summary.en: Acharei-Kedoshim falls in the middle of Sefirah, the week of netzach, the axis around which Sefirah turns. The Rav shows that almost all the halachos of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah are found in the parshiyos read during Sefirah, and even the few exceptions connect to Shavuos or are hinted there.

title.en: The Ramban on kedoshim tihyu

summary.en: The Rav reads the Ramban that 'kedoshim tihyu' warns against being a glutton within the Torah's permission and commands sanctifying oneself in what is permitted, which is the repair of middos rather than deeds. He brings Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 231, that all one does should be for Hashem, and says that our weak generation cannot demand great things of itself.

title.en: Kedoshim for everyone; grow with nature

summary.en: Since the parsha was said to the whole congregation, the Rav says 'kedoshim tihyu' is for everyone, each by his own measure and with sense: stopping now and then from an extra treat, eating enough to serve Hashem with joy, and not fooling oneself. He closes by urging the listeners to use the remaining weeks of Sefirah, to look at nature growing each day and to grow with it until Shavuos.

catalogTitle: תיקון המדות הנוגע למעשה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the weeks of Sefirah are the time to become a true 'adam' through good middos, above all by never shaming another person, since Torah can only be received by people of good character.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining that the seven weeks of Sefirah are for refining the seven middos, which is why Pirkei Avos is learned then; Rabbi Chaim Vital teaches that middos are not written in the Torah because they are the prerequisite for receiving it. Over Sefirah a person must become an 'adam', and in the generation before Moshiach, marked by chutzpah, this work is urgent. He then brings a chain of examples from Sefer Bereishis and Chazal: Beis Hillel's humility, Rachel handing the simanim to Leah, Tamar ready to be burned rather than shame Yehuda, Yosef risking his life not to shame his brothers, the chol bird, and Shaul with his servant. He warns against frumkeit that shames others, contrasts Tamar with Potiphar's wife, and stresses kavod habriyos, ahavas Yisrael and respect for another's opinion. He closes with the Kohen Gadol who must tend to a meis mitzvah even on Yom Kippur.

en: The seven weeks of Sefirah are given for perfecting the seven middos, which are the entrance requirement for receiving the Torah on Shavuos.
In the era before Moshiach, whose main sign is chutzpah, one must work especially hard to become a mentsch.
Rachel, Tamar and Yosef merited the geulah, the kingship of David and great blessings because they refused to shame another person.
Frumkeit that is used to shame and attack others is, according to the Rav, a bad middah; one must be ehrlich, and rebuke only gently and with love.
The Torah is particular about kavod habriyos, which can even override the Kohen Gadol's Yom Kippur service.
Love of a fellow Jew is bound together with love of Hashem and love of Torah.
What a person learns shapes his middos: Torah study in a given area brings care in that area.

title.en: Sefirah as the time for perfecting middos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seven weeks of counting are for refining the seven middos, character traits rather than piety, and that this is why Pirkei Avos is learned between Pesach and Shavuos. He brings Rabbi Chaim Vital that middos are hardly written in the Torah because they are the entrance requirement for receiving it.

title.en: Becoming an 'adam' by Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav brings the siddur of the Yaavetz that the blessing of Sefiras HaOmer hints to the name of Hashem whose spelled-out letters equal 'adam', and contrasts the barley Omer, animal food, with the human food brought on Shavuos. He then brings the Gemara at the end of Sotah that chutzpah marks the time before Moshiach and the Arizal's words about his generation.

title.en: Simple middos and Beis Hillel's humility

summary.en: The Rav announces that in the coming weeks he will speak about simple middos, not sharp chiddushim, since simplicity is the beauty of a Jew. He brings the Gemara that Beis Hillel merited that the halacha follows them because they were gentle and humble, quoting Beis Shammai's view first.

title.en: Rachel's simanim and the redemption

summary.en: The Rav retells how Rachel gave Leah the signs she had arranged with Yaakov so that her sister would not be shamed, and how she never revealed it. Through the Midrash on 'Rachel weeps for her children' he shows that the redemption comes in her merit, and explains that her test was one of middos, not of tefillah or mitzvos.

title.en: Tamar, and frumkeit that shames

summary.en: The Rav tells how Tamar was ready to be burned rather than publicly shame Yehuda, and how she merited the kingship of David; the Gemara learns from her that one should rather be thrown into a fire than shame another. He applies this to people who shame others in the name of frumkeit, bringing the sayings of the Belzer Rav and the Ropshitzer, and says rebuke must be private and with love.

title.en: Yosef's danger rather than shaming his brothers

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that Yosef put himself in mortal danger by sending everyone out before revealing himself, so as not to shame his brothers before the Egyptians, and that his greatness came from these middos. He adds that Sefer Bereishis has almost no mitzvos and teaches middos, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that this is why Avos is learned before Matan Torah.

title.en: Covering for sinners at war; the chol bird

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah sends home newlyweds and others from war so that one who is afraid because of his sins will not be recognized and shamed. He then tells the Gemara of the chol bird that did not ask Noach for food so as not to burden him, and was blessed never to die.

title.en: Middos as the foundation; Yosef avoids his father

summary.en: The Rav says good middos are the foundation of yiras Shamayim, of chassidus and of Torah, and that a chassid without them is a false chassid. He brings from the Rishonim that Yosef avoided being alone with Yaakov for seventeen years so that he would not have to tell how his brothers sold him.

title.en: Tamar and Potiphar's wife: both for Heaven's sake

summary.en: The Rav asks why, if both Tamar and Potiphar's wife acted for Heaven's sake, as Rashi says, one is praised and the other shamed forever. He answers that Tamar would not shame Yehuda, while Potiphar's wife threw Yosef into prison; he applies it to zealotry that shames people, and brings the Divrei Chaim's proof that burying a rasha is no mitzvah.

title.en: Shaul and his servant; kavod habriyos in Shema

summary.en: The Rav shows how Shaul, searching for the lost donkeys, spoke of his father worrying about 'us', putting his servant on a par with himself, and was told that this is why he would become king. He then brings the Mishnah that one may interrupt Kriyas Shema to greet out of respect, though one may not even gesture, showing how the Torah values kavod habriyos.

title.en: Parshas Kedoshim and the three loves

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's students rejoiced when Parshas Kedoshim came, since it holds 'love your fellow as yourself', Rabbi Akiva's great principle. He connects love of a fellow Jew to love of Hashem, brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's three loves, and says one should accept this mitzvah before davening so the tefillah is accepted.

title.en: The poor man's offering and a bochur's chiddush

summary.en: The Rav explains that only by the poor man's mincha does the Torah say 'nefesh', and that the poor man's bird is burned with its feathers despite the bad smell, yet it is a pleasing aroma to Hashem; he brings the Rambam that the incense was to counter the smell of the offerings. He applies this to a bochur who offers a weak chiddush to a great lamdan, who should accept it warmly.

title.en: Different faces, different opinions

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that just as people's faces differ so do their opinions, and explains that each person has a different neshamah and root, as Hillel came from chessed and Shammai from gevurah, so their faces and rulings differed. He concludes that one may prefer his own view but may never say another's view is nothing.

title.en: Rav Aharon Kotler: learning shapes middos

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Aharon Kotler's observation that Litvishe Jews are more careful in bein adam lachaveiro and chassidim in bein adam laMakom, because chassidim learn mostly Seder Moed and Brachos while Litvishe yeshivos learn the Bava's, and Torah instills what one learns. He adds the tzaddikim's teaching to learn a Yom Tov's masechta before the Yom Tov.

title.en: The Kohen Gadol and kavod habriyos

summary.en: The Rav tells of a member of the Gerer family who delayed breaking his fast after Yom Kippur to finish Masechta Yoma, then brings the case of a Kohen Gadol on Erev Yom Kippur who finds a meis mitzvah and must become tamei even at the cost of the avodah, because kavod habriyos is great. He closes that Sefirah is the time to reflect on how to improve in bein adam lachaveiro, ahavas Yisrael and kavod habriyos.

catalogTitle: A יו”ט for the Latecomer - Don't Waste it!

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Purim is a Yom Tov for the Jews at the edge of the camp, the latecomers and those who stumbled, because Hashem never rejects any Jew, and he urges his listeners not to waste it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Haman's ten thousand kikar of silver, which Tosafos matches to the half-shekels the Jews gave, and with the extra 1,775 shekels whose use Moshe Rabbeinu forgot. He explains that the Torah's 600,000 letters correspond to 600,000 Jewish souls; the Jews beyond that number were those of Shevet Dan whom the clouds expelled, and Amalek attacked them thinking Hashem had rejected them. Achashverosh's feast celebrated that the Beis HaMikdash would not be rebuilt, and Haman, repeating Amalek's mistake, thought sinning Jews were ownerless. The extra silver became the hooks outside the holy courtyard, matching the last eight pesukim of the Torah, pesukim of forgetting; Moshe forgot, but Hashem forgets no Jew. Purim is therefore the Yom Tov of the latecomers, the Adar Jews of the last generation. The Rav closes with a call to use Purim for tefillah, tzedakah beyond one's strength and acceptance of Torah.

en: The Torah's 600,000 letters correspond to 600,000 Jewish souls, and each Jew has his letter in the Sefer Torah.
Amalek, and later Haman, attacked on the assumption that sinning Jews are rejected and ownerless; the Rav says no Jew is ever rejected by Hashem.
The Jews in Shushan were punished for attending Achashverosh's feast because it celebrated the Beis HaMikdash not being rebuilt.
Purim is a Yom Tov for the nechshalim, the stragglers and latecomers at the edge of the camp.
Just as the year runs from Nisan to Adar, Jewish history does too, and the generation before Moshiach consists of Adar Jews.
The Rav urges using Purim for tefillah, for tzedakah beyond one's strength and for hearing the Megillah properly, not wasting it on drinking.

title.en: Haman's silver and the forgotten shekels

summary.en: The Rav brings Tosafos's calculation that Haman's ten thousand kikar matched the half-shekels, asks how that fits the hundred kikar in Parashas Pekudei, and explains that Haman's money was charity meant to neutralize the Jews' merit. He then describes how Moshe Rabbeinu forgot what he did with the extra 1,775 shekels until he was reminded.

title.en: Why Moshe forgot; 600,000 letters

summary.en: The Rav asks how Moshe Rabbeinu, who never forgot Torah, could forget. He explains that the half-shekels counted 600,000 Jews, matching the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah, so that one should see the letters at hagbah, and notes that the count came to a few thousand more than 600,000.

title.en: Amalek attacks the expelled Jews

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek attacked the Jews of Shevet Dan whom the clouds of glory had expelled, thinking Hashem had rejected them. He answers that every Jew is dear to Hashem, compares it to a parent who alone may discipline his child, and says these Jews will yet do teshuvah.

title.en: The sin of Achashverosh's feast

summary.en: The Rav describes the extravagance of Achashverosh's feast, where everything was kosher, and asks why the Jews were punished for attending. He explains with the Gemara that Achashverosh calculated the seventy years had passed, and the feast celebrated that the Beis HaMikdash would not be rebuilt, which touches on denying the geulah.

title.en: The extra silver outside the courtyard

summary.en: The Rav says Haman repeated Amalek's mistake, thinking sinning Jews were ownerless, and so paid only for 600,000. He then explains that all the silver went into the holy courtyard except the vavim, the hooks that protruded outside the hangings, and that this was the silver of the extra Jews who had been expelled from the camp.

title.en: The last eight pesukim: verses of forgetting

summary.en: The Rav explains that the last eight pesukim of the Torah stand outside the rest of it and speak of forgetting: Moshe's passing, when halachos were forgotten, and the breaking of the luchos. The extra souls belong to those pesukim, so Moshe forgot their silver, but Hashem, who forgets no Jew, reminded him; Haman made Amalek's mistake by not paying for them.

title.en: Purim, the Yom Tov of the latecomers

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Purim is a Yom Tov for the nechshalim, which is why those less careful rejoice most on it. He points to the Megillah's name 'Yehudim', written five times with an extra yud, and to the halachah that a Megillah with letters half rubbed out is still kosher, and explains with Onkelos that the nechshalim are the latecomers.

title.en: Nisan Jews and Adar Jews

summary.en: Bringing Sefer Yetzirah's teaching that the world was created in time, place and soul, the Rav explains that the months, like the letters, correspond to Jews: Nisan Jews who are zealous like those baking matzos, and Adar Jews who are last. Jewish history too runs from Nisan to Adar, and the generation before Moshiach are Adar Jews; Haman erred in thinking the Jewish year ends with Adar.

title.en: Our generation and the chizuk of Purim

summary.en: The Rav says his generation, as Adar Jews, feels Purim more than earlier ones, and that Parashas Zachor gives Jews simchah because Hashem loves them and fights for them. He points to the miracles in Eretz Yisrael, says one should know what is happening with fellow Jews as Moshe went out to his brothers, and calls Purim a source of chizuk for every Jew.

title.en: Don't waste Purim: tefillah and tzedakah

summary.en: The Rav calls Purim a time when tefillos are accepted and urges davening for Jews everywhere, not wasting the night on drinking. He urges tzedakah beyond one's strength, tells how the Satmar Rav had his congregation pledge a second round beyond their means, and compares Purim tzedakah to an esrog elevated on Sukkos.

title.en: The holiness of Purim and its seudah

summary.en: The Rav urges hearing every word of the Megillah and giving matanos la'evyonim, brings the Kedushas Levi that every bite of the Purim seudah should carry a kabbalah to keep the Torah, and the Chasam Sofer that the holiness of Megillas Esther exceeds that of the Torah. He closes by calling Purim a gift to use for oneself and for Klal Yisrael.

catalogTitle: יציאה ממ"ט שערי טומאה בימי ספירה ובכלל - בזמן הגלות. ביאור - אנא בכח; למנצח; לימוד מס' סוטה; משנה בסוף מס' סוטה - בעקבות משיחא חוצפא יסגא וכו'

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the 49 days of sefirah as a climb out of the 49 gates of impurity, mirrored in the desert journeys, in Ana Bekoach, in Lamenatzeach and in the 49 dafim of Masechta Sotah, whose closing mishnah on the footsteps of Moshiach he finds fulfilled in our own days.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the exodus: on the night of the Seder Hashem took the Jews out of the 49 gates of impurity as a free gift, and from the second day of Pesach they must earn it themselves, counting 49 days and refining the seven middos to reach the fiftieth day of Matan Torah. What each Jew does in sefirah, the whole people does in the desert and in galus: Parshas Masei lists 42 journeys, and with the seven they went back, as Rashi brings, there are 49. The same pattern of 42 plus seven appears in the 42-letter Name in Ana Bekoach and in Lamenatzeach. He then explains the custom of learning a daf of Sotah each day: the Jews were tested like a sotah, as the barley omer shows. The masechta ends with the mishnah on the footsteps of Moshiach, and he shows its signs today: chutzpah, rising prices, kingdoms turning to heresy, schools corrupted, the Galil in ruins, and the conclusion to rely only on our Father in Heaven.

en: On the Seder night the Jews were taken out of the 49 gates of impurity as a gift; from the second day of Pesach they must leave them by their own work, one gate each day of sefirah.
The 49 days of sefirah, the 49 journeys in the desert and the long galus are one path of 49 levels leading to the fiftieth: Matan Torah, Eretz Yisroel, the geulah.
The count of 49 is built as 42 plus seven: 42 journeys and seven retraced, 42 letters of the Name in Ana Bekoach and the line repeated at the end of each week.
Masechta Sotah, with its 49 dafim, belongs to sefirah: the Jews were tested like a sotah, which is why the omer, like the sotah's offering, is of barley, while on Shavuos the two loaves are of wheat.
The last daf of Sotah, reached on erev Shavuos, corresponds to malchus shebemalchus, the lowest level, and its mishnah describes the footsteps of Moshiach, the period the Rav says we are in now.

The Rav goes through the signs of the mishnah, chutzpah, high prices, kingdoms turning to heresy, places of study turned to immorality, the Galil destroyed and people wandering from city to city, and shows each one in the world of today.
