title.en: From a free gift to forty-nine days of work

summary.en: The Rav explains that on the Seder night Hashem took the Jews out of the 49 gates of impurity in one moment as a gift, and from the second day of Pesach they must leave them by their own work. Each day of sefirah a Jew refines one of the seven times seven middos, to reach the fiftieth day of Matan Torah and the root of the Avos.

title.en: Forty-nine journeys in the desert and in galus

summary.en: The Rav says what each Jew goes through in sefirah, the whole people goes through on a larger scale: the 49 journeys in the desert, each a place of impurity, and the long galus, where each period passes one journey until the geulah. He shows from Parshas Masei and Rashi that the 42 listed journeys are 49 with the seven the Jews went back.

title.en: Ana Bekoach and Lamenatzeach: 42 plus seven

summary.en: The Rav explains the 42-letter Name and the tefillah of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah built on it, and asks how its 42 letters fit the 49 days; the answer is that at the end of each week the whole line is said again. He shows the same count of 49 in Lamenatzeach and its middle passuk, and ties it all to the 49 stations of the desert, sefirah and galus.

title.en: A daf of Sotah each day of sefirah

summary.en: The Rav describes the custom of learning a daf of Masechta Sotah each day of sefirah, finishing on erev Shavuos, and gives the simple reason, to keep track of the count. He then explains the deeper link: the Jews were tested like a sotah, which is why the omer is of barley like the sotah's offering, and each daf brings them a day closer to Har Sinai.

title.en: The last daf: chutzpah and rising prices

summary.en: The Rav explains that the last daf of Sotah, learned on erev Shavuos, is malchus shebemalchus and opens with the footsteps of Moshiach, which the Chofetz Chaim already saw in his time. He illustrates the chutzpah of today from his own memories of respect for teachers, then explains the law of supply and demand to show how the mishnah's rising prices defy it.

title.en: The kingdom turns to heresy

summary.en: The Rav explains that minus means believing in nothing, and that even an idolater restrained himself out of belief; he tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov jumped off a wagon whose driver did not cross himself before a priest. He contrasts the old kings and early America with today's unbelief, then shows how the school buildings of Williamsburg illustrate the house of study turned to immorality.

title.en: The Galil, the wanderers, and our Father in Heaven

summary.en: The Rav shows the Galil emptied by rockets and the people of Eretz Yisroel going from city to city collecting to marry off their children, and concludes that everything in the mishnah is being fulfilled. Its last words teach that one can rely only on our Father in Heaven, and he calls on ehrliche Yidden to be the exceptions of the generation.

catalogTitle: ביאור הזוהר “בשבועות יפקון מגלותא;“ הלכות טהרה וקדושה בפרשיות הספירה; לימוד פרקי אבות - דרך ארץ קדמה לתורה

oneLiner.en: Starting from the tumah of a yoledes in parshas Tazria, the Rav shows how the days of Sefirah are counted days of purifying and refining one's midos, so as to be let into Yerushalayim and Har Sinai on Shavuos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the parsha of the yoledes and asks why a mother who brought a Jewish child into the world becomes tamei. Following the Ohr HaChaim's explanation of why a Jewish corpse defiles in an ohel, he explains that the holiness she carried has emptied out, and asks why a boy then brings less tumah than a girl. The answer is the bris: Eliyahu, who never ate from the Etz HaDaas, comes, and the tumah is cut short; this is why the verse of milah interrupts the passage. From there he turns to Sefirah as preparation for the fiftieth day, explains the Zohar that the redemption will come 'on Shavuos', and shows that the Sefirah parshiyos hold Rambam's Sefer Taharah and Sefer Kedushah. The counted days are too precious to be nullified. He closes with Pirkei Avos and derech eretz before Torah, Rabbi Akiva's students, and lashon hara, which drives a person out of Yerushalayim.

en: A yoledes becomes tamei because the great holiness she carried, a child learning the whole Torah with an angel, has emptied out of her.
At a bris, Eliyahu HaNavi comes and the tumah is cut short, which is why the verse of milah on the eighth day interrupts the laws of the yoledes.
The days of Sefirah prepare for the fiftieth day, a day of yovel, return and redemption; this is how the Rav reads the Zohar that the redemption will come on Shavuos.
The parshiyos read during Sefirah contain nearly all of Rambam's Sefer Taharah and Sefer Kedushah, because these are the weeks of becoming pure and holy.
The days of Sefirah are counted, a davar shebeminyan, and like any counted thing they are too precious ever to be nullified.
Good midos are a prerequisite for receiving the Torah, so in the weeks before Shavuos one learns Pirkei Avos and refines one's midos.
Lashon hara drove the Jews out of Yerushalayim, and today it keeps a person from reaching Yerushalayim in his tefillah and from the light of a blatt Gemara.

title.en: Why does a yoledes become tamei?

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening verses of Tazria and asks why a mother who brought a life into the world, and carried a child learning Torah with an angel, should become tamei. He also asks why the verse of milah on the eighth day appears in the middle of the laws of tumah.

title.en: The Ohr HaChaim: holiness that has emptied out

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim's parable of flies drawn to an emptied barrel of honey to explain why a Jewish corpse defiles in an ohel and a gentile's does not, and applies it to the yoledes. He then asks why a boy, whose holiness is greater, brings only seven days of tumah and a girl fourteen.

title.en: Closeness of family between souls

summary.en: The Rav explains that close family ties reflect a closeness between souls and create halachos, as with aveilus. He asks why the mother may wear Shabbos clothes at a bris on Tisha B'Av though she has no obligation in the milah, and answers that her closeness to the child brings her into its simcha.

title.en: Eliyahu at the bris cuts off tumah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Eliyahu never ate from the Etz HaDaas, so at a bris, a moment of the days of Moshiach, tumah is nullified. This answers why a boy brings less tumah and why the verse of milah interrupts the passage, and through the rule of lo plug it applies even when the milah is delayed.

title.en: The Zohar: redemption on Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav describes the days of Sefirah as preparation for the fiftieth day, the day of yovel. He brings the Zohar that the redemption will come on Shavuos, contrasts it with the Gemara's Nissan or Tishrei, and explains it through the distinction between 'b'itah' and 'achishena': Shavuos is a time especially suited for Moshiach.

title.en: Shavuos as the eighth day; Rambam's two books

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shavuos, the fiftieth day and the first of the eighth week, is like the eighth day on which a tamei person may immerse, and that the day itself is a mikveh. He then explains the name Yad HaChazakah and shows that two of its fourteen books, Sefer Taharah and Sefer Kedushah, are found in the Sefirah parshiyos.

title.en: Counted days of taharah and kedushah

summary.en: The Rav goes through the parshiyos from Shemini to Emor and shows the laws of tumah and taharah and of kedushah in each. He brings the Gerrer Rebbe that these are counted days, and explains through the halacha of davar shebeminyan that counted days are too precious to be nullified; in them a person can be entirely renewed.

title.en: Iyar, the month of ziv

summary.en: The Rav explains why Iyar is called the month of ziv: the fields blossom then because above, too, there is a radiance, the month the Beis HaMikdash was completed. A person is like a tree of the field, and through the mitzvah of Sefirah, which fills all of Iyar, he should blossom by purifying his seven midos.

title.en: Pirkei Avos: derech eretz before Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the original custom is to learn Pirkei Avos between Pesach and Shavuos because it deals with refining midos, derech eretz that precedes Torah. He brings Rabbi Chaim Vital that the Torah hardly speaks of midos because they are a prerequisite for learning it, and explains that Rabbi Akiva's students died in these weeks because midos are demanded more then.

title.en: Lashon hara and exile from Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that tzaraas comes from lashon hara and that the metzora is sent out of all of Yerushalayim, and that the whole galus, symbolized by Kamtza and bar Kamtza, came from sins between man and his fellow. Today such a person is barred from Yerushalayim in his Shemoneh Esrei and from the light of the Gemara; he closes that Sefirah must be counted with the aim of refining one's midos.

catalogTitle: לימוד מס' סוטה - בירור טהרת כלל ישראל. דף מ"ט כנגד זמננו עקבתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that learning Maseches Sotah during Sefirah testifies to the purity of Klal Yisrael, and that its last daf, with the baraisa of the heels of Moshiach, corresponds to our generation, whose task is emunah, strengthened above all through heartfelt tefillah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the custom of learning a daf of Sotah each day of Sefirah. Beyond keeping count, he explains, both the sotah's offering and the Omer are of barley, and both come to show that Klal Yisrael kept its sanctity. He then describes Klal Yisrael across the generations as the full form of Adam HaRishon: the generation of the desert was the head, which learned Torah, David HaMelech's era the heart, which sang and davened, and our generation the heel, the darkest and lowest, the forty-ninth level before the fiftieth. The forty-ninth daf of Sotah, with the baraisa of the heels of Moshiach, is our generation, and what remains is to rely on our Father in Heaven, that is, emunah. Emunah is cleansed through Torah for the head and tefillah for the heart. He closes with the place of tefillah, including a child's kvitel at the Kosel, as the work of these times.

en: Sotah is learned during Sefirah because the sotah's offering and the Omer are both barley, and both come to clarify the sanctity of Klal Yisrael.
The generations of Klal Yisrael together form the full stature of Adam HaRishon, from the head down to the heel.
Our generation is the heel of Moshiach, the forty-ninth and lowest level, which will suddenly be overturned into the head of all generations.
The last daf of Sotah, 49b, with the baraisa ending that we can rely only on our Father in Heaven, corresponds to our generation; its task is emunah.
Emunah is purified by cleansing the head with Torah and the heart with tefillah, and a person needs both.
Tefillah is itself emunah, since one speaks to Hashem and asks of Him; even a prayer for small things expresses faith that He can give.

Klal Yisrael as the form of Adam HaRishon

title.en: Why Sotah is learned during Sefirah

summary.en: The Rav brings the custom of learning one daf of Sotah's forty-nine each day of Sefirah, which keeps the count. The inner reason: the sotah's barley offering and the barley Omer both come to clarify the sanctity of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Klal Yisrael as the form of Adam HaRishon

summary.en: From the Midrash that all souls hang on the limbs of Adam HaRishon, the Rav explains that each Jew belongs to a limb: Torah scholars to the head, those whose avodah is tefillah to the heart, givers of tzedakah to the hands, and the lowest souls to the heel, which is always in darkness.

title.en: The generations from head to heel

summary.en: The Rav lays the generations along the body: the generation of the desert was the head, David HaMelech the heart, and our generation the heel. Like Adar turning into Nisan, the forty-ninth and lowest level will suddenly be overturned into the head of all generations.

title.en: Daf 49b: our generation and emunah

summary.en: The last daf of Sotah holds the baraisa of the heels of Moshiach, which describes our generation and ends that we can rely only on our Father in Heaven. The Rav explains that in a world full of heresy the task is emunah: Klal Yisrael began with Avraham's emunah and with Anochi at Sinai, and it ends with emunah.

title.en: The summit of Amanah and a child's emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that at the ingathering the Jews will stand on Mount Amanah and sing, meaning they will strengthen themselves in emunah. Every Jew, even a small child, has simple emunah, which can become sick and lose its appetite for holiness; he tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov as a melamed asked children whether they remembered standing at Sinai.

title.en: Cleansing the head with Torah, the heart with tefillah

summary.en: The Rav explains how one works on emunah: the head is cleansed with Torah and the heart with tefillah. In the time before Moshiach the main thing is tefillah, yet bochurim must invest in Torah; learning without davening and davening without learning are each worthless, as a person cannot live without a brain or a heart.

title.en: Tefillah is emunah: the kvitel at the Kosel

summary.en: The Rav speaks of pouring out the soul in tefillah, with tears, as David HaMelech and the authors of Yedid Nefesh and Shir HaShirim did, and says tefillah is the way toward Moshiach because it is emunah. He tells of a kvitel from the Kosel in which an Israeli boy asked Hashem for a dog and a bicycle, and explains that such a request too is emunah.

title.en: Tefillah stands at the height of the world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that tefillah stands at the height of the world yet people treat it lightly, and urges investing in davening. He stresses David HaMelech's Pesukei d'Zimra as the root of tefillah, tied to Moshiach through the word sichah, and closes with asking Hashem for understanding and attachment rather than a bicycle.

catalogTitle: A Day in which Sublime עולמות are Revealed

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Purim a sublime world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of all Jewish souls where no accuser can reach, is revealed, so that Hashem's unconditional love reaches even the most forgotten Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying Purim is misunderstood: Chazal and the Chasam Sofer place it above Pesach and Shavuos. Following the Noam Elimelech, he describes a world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of the souls, where the trace of holiness in every Jew can never be erased. The Jews at the 'end of the Sefer Torah', whom Moshe Rabbeinu forgot and Amalek and Haman thought were forgotten, are remembered there by Hashem. That world is revealed on Purim. The Megillah reveals Hashem's hidden love: He loves the generation of concealment most, like a king who visits his bride even in a tannery. Purim, like Yom Kippur, is decided by a lottery, the expression of a will beyond reason, and carries the holiness of Keser. The Megillah is a personal letter, unrolled without fear of accusers. Finally, Purim, like Yom Kippur, depends on the unity of all Jews, which is why Shushan keeps Purim with Yerushalayim.

en: The Rav says Purim is not a day of frivolity; it is higher than every other day of the Jewish calendar, even Pesach and Shavuos.
There is a world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of the Jewish souls, where no Jew is rejected and the Satan has no access, and it is revealed on Purim.
The Megillah reveals Hashem's love in a time of concealment: Hashem loves the generation of hastarah more than all others, even when it cannot see Him.
Purim and Yom Kippur are both decided by a lottery, which expresses Hashem's will that has no reason, and both draw from the level of Keser.
The Megillah is called an iggeres, a letter Hashem addresses personally to each Jew, especially those weak in Yiddishkeit.
Like Yom Kippur, Purim comes from the unity of all Jews, which is why Shushan, where the Jews gathered together, keeps Purim on the day Yerushalayim does.

candidateTopics: the lottery and the will beyond reason

title.en: Purim is higher than every other day

summary.en: The Rav opens by saying Purim is misunderstood as a day of frivolity, and brings the Chasam Sofer that it is greater than Pesach and Shavuos, and the Rambam that the Megillah will remain when other festivals are nullified. He then introduces, from the Noam Elimelech, a world called 'Kol Yisrael', connected to the Mishnah's 'all of Israel has a share'.

title.en: No Jew is lost at the root of Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the question what becomes of a sinner, answered by Hashem with teshuvah, and explains that in the deepest level of Torah no Jew is rejected and the trace of holiness is never erased. He describes the Avos as the trunk of the tree and the point of Yaakov in every Jew, and the 'forgotten' Jews at the end of the Sefer Torah, whom Moshe Rabbeinu forgot like the hooks of the pillars.

title.en: Amalek's mistake and the hidden bond

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek and Haman attacked the Jews on the fringes, thinking they were forgotten, but in the world of 'Kol Yisrael', revealed on Purim, every Jew is remembered and the Satan cannot reach. He discusses Achashverosh's feast celebrating that the Beis HaMikdash would not be rebuilt, and the Gemara's opening verse that Hashem never despises His people, and a Midrash reading Achashverosh as Hashem.

title.en: Megillas Esther reveals the concealment

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world of Purim never opened, not even on Pesach or Shavuos, until the Megillah, which reveals the hastarah (concealment) alluded to in 'haster astir'. He describes today's confusing concealment, how the Megillah is understood only at its end, and a sefer's teaching that one should tremble at the blessing 'al mikra Megillah', which calls down that world.

title.en: The King loves the generation of concealment

summary.en: The Rav reads 'the king loved Esther more than all the women' as Hashem's love for the generation of concealment, which thought it was forgotten. He explains the hidden vav of 'kalaso' as the hidden Groom, and the Zohar's parable of the king who visits his bride in a tannery: the Megillah tells that Hashem is bound to His people in every state.

title.en: Purim, Yom Kippur and the lottery

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Yom Kippurim, a day like Purim': on both days the main thing is a lottery. From the two identical goats of Yom Kippur and Rav Tzadok's teaching, he explains that Yaakov may look like Esav but Hashem knows he is His, and that a lottery, like a will that has no reason, shows Hashem's choice of His people is beyond explanation.

title.en: The crown of Keser and the personal letter

summary.en: The Rav explains the Kedushah of Keser said at Musaf on Shabbos and all day on Yom Kippur, and that, per the Arizal, a Jew has this holiness the whole day of Purim; he touches on the threefold Purim in Yerushalayim that year. He then explains why the Megillah is called an iggeres: a letter addressed personally to each Jew, like a letter to grandparents, sent especially to the weak, and he likens Purim to the crown on the yud.

title.en: Above the Name: an uncovered Megillah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'lifnei Hashem tit'haru' as a level above the Name Havayah, and that the Megillah, which lacks Hashem's Name, is wholly above it, like a person who is more than his name. He contrasts holy objects that are kept covered for fear of the Satan, such as matzah, the Sefer Torah and the shofar, with the Megillah, which is unfolded entirely because on Purim there is no accuser.

title.en: The unity of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that the essence of Purim, like Yom Kippur, is the world of 'Kol Yisrael' where all souls merge into one; Yom Kippur does not atone for one who is at odds with another Jew. Haman's accusation was that the Jews were scattered and divided, and Esther answered by gathering them together; he connects this to Yerushalayim, which joins all Jews together.

title.en: Shushan like Yerushalayim; blessings

summary.en: The Rav compares Purim's single shared feast and mishloach manos to an eruv uniting all Jews, and says Shushan merited to keep Purim with Yerushalayim because of that unity. He closes with blessings for a joyous Purim, notes a sefer that a year when Purim falls on Friday is a sign for the geulah, and mentions his plan to travel to Eretz Yisrael for the threefold Purim.

catalogTitle: תיקון המדות הנוגע למעשה - הוכחות מתנ"ך ומהלכה על חומר הענין

oneLiner.en: In the days of Sefirah the Rav gathers proofs from Tanach, Chazal and halachah that one must guard the honor of every person and every creature, and never shame anyone.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the students of Rabbi Akiva, who died in the days of Sefirah because they did not treat one another with respect, and explains that good middos are the vessel for receiving the Torah, so these weeks are the time to work on them. He announces that in the coming weeks he will speak about middos between man and his fellow, and he even rebukes his own community for weak middos. He then brings a long chain of proofs: Avraham's hospitality, Beis Hillel, Rachel, Yosef, Tamar, the punishment of Yaakov for Esav's cry, Boaz and Manoach, the stones of the mizbe'ach, the Etz HaDa'as, the soldiers who return from war, and the bird offered with its feathers. He compares Tamar to the wife of Potiphar and explains that shaming someone is worse than taking one's own life, illustrated with stories of the Bluzhever Rebbe. He ends with practical cases: different opinions, curses, children, Purim jokes and correcting the Torah reader.

en: Good middos are the vessel for Torah, so the Sefirah days before Shavuos are the time to repair them, and the students of Rabbi Akiva were punished then for lacking respect for one another.
Every creature was made by Hashem with wisdom, so one must respect and have mercy even on animals, plants and stones.
Shaming another person in public is so grave that Tamar preferred to be burned rather than shame Yehudah, and the Rav says it is worse than taking one's own life.
Tamar and the wife of Potiphar both acted for the sake of Heaven to bring Moshiach, and the difference between them was only good middos.
Just as faces differ, so do opinions, and one may not resent another person for thinking differently.
The Rav applies kavod habriyos to daily life: encouraging a weak answer or a small gift, not cursing any Jew, not embarrassing children or making jokes at another's expense.

title.en: Sefirah and the students of Rabbi Akiva

summary.en: The Rav asks why the students of Rabbi Akiva were punished specifically in Sefirah, and explains that these days are for preparing good middos, the vessel for receiving the Torah. He announces that in the coming weeks he will speak about improving middos between man and his fellow.

title.en: A hard word about the community's middos

summary.en: Saying it may give offense, the Rav states that his community in Boro Park and Flatbush is not distinguished for good middos, and attributes this to the inhuman conditions the young survivors of the camps had to live through. Since a Jew is good by nature, he expects this foreign trait to be rejected over time, and calls for a cheshbon hanefesh in these days.

title.en: Avraham, Beis Hillel and Rachel

summary.en: The Rav begins the proofs from Tanach and Chazal: the saying to be careful with a friend's honor, Avraham's hospitality right after his milah, Beis Hillel who always quoted Beis Shammai first, and Rachel who gave Leah the signs so she would not be shamed, in whose merit the children return.

title.en: Yosef, Tomer Devorah and respect for every creature

summary.en: The Rav shows how Yosef sent everyone out so his brothers would not be shamed, brings the Tomer Devorah that one must respect every creature since Hashem made it with wisdom, and the Gemara that Rebbi's suffering ended through his mercy on small animals. He adds that shaming someone in public costs one's share in the World to Come, and that one who causes pain must ask forgiveness even after paying.

title.en: Esav's cry and Boaz's sixty children

summary.en: The Rav explains that even Yaakov, who caused Esav to cry out, remained in debt until the cry of Mordechai generations later, and brings the Zohar about Esav's tears. He then tells the Gemara that Boaz lost his sixty children because he never invited the childless Manoach to his weddings.

title.en: Honor even for a stone, a tree and a sinner

summary.en: The Rav brings that the Torah guards the honor of the mizbe'ach's stones with a ramp, hides which tree was the Etz HaDa'as so it should not be shamed, sends home all exempt soldiers to cover for the sinner, killed Bilam's donkey for Bilam's honor, and lowers the thief's payment when he carried a sheep. From here he argues one must not jump to accuse and shame people.

title.en: The plague that hides, and the chol bird

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a plague which takes mamzerim takes others with them so no family is singled out, and the Midrash that the chol bird in Noach's ark did not ask for food so as not to burden Noach, and was blessed to live forever. He notes that a bird's good nature is a lesson for people.

title.en: Tamar and the wife of Potiphar: two Moshiachs

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the story of Tamar is placed next to that of Potiphar's wife because both acted for the sake of Heaven, and explains that the two parshiyos speak of the two Moshiachs, ben David from Yehudah and Tamar and ben Yosef from Yosef. He describes how Tamar, knowing Moshiach would come from her, still would not name Yehudah when taken to be burned.

title.en: Potiphar's wife, Osnas and Shaul

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Potiphar's wife, who also meant to bring Moshiach but had Yosef thrown into prison when he refused, with Tamar, and concludes that the difference was good middos; she merited nothing, as Osnas was only her adopted daughter, the daughter of Dinah. He adds that Shaul merited kingship because he spoke of his servant as an equal.

title.en: Worse than taking one's own life

summary.en: The Rav explains why one who takes his own life loses his share in the World to Come: death itself atones for a person, but here the death is the sin. Even so, he concludes, Tamar chose to be burned rather than shame Yehudah, so shaming another in public is graver still.

title.en: Two stories of the Bluzhever Rebbe

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Bluzhever Rebbe, who told the king's doctor that six days before Matan Torah a Jewish heart cannot beat normally, and of the responsum of his grandfather, the Tzvi LaTzaddik, forbidding even passive self-destruction, which later saved the Rebbe in the camps when he decided to eat his bread.

title.en: The poor man's bird with its feathers

summary.en: The Rav asks why a bird offering is burned with its feathers despite their foul smell, and brings Chazal that it is so the mizbe'ach be adorned with the poor man's korban. He applies this to a small gift at a simcha and to a simple answer in learning, which one must welcome and praise.

title.en: Different faces, different minds

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that as faces differ so do opinions, explains with the Midrash of the coins that every person is a different stamp of the image of G-d, and that the face shows what is inside a person, citing the wisdom of reading faces in the Zohar on Yisro. He concludes that one cannot hold it against another that he thinks differently.

title.en: The housewife and the cat; the Kohen's brachah

summary.en: The Rav tells how Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan compared himself and his Zionist secretary to a housewife and a cat: both want no mice, but only the cat enjoys finding them. He then brings the Imrei Emes' answer why a Kohen does not bless 'who did not make me a Yisrael': it would be gaining honor through another's shame.

title.en: Seeing the good, and never cursing a Jew

summary.en: The Rav shows that the Torah first mentions the pig's kosher sign before its flaw, that Chazal instituted silent prayer so sinners would not be shamed, and brings the story in Chovos HaLevavos of the chassid who saw a carcass's white teeth. He warns never to curse or speak badly of a Jew except for the sake of Heaven, proves from yibum that one may not say 'may his name be erased' even of an apostate, and cites the Satmar Rav who said he never cursed a Jew.

title.en: Children, Purim jokes and the Torah reader

summary.en: The Rav warns against quizzing other people's children to embarrass them and against Purim jokes at another's expense, explains that one corrects a Torah reader only for a mistake that changes the meaning, notes the custom of singing during a chasan's drashah, and closes with the Chofetz Chaim, who had gebrokts served for a guest so as not to offend him.

catalogTitle: תיקון המדות הנוגע למעשה - דוגמאות וסיפורים

oneLiner.en: Through many examples and stories of gedolim, the Rav shows how careful one must be with another person's feelings and dignity, and ties the low state of middos to churban, past and present.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the churban that came through sinas chinam, and with the Maharal's reading that Kamtza, who did nothing, was blamed as the friend of the one who made the machlokes. From the passuk that Hashem judges 'every hidden thing' he moves to hidden wrongs between people: disgusting habits in front of others, staring at a blemish, embarrassing questions, unclear letters, names that shame a child. A nisayon can come at any moment, as in the story of R' Yosef tested by a poor guest. He shows how halachah itself avoids shaming the poor and the unlearned, and tells many stories of the Chasam Sofer, R' Akiva Eiger, R' Yisrael Salanter, R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and others. He says great rabbanim attributed the churban in Europe to low middos, warns of the danger facing Klal Yisrael today, and calls for teshuvah as Shavuos approaches.

en: Every punishment reveals its sin: the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed through sinas chinam, and even the friend of a baal machlokes shares the blame.
Hashem judges even 'hidden' wrongs that people do not count as sins, such as behaving disgustingly in front of others or causing someone embarrassment.
What distinguishes an eved Hashem is not the big mitzvos everyone keeps but a hundred small things, above all in how he treats people.
Halachah and Jewish custom were built to avoid shaming those who have less, as with the wood for a tamei korban Pesach, the baal korei and the borrowed clothes of Tu B'Av.
Heaven is exacting about the feelings of others: the stories of Levi, R' Mordechai Banet and the soul that came to R' Moshe of Savran show punishment for causing distress or shame.
The Rav reports hearing from great rabbanim that the churban in Europe came because middos had fallen so low, and he warns of the danger facing Klal Yisrael today.
With Shavuos approaching, he calls for teshuvah and for accepting the yoke of Torah, mitzvos and fear of Heaven, turning only to the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Sinas chinam and the friend of Bar Kamtza

summary.en: The Rav explains that every punishment reveals the sin behind it, so the churban shows it came from sinas chinam. He asks why the Gemara blames Kamtza, who did nothing, and brings the Maharal: Kamtza was the friend of the man who made the machlokes.

title.en: Hidden wrongs between people

summary.en: From the passuk that Hashem judges every hidden thing, the Rav lists wrongs people do not see as sins: disgusting habits in front of others, staring at a blemish, asking one's rebbi an unprepared question in public, and writing letters and addresses unclearly.

title.en: Names that shame a child; the Bas Ayin's Hadas

summary.en: The Rav warns against giving a child a name he will be ashamed of among his friends, and tells of the Bas Ayin in Tzfas who insisted a girl be named Hadas rather than Hadassah, which seventeen years later made her shidduch possible.

title.en: Small things make the eved Hashem

summary.en: The Rav speaks of davening a long Shemoneh Esrei where one does not block others, of listening attentively when someone speaks, and says the eved Hashem is recognized in a hundred small things. He brings R' Sholom of Belz on the 'frummer' and says a person can be tested at any moment, even while leading his child to the chuppah.

title.en: R' Yosef and the hungry guest

summary.en: The Rav tells of R' Yosef, a tzaddik who took in the guests nobody wanted, who was tested by the Satan disguised as a starving poor man, and passed. He adds the story of Dovid HaMelech and Nasan HaNavi: a person never knows when his test comes.

title.en: Doing a favor completely

summary.en: The Rav says a person with good middos marks his house number clearly and says a phone number slowly. He tells of a young Belzer Rebbe who as a child told the exact time, and of R' Elchonon Wasserman, who asked a driver to take him all the way to the house: a chessed should be done completely.

title.en: Halachah that protects the poor from shame

summary.en: The Rav says the Shechinah stands with the poor man, and shows from a tamei korban Pesach burned with Mikdash wood, from the baal korei, from singing at a hakafah of yichus, and from the borrowed clothes of Tu B'Av that Chazal built practices to avoid shaming. He gives the rule of 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your friend'.

title.en: Appeasing, private tzedakah, and Levi

summary.en: The Rav says one who shamed a friend must appease him, even by letter, and that tzedakah to a person of good family should be given privately. He brings the Gemara that Levi was kept outside the heavenly beis medrash for not attending R' Afes's shiurim and causing him distress.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's delayed teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav tells the story behind a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer about reburying R' Mordechai Banet in Nikolsburg. The answer was held back six months because R' Mordechai Banet appeared in a dream: he had to remain buried there for six months, for not defending a girl who was shamed by a broken shidduch.

title.en: A sharp bochur and a soul seeking tikkun

summary.en: Through R' Shlomo Bloch the Rav tells of a great rosh yeshiva whose children died, because as a bochur he had shamed a visiting rav in public. Then he tells of a soul that came to R' Moshe of Savran: it had repented for everything except shaming a chassan who erred in Tehillim before his father-in-law.

title.en: R' Akiva Eiger guards others' honor

summary.en: The Rav tells three stories of R' Akiva Eiger: he kept silent at shared sheva brachos so as not to outshine another chassan, spilled his own wine at the Seder when a guest spilled his, and left a kushya of R' Mordechai Banet unanswered in public so as not to embarrass the town's rav. He then warns young people against nicknames.

title.en: R' Yisrael Salanter and the shamed shoemaker

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Yisrael Salanter gave up a rosh yeshiva position rather than overshadow the other rosh yeshiva, and how he said the rabbanim of Vilna would be held accountable when a rich man shamed a shoemaker at his daughter's chuppah. He then says he heard from great rabbanim that the churban in Europe came because middos had sunk so low.

title.en: The Imrei Emes' warning and today's danger

summary.en: The Rav brings the Imrei Emes' drashah at the Knessia Gedolah on 'Vayischazeik Dovid', understood only after the churban of Hitler, and the Gemara that the world trembled until the Torah was given. He describes the danger to Eretz Yisrael today and tells how his father-in-law's kehillah in Vienna argued over petty matters while Hitler threatened.

title.en: Not relying on America; teshuvah before Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav says Jews cannot rely on America, now that it no longer needs Israel against Russia, and warns that rising racism and antisemitism resemble how things began in Germany. The only answer is teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah; Sivan is a time of teshuvah, as Klal Yisrael came to Sinai in teshuvah, and one must accept the yoke of Torah.

title.en: R' Yisrael Salanter: the maid and his last night

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Yisrael Salanter agreed to eat at a wealthy host only if the Shabbos meal took an hour and a half, to spare the tired widow who served. Then he tells of his last night, when he spent his final moments calming his roommate's fear of being alone with a dead body.

title.en: A kept secret and a kerosene cholent

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Yitzchak Elchanan refused even a hundred rubles to reveal who a collection was for, and the donor then confided that he too had lost his fortune. Then R' Avigdor Halberstam, brother of the Divrei Chaim, ate a whole pot of cholent cooked with kerosene so the hostess would not be shamed.

title.en: R' Shmuel Salant, the shofar, and the brazen

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Shmuel Salant rebuked students who laughed at an old woman's question, and how he told a baal tokea that he failed because he felt pride at another's failure. He tells of the Chofetz Chaim expelling a bochur who was insolent to his host, explaining from the Mishnah that the brazen never do teshuvah, and of the Satmar Rav expelling a bochur who refused to collect money.

title.en: R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's sensitivity

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld spared the Lubliner Rav's feelings when visitors came only to him, gave the Mussaf to the late chazzan's son to comfort the widow, and asked to return to the Old City before his passing so the people carrying him would not have far to go.

catalogTitle: תיקון המדות הנוגע למעשה - ספורי צדיקים

oneLiner.en: Through practical examples and many stories of tzaddikim, the Rav teaches that refined middos mean constant chesed in small things and taking great care never to embarrass or pain another Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with everyday chesed: writing clearly, putting a visible address on a house so Hatzalah can find it, giving a phone number slowly, and not pushing into a line, which can cause a chillul Hashem. Doing chesed, he says, draws chesed onto oneself. He then shows how Jewish customs are built on not shaming those who cannot: singing during a chasan's drasha, the baal korei reading for everyone, the mesader kiddushin saying the brachah, and the daughters of Yerushalayim borrowing garments. A long chain of stories follows: R' Nachum of Chernobyl and the spoon, R' Levi Yitzchak's matzah takanah, R' Mordechai Benet's punishment for a shamed kallah, R' Akiva Eiger, R' Yisrael Salanter and the cook, the Chofetz Chaim, R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, R' Chaim Ozer and the Satmar Rav. In each, a tzaddik goes out of his way to spare another person's feelings.

en: Small courtesies, like a clear address or a phone number said slowly, are real chesed, and through them a person draws Hashem's chesed onto himself.
Many minhagim, such as singing during the chasan's drasha and the baal korei reading for everyone, exist so as not to shame those who cannot.
Heaven is exacting with tzaddikim even over causing shame indirectly, as R' Mordechai Benet's burial away from Nikolsburg showed.
A person must be farginen, glad for another's success, and lacking this is a deep flaw in middos.
The Chofetz Chaim requires one who spoke lashon hara to appease the victim, but R' Yisrael Salanter held that one should not do so if telling him would cause him pain.
A tzaddik who is used to thinking of another's feelings finds, in the moment, a way to spare him shame or trouble, even at a cost to himself.

title.en: Chesed in everyday small things

summary.en: The Rav lists small acts of chesed: writing legibly, a clear house address so Hatzalah can find it, not pushing into a line, which can make a chillul Hashem, and saying a phone number slowly. He concludes that doing chesed draws chesed onto oneself.

title.en: Minhagim built on not shaming others

summary.en: The Rav explains that singing during the chasan's drasha, the baal korei reading for everyone, and the mesader kiddushin saying the brachah all exist so as not to shame those who cannot. He brings the daughters of Yerushalayim borrowing garments and the bikkurim baskets, and applies it to not making an extravagant wedding.

title.en: R' Nachum of Chernobyl and R' Levi Yitzchak

summary.en: The Rav tells how R' Nachum of Chernobyl said he gave a poor man the silver spoon he took, and then gave him more for the shame he suffered. Then R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, asked for stricter matzah takanos, ruled that one may not knead Jewish blood into the matzos by pressuring the poor women who bake them.

title.en: R' Mordechai Benet and the shamed kallah

summary.en: R' Mordechai Benet died away from Nikolsburg, and the Chasam Sofer delayed his ruling on reburial for six months after R' Mordechai appeared in a dream: he had ruled correctly that a shidduch could be broken, yet a kallah was shamed, and his punishment was to lie beside her. The Rav adds the mashal of an ink stain on a sack versus a silk shirt: tzaddikim are judged to a hairsbreadth.

title.en: R' Akiva Eiger's sensitivity

summary.en: At his Seder, R' Akiva Eiger spilled his own wine after a guest spilled his, saying the table was crooked. When he could not answer R' Mordechai Benet's kushya at a drasha, he later gave the answer privately, explaining he would not shame the rav of the city; R' Mordechai Benet then publicly repeated the answer the next day.

title.en: Nicknames, a shamed shoemaker, and farginen

summary.en: The Rav warns against nicknames and tells of a former shoemaker in Vilna shamed on the way to his son's chuppah, after which R' Yisrael Salanter said the earlier rabbanim of Vilna were judged for not teaching mussar. He stresses farginen, citing Aharon's joy at Moshe's mission and the moon's flaw.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim and appeasing after lashon hara

summary.en: The Rav describes the impact of the sefer Chofetz Chaim, the Gerrer Rebbe's letter urging Chassidim to learn it, and how it healed the rift between Chassidim and Misnagdim. He brings the Chofetz Chaim's ruling that one must appease the person spoken against, and R' Yisrael Salanter's disagreement: telling him would only cause him pain.

title.en: R' Yisrael Salanter and the widowed cook

summary.en: R' Yisrael Salanter agreed to eat at a rich man's Shabbos meal only if it lasted two hours. Afterwards he called in the cook, a widow, who told how the long meals exhausted her, showing the host why he had asked to hurry.

title.en: Chesed until the last moment

summary.en: The Rav tells of a great chassid who held a separate Friday night table for taxi drivers, of a rebbetzin carrying food to poor families, and of a tzaddik who on his last night calmed his roommate's fear of the dead, so that he would not be frightened when he passed away beside him.

title.en: R' Yitzchak Elchanan and the Dukla Rav

summary.en: A rav arriving in Brisk refused to sit until the delegations of tailors and shoemakers were invited. R' Yitzchak Elchanan refused to reveal for whom he was collecting even when a donor offered more, and the donor turned out to be the impoverished man himself. The Dukla Rav ate an entire cholent spoiled with kerosene so the maid would not be shouted at.

title.en: Not mocking, and the brazen bochur

summary.en: R' Yisrael Salanter answered a simple woman's question about a cat seriously and rebuked his laughing students. The Rav tells of two bochurim: one who sinned was kept in the yeshiva, while one who insulted the woman who fed him was sent away, explained by 'az panim l'Gehinom', since a brazen person does not do teshuvah. He adds the Satmar Rav's guidance and his emphasis on tzedakah.

title.en: R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's consideration

summary.en: R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld let the son of a deceased baal mussaf lead the Yamim Noraim prayers so his widowed mother would be comforted. When old and ill, he asked to return to the cramped Old City so that the people carrying his coffin would not have far to walk.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim at the window; R' Moshe Kliers' eruv

summary.en: R' Meir Dan Plotzki persuaded the Chofetz Chaim to show himself at a train window so the crowd would have pleasure. R' Moshe Kliers learned a sugya with the Sephardi chacham whose eruv was questioned, and when the chacham realized his error, reassured him that for kavod habriyos and kavod chachamim one could rely on the eruv. The Rav notes that many do not make this calculation.

title.en: R' Chaim Ozer, the seforim seller, and the Satmar Rav

summary.en: R' Chaim Ozer chose the plainer apartment so the maid would not walk far from kitchen to table. A tzaddik bargained over a sefer so the seller would not regret his price, and the Satmar Rav gave a man $9,500 rather than the $10,000 he asked, for the same reason. The Rav closes on doing chesed so the other does not feel it.

catalogTitle: The Message of the "אגרת הפורים": Hashem is Near to You!

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Purim heaven comes down to earth, so the Megillah is a personal letter from Hashem to every Jew, and its mitzvos, above all tzedakah and the seudah, open doors that stay closed the rest of the year.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying Purim is beyond understanding, as the Gemara's 'ad d'lo yada' hints. Following the Maharal, he explains the haste in the Megillah: the miracle comes from heaven, where there is no time, and pushes time aside. Purim is therefore like Shabbos, a taste of the world to come, and Klal Yisrael accepted the Torah then with love. He describes three days of preparation before Purim and the idea that Hashem is a person's shadow. He shows hidden names of Hashem in the Megillah, spelled for din or for chesed, then explains why the Megillah is called an iggeres: a personal letter, sweet only to the one it is addressed to. The four mitzvos of Purim correspond to the four letters of Hashem's name; tzedakah on Purim lights up far higher worlds. He ends with the joy of the seudah as a day of reconciliation, and two stories showing what Purim accomplishes.

en: The miracle of Purim comes from heaven, where there is no time, so on its way down it pushes time aside; this is why everything in the Megillah happens in a hurry.
On Purim heaven comes down to earth; it is a taste of the eternal Shabbos, which is why Shabbos clothes are worn on Purim though it is a weekday.
The Megillah is called an iggeres because it is a personal letter: sweet and meaningful only to one who has a bond with Hashem.
The four mitzvos of Purim correspond to the four letters of Hashem's name, which Amalek keeps from being complete.
Tzedakah on Purim is like pressing the master switch: the same act lights up far higher worlds than tzedakah during the year.
Just as on Purim tzedakah is given to whoever stretches out a hand, Hashem gives on Purim to whoever turns to Him, even the undeserving.
The Purim seudah is a feast of reconciliation with Hashem, like Yom Kippur, and should be eaten alert and aware of its purpose.

hidden names of Hashem in the Megillah

title.en: Purim above time: heaven comes down

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'ad d'lo yada' and, following the Maharal, explains why everything in the Megillah happens in haste: the miracle comes from heaven, where there is no time. On Purim heaven comes down to earth, a preview of the eternal Shabbos.

title.en: Shabbos clothes and three days of preparation

summary.en: The Rav explains why Shabbos clothes are worn on Purim, brings that the Torah was accepted with love on Purim and the Chasam Sofer on the light of the Megillah, and describes the days before Purim as days of preparation. Since Hashem is a person's shadow, one prepares with kedushah to receive His gifts.

title.en: Hidden names of Hashem in the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav shows three places where Hashem's name is hidden in the first or last letters of words: Haman draws down din with letters spelled backwards at word ends, Esther answers with chesed in letters spelled straight at word beginnings, and in Haman's downfall din comes mixed with chesed.

title.en: The Megillah as a personal letter

summary.en: The Rav brings an explanation from a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov of why the Megillah is called an iggeres, with the parable of a family letter full of small talk that is precious to the parents and meaningless to a stranger. So the Megillah is sweet to one bound to Hashem, and every word should be heard.

title.en: Four mitzvos and the four letters of Hashem's name

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek keeps Hashem's name incomplete and that the four mitzvos of Purim correspond to its four letters; completing them perfectly would bring the geulah. He urges learning the Megillah beforehand from holy sources and preparing much money for tzedakah.

title.en: Tzedakah on Purim: the master switch

summary.en: The Rav explains that tzedakah forms Hashem's name through the coin, the hand, the arm and the receiver, and that on Purim it carries an added mitzvah. With a parable of two identical switches, one lighting a room and one a whole tower, he shows that Purim tzedakah reaches far higher worlds.

title.en: The seudah: reconciliation like Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Rav explains the joy of the seudah through 'kimu v'kiblu': Purim is like Yom Kippur, a day of making up with Hashem, as in the old Purim song about reconciling. The sins that insulate a person from Hashem are removed, and every word of the Megillah creates a malach.

title.en: Whoever stretches out a hand: doors open on Purim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Purim tzedakah is given without checking who asks, and so Hashem gives on Purim to whoever turns to Him in emunah. Purim opens doors closed all year, as the Gemara's opening 'pischa' and Mordechai's name Pesachyah hint, and even neshamos are helped then.

title.en: The Spinka Rebbe and the heavenly chamber

summary.en: The Rav tells the Spinka Rebbe's story of a young man who read the Megillah on the second night of Pesach, and a neshamah that came to ask him to rule whether this made it Purim, so that a heavenly chamber open only on Purim would let it in. He concludes that Purim can do what even the Seder cannot.

title.en: A seudah by day, and the dike of Amsterdam

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara that a Purim seudah eaten at night does not count as a call to eat it with the brightness of day, and tells how Rabbi Lazar of Amsterdam saved the city from a leaking dike by feasting on Purim. He closes with the importance of hearing Parshas Zachor on the coming Shabbos.

catalogTitle: ביאור על פי פשט בעשר ספירות

oneLiner.en: In the days of sefirah, when the midos are to be refined, the Rav explains the ten sefiros in simple terms as the ten utterances of creation and the seven midos every person carries.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that the days of sefirah are the time to refine one's midos, and that the Tanya, unlike seforim on the parsha, explains matters step by step. He identifies the ten utterances with which the world was created with the ten sefiros, a key to much in Chassidic seforim. He divides them into the upper three and the seven lower ones, and explains that time itself is a creation, so the Torah's preceding the world by two thousand years means two levels above chesed. He then explains each midah: chesed as giving, gevurah as withdrawal, tiferes as a beautiful blend like a picture of many colors, netzach and hod as winning and yielding, yesod as guarding the bris, and malchus as accepting Heaven's rule. He ties the weeks of sefirah to the midos, explains chochmah and binah, and closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov on misused chesed.

en: The Rav says the days of sefirah are the time to refine the midos, and the Tanya explains them in an orderly way, from the easy matters upward.
The ten utterances of creation are the ten sefiros: three upper ones above the world, and seven lower ones that are the midos a person has.
Chesed is giving out of oneself, gevurah is pulling back into oneself, and tiferes is the blend of the two, as in Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov.
Netzach and hod give a person a firm existence, one by winning and the other by yielding; yesod is guarding the bris, and malchus is accepting the rule of Heaven.
Each week of sefirah refines one midah, and since every midah contains all the others, each day is a different combination.
Above the seven midos are the mochin: chochmah is acquiring knowledge, and binah is building one idea on another to reach a new understanding.

title.en: Sefirah, the Tanya, and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Rav says the days of sefirah are for refining the midos and explains why he learns Tanya: its advice in avodas Hashem, and its orderly explanation of matters rather than drush on the parsha. He then states that the ten utterances of creation are called the ten sefiros, a key to much in Chassidic seforim.

title.en: Three upper sefiros, seven midos, and time

summary.en: The Rav divides the sefiros into the upper three and the seven lower ones that parallel the seven days of creation, and names them all. He asks how the Torah could precede the world by two thousand years when there was no time before creation, and answers that time itself was created, so the 'years' are levels above chesed.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and tiferes

summary.en: The Rav explains chesed as giving out of oneself, gevurah as its opposite, holding back into oneself, and tiferes as a blend of the two, matching Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov. He illustrates tiferes with the colors of the midos, white and red making pink, and a picture whose beauty comes from the harmony of many colors.

title.en: Netzach, hod and yesod

summary.en: The Rav explains netzach as winning over another, with a mashal of a man with a stick who overcomes a dog, and hod as bowing and yielding; both give a person a lasting existence. He then explains that yesod is connected to the bris kodesh and is called foundation because guarding it is the foundation of Yiddishkeit.

title.en: Malchus, and midos before Torah

summary.en: The Rav describes malchus as awe and accepting the yoke of Heaven, and speaks of serving Hashem with love and with fear, and of tzaddikim who served with netzach or with yesod. He explains that after leaving Mitzrayim one must refine the midos in order to merit receiving the Torah.

title.en: The weeks of sefirah and their midos

summary.en: The Rav goes through the weeks of sefirah: the first week repairs chesed, love that has been turned to bad things; the second repairs gevurah, whose holy form is fear of Hashem; and so on to malchus. He explains that each midah contains all the others, chesed shebechesed, gevurah shebechesed and so on, and applies it to the days of the current week.

title.en: The mochin, and chesed misused

summary.en: The Rav links the seven midos to the limbs of the body and to Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef and Dovid, then explains the mochin above them: chochmah as learning knowledge, binah as building on it to make a chiddush, and da'as. He closes with the passuk in Kedoshim calling a forbidden relationship 'chesed' and the Ba'al Shem Tov's explanation, concluding that the midos must be refined.

catalogTitle: צירוף החודש - יתהלל המתהלל השכל ויודע - לימוד תורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the letter combination of the month of Iyar, drawn from the passuk 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a', marks Iyar as the month of Torah, and calls for strengthening in learning, davening and counting Sefirah, ending with Rosh Chodesh as the day of Dovid HaMelech.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Bnei Yissaschar that each month has its own combination of the letters of Hashem's Name, to be borne in mind at Mussaf of Rosh Chodesh. Nisan's is the straight order; Iyar's, from the initials of 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a' in Yirmiyahu, reverses the second half and carries some din. Knowing Hashem means seeing Him filling every place, and more inwardly, understanding Torah, which is G-dliness itself. He tells the bochurim that kavanos are not for everyone, then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the mann began falling in Iyar and Miriam's well came, with the Arizal giving Rav Chaim Vital its water to drink: Iyar is the month of Torah. The days of Sefirah judge a person more than Tishrei and are days of cleansing; the week of Tiferes is Torah. He closes with the two simanim in Shulchan Aruch on the Rosh Chodesh meal and melaveh malkah, both tied to Dovid HaMelech.

en: Each month has its own combination of the letters of Hashem's Name; Iyar's comes from the initials of 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a' and has the hei before the vav, a touch of din.
Knowing Hashem means recognizing that He fills and surrounds every place, and more inwardly, understanding Torah, which is G-dliness itself.
Iyar is the month of Torah: the mann began to fall in it and Miriam's well came then, and Chazal say the Torah was given only to those who ate the mann.
The days of Sefirah leave a deeper mark on a Jew than Tishrei; they are judgment with chesed and days of cleansing the seven middos.
The Rosh Chodesh meal and melaveh malkah each have a siman in Shulchan Aruch, and both belong to Dovid HaMelech.

title.en: The letter combination of Iyar

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that each month has its own combination of Hashem's Name, and shows that Iyar's comes from 'yishallel hamishallel haskel veyado'a'. He explains knowing Hashem as seeing Him in all of creation and, more inwardly, as understanding Torah.

title.en: Kavanos, the mann and Miriam's well

summary.en: The Rav tells the bochurim that kavanos are not for everyone and that one should daven with the meaning of the words. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Iyar is the month of Torah because the mann fell and Miriam's well came in it, with the Arizal and Rav Chaim Vital at the Kinneret, and ties Iyar to chochmah and the tefillin of Rabbeinu Tam.

title.en: The days of Sefirah and the week of Tiferes

summary.en: The Rav calls for strengthening in Torah as the new zman begins in Iyar, and brings Rav Pinchas of Koretz that the days of Sefirah judge a person more than Tishrei, with din tempered by chesed. He explains the week of Tiferes as Torah and Yaakov Avinu, and urges counting Sefirah with a minyan and with fervor.

title.en: Rosh Chodesh and melaveh malkah, the day of Dovid

summary.en: The Rav notes two simanim in Shulchan Aruch, on the Rosh Chodesh meal and on melaveh malkah, and explains that both belong to Dovid HaMelech: the three Shabbos meals match the three tefillos of the Avos, and melaveh malkah matches tikkun chatzos. Rosh Chodesh, the renewal of the moon, is Dovid's day and a sign of the redemption, and he ends with a l'chaim and a wish for Torah.

catalogTitle: פורים Reveals the Essence of the אידישע נשמה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Purim reveals the innermost root of every Jewish soul, where even the lowest Jew wants Hashem's will and remains beloved, which is why Purim stands higher than Yom Kippur.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by rejecting the view of Purim as a carnival and cites the Chasam Sofer and Rav Tzadok HaKohen that its holiness surpasses even Yom Kippur. Since each sedra shapes its week, illustrated by stories of the Rebbe of Belz and of the Ba'al HaTanya with the Maggid, he turns to the lechem hapanim in the first sedra of Adar. With the Noam Elimelech he describes Knesses Yisrael, the root where all souls are one and no sin reaches. The Rambam's explanation of coerced consent shows that every Jew inwardly wants Hashem's will; this root, 'reishis', is above letters and thought. Yom Kippur reaches it after ten days, Purim reveals it even in the lowest. Shevet Dan, Adar and the stale-bread taunt of the mekalel and Haman show the claim that low Jews are discarded, refuted by the ever-fresh lechem hapanim. Purim is Hashem's love for the lowest Jew.

en: Purim is not a Jewish carnival; its holiness is greater than Yom Kippur.
Every sedra is the fabric of its week, and the first sedra of Adar contains the passuk of the lechem hapanim.
All Jewish souls are rooted in Knesses Yisrael, a level where they are one soul and no sin can enter.
In his innermost self every Jew wants to do Hashem's will; the yetzer hara only covers it, as the Rambam explains.
Even the lowest Jews, like Shevet Dan at the end of the camp, are rooted in 'reishis', and Haman's claim that they were cast off was false.
The lechem hapanim, which stayed fresh all week, shows that no Jew becomes stale before Hashem; it corresponds to Purim.
Purim is the day Hashem shows His love to every Jew, even the lowest, which is why the less observant are often the happiest on Purim.

title.en: Purim higher than Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Rav sets aside the regular shiur to speak about Purim, rejecting the view of it as a 'Jewish Halloween'. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the holiness of the Megillah is higher than Toras Moshe, and Rav Tzadok HaKohen that Purim is far greater than Yom Kippur.

title.en: The sedra shapes the week

summary.en: The Rav explains that the weekly sedra is the fabric of the week. He tells of lumber merchants whose river stayed frozen because the children learned Miketz, and of the Ba'al HaTanya, who became the Maggid's ba'al korei because he knew the sedra's bond with each week, day and person called up.

title.en: Lechem hapanim and Knesses Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav notes the passuk of the lechem hapanim in the first sedra of Adar. He brings the Noam Elimelech that there is a world called Knesses Yisrael where all Jewish souls are fused into one and no sin or accusation enters, and identifies it with the yechidah, the innermost level of the soul, where no Jew wants to sin.

title.en: Retzon Hashem, reishis, and Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Rav explains the Rambam on coercing a Jew until he says 'I want': inwardly every Jew wants Hashem's will. He brings the Maggid that the maamar of 'Bereishis' is above letters and thought, and that Jews are called 'reishis'. Yom Kippur reaches this root after ten days; Purim revealed it even when the Jews had sinned.

title.en: The lowest Jews: Dan, Adar and Haman

summary.en: The Rav explains that the lowest souls are at the end of the Torah, like Shevet Dan, who were outside the clouds of glory and exposed to Amalek, and like the month of Adar. Haman thought he could prevail over these low Jews, but Hashem showed that every Jew is rooted in Bereishis; this is why Purim, kept in the second Adar next to Nisan, is greater than Yom Kippur.

title.en: The mekalel and the fresh lechem hapanim

summary.en: The Rav tells of the son of the Egyptian man who was turned away from Shevet Dan and mocked the nine-day-old lechem hapanim, meaning that Hashem no longer cares for the lowest Jews. He answers that the lechem hapanim miraculously stayed fresh, so no Jew becomes stale before Hashem, and says Haman made the same claim; the Kabbalists say Haman was a gilgul of that man's father.

title.en: Memuchan, Purim as lechem hapanim, and matanos la'evyonim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the names of Achashverosh's ministers allude to the korbanos, with Memuchan alluding to the lechem hapanim, and that the shemen zayis corresponds to Chanukah and the lechem hapanim to Purim. Purim is the day Hashem shows His love to the lowest Jew, which is why the less observant are happiest on it. He closes with Purim wishes and explains that matanos la'evyonim reaches higher than ordinary tzedakah.

catalogTitle: יום שכל יהודי נכנס בפנמיותו - ה'סוד' שיש בו (שייכות לפרשת אמור)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Jew carries an inner point of holiness, a 'Holy of Holies' in the heart where all Jews are equal, and that Lag BaOmer, the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, is the day this secret point is revealed, so that even the lowest Jew can draw strength from it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash on parshas Emor, 'imros Hashem imros tehoros': learning even about tumah brings purity, and the days of Sefirah are days of purification. He then asks why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's passing is a day of joy, and why the Beis Aharon says that Rashbi is 'for everyone, even the lowest', when his teaching is the hidden Torah. Through the sefirah of hod, which the Gemara links to the Beis Hamikdash, he shows that Aharon HaKohen is the living Beis Hamikdash, the Holy of Holies of the Jewish people. Every Jew has such an inner point where he cannot be a rasha and where all are equal; this explains the minyan, the mumim of the kohanim, the sin of Rabbi Akiva's students, and why the Kohen Gadol does not mourn. Rashbi, the Holy of Holies after the churban, revealed the inner Torah, so his day has no mourning and every Jew can take chizuk from it.

en: Learning the Torah's portions about tumah does not draw impurity onto a person; Hashem's words are pure and bring purity, especially in the days of Sefirah.
Hod is the power to bow and submit to Hashem, to tzaddikim and to the Torah, and the Gemara calls the Beis Hamikdash 'hod'.
Everything in creation exists in place, time and soul; the Holy of Holies, Yom Kippur and the Kohen Gadol are the innermost point of each, so Aharon is the living Beis Hamikdash.
Every Jew has an inner point that is truly G-dly, that can never be extinguished, and in which the worst Jew is equal to the greatest.
Because every Jew has a unique purpose, every Jew deserves respect; Rabbi Akiva's students failed in this, and Lag BaOmer repairs their sin.
Rashbi is the Holy of Holies and Kohen Gadol of the world, who revealed the hidden Torah after the churban, so his day is joy without mourning.
Faith that one carries this secret point in the heart lets even the lowest Jew draw chizuk from Rashbi on Lag BaOmer and not give up.

title.en: Pure words in the parshiyos of tumah

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash on Emor, 'imros Hashem imros tehoros'. Though speaking of bad things can draw bad onto a person, learning the Torah's portions of tumah in the Sefirah weeks brings purity, refined 'seven times seven'.

title.en: Why Rashbi's passing is a day of joy

summary.en: The Rav asks why the hilula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is a joy when other tzaddikim's yahrzeits are not, and finds an earlier answer unsatisfying. He brings the Beis Aharon that whoever believes in Rashbi can draw chizuk from him, 'for all, even the lowest', and asks why, since Rashbi's mark is the hidden Torah meant for the few.

title.en: The seven middos and the week of hod

summary.en: The Rav explains that each Sefirah week refines one middah toward Hashem: love, fear and beauty only for Him. Netzach and hod are a person's two legs: netzach stands firm against opposition, while hod bends like grass in the wind; a Jew's beauty is his ability to submit.

title.en: Aharon HaKohen, the living Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: From the Gemara in Berachos that hod is the Beis Hamikdash, the Rav explains why Aharon embodies hod. Using olam, shanah, nefesh, he shows that the Kohen Gadol is the Holy of Holies in the realm of souls, and that Aharon's death in Av, the month of hod, foreshadowed the churban.

title.en: The inner point in every Jew

summary.en: The world is a camouflage over Hashem's presence, and its inner point is G-dliness itself. Likewise every Jew has an inner point that is G-dly, never extinguished and equal in all Jews, like the circle of tzaddikim and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'like the children of Kush'. It is a private Holy of Holies that a person himself cannot enter.

title.en: The minyan and the Kohen without blemish

summary.en: The Rav asks how the minyan for a davar shebikdusha can be learned from the meraglim, reshaim, and answers that ten Jews reveal the inner point where none is a rasha, so ten reshaim make a minyan and nine tzaddikim do not. He adds the Ramban on why the parsha of mumim names the sons of Aharon and not Aharon: in that inner point there is no blemish.

title.en: Every Jew's unique purpose and Rabbi Akiva's students

summary.en: Based on 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', the Rav explains that every Jew has a unique purpose, as every face differs, in which even the worst Jew is greater than the greatest tzaddik; so one must respect every Jew. Rabbi Akiva's students died for lacking this, and he then taught 'love your fellow as yourself' as the great principle, being himself the inner soul of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The Beis Hamikdash, place of bowing and equality

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Beis Hamikdash, the place of hod, is always tied to bowing, and that there even a king receives no special honor, for all are equal before Hashem. Since it is the place of the united soul of Klal Yisroel, sinas chinam struck at its very essence.

title.en: Mourning belongs to the outside, not the inner self

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's parable of the king's children on 'banim atem... lo sisgodedu': a Jew who passes away returns to his Father, so excessive mourning is forbidden. Mourning comes from the body, not the inner soul; Chazal derive it from 'I will turn your festivals into mourning', and Tisha B'Av falls on the weekday of Pesach. Thus the Kohen Gadol, the inner point, barely mourns.

title.en: Rashbi, the Holy of Holies after the churban

summary.en: From 'lo sisgodedu' the Rav shows that all Jewish souls are one, and that the Torah too has an inner part, sod, about G-dliness itself. After the churban Hashem sent Rashbi's soul to take the Beis Hamikdash's place; hidden in the cave he revealed the secrets of the Torah, and as the world's Kohen Gadol, his day of passing has no mourning, only joy.

title.en: The week of hod and the crowds at Meron

summary.en: The Rav connects this to the custom of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples to celebrate the yahrzeits of masters of the inner Torah. The week of hod begins with Pesach Sheni, when even the tamei were granted a share, and peaks at Lag BaOmer. That is why all kinds of Jews, even those far from Yiddishkeit, are drawn to Meron: their inner point, where there is no blemish, pulls them to Rashbi.

title.en: Emunah in the hidden point, the meaning of the Beis Aharon

summary.en: Returning to the Beis Aharon, the Rav explains that 'emunah in Rashbi' is not intellectual entry into the pardes, which is forbidden to most, but faith and instinct that one's heart holds a secret, shining point. 'Ohr' equals 'raz': the secret is hidden yet gives light, which is why simple Jews dance with joy over the secrets of the Torah.

title.en: Chizuk for the broken Jew of ikvesa d'meshicha

summary.en: The Rav speaks to the Jew broken by the yetzer hara in ikvesa d'meshicha, who feels unworthy of tefillin or a kapitel Tehillim: on Lag BaOmer he must take chizuk and carry it through the year. The day repairs the sin of Rabbi Akiva's students, since even the lowest has a point deserving honor; it is hod shebehod, and it always falls on Purim's weekday.

title.en: Tzedakah of time and a closing wish

summary.en: The Rav describes the beis medrash initiative of giving 'tzedakah of time', learning at night with weaker bochurim, and urges joining it, noting that whoever gives his time for another loses nothing. He closes with the wish that everyone feel the secret of the day: that every Jew carries the inner G-dliness of the hidden Torah.

catalogTitle: היום נתגלה נקודה פנימיות של כל ישראל שנקרא קודש קדשים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai stands above the churban like the hidden Kodesh HaKodashim, and that on Lag Ba'omer the hidden point of love in every Jew, even the most distant, is revealed.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Satmar Rav, who explained the singing in Meron during the Nine Days with the words "oz vechedvah bimkomo", and with the Likutei Torah that the churban had no hold on Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. He tells of a student of the Arizal punished for saying Nachem on Rashbi's day. In the Kodesh HaKodashim there was no churban: Shlomo HaMelech hid the Aron in tunnels beneath it, and so every Jew's heart holds a hidden point, the ahavah mesuteres, that churban cannot reach. Moshe forgot the vavim made from the half-shekels of the Jews outside the camp, and Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him; Rashbi, Rabbi Akiva's continuation, declares that Torah and the forgotten Jews are never forgotten. After singing, the Rav explains that on Lag Ba'omer, completing hod shebehod, Klal Yisrael seizes Yishmael's bow, and connects the 70 tikkunim of Rashbi to "vayehi roveh kashes". He closes with a tefillah for kiddush Hashem.

en: The churban had no hold on Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, just as there was no churban in the Kodesh HaKodashim.
Shlomo HaMelech hid the Aron in tunnels under the Beis HaMikdash, and in the same way every Jew's heart holds a hidden point, the concealed love of Hashem, that churban cannot reach.
The Jews who fell outside the camp are the forgotten souls; Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded Moshe of them, and Rashbi carries on that role.
Lag Ba'omer is a secret that Jews feel without understanding: the revealing of the hidden love, which strengthens every Jew, even the posh'im.
Rashbi declares that the Torah will never be forgotten; the Torah is scattered like the Jews in galus, but neither the Torah nor any Jew is forgotten.
On Lag Ba'omer Klal Yisrael seizes Yishmael's weapon, the bow, just as David HaMelech killed Goliath with his own sword.

title.en: The hidden Aron and the hidden love

summary.en: The Rav explains that there was no churban in the Kodesh HaKodashim, since Shlomo HaMelech hid the Aron in tunnels beneath it. He ties Shlomo to Shir HaShirim, the holy of holies, and says every Jew's heart has a hidden point, the ahavah mesuteres, which is the hidden Aron.

title.en: The forgotten vavim and the forgotten souls

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshe forgot the vavim, the only part of the Mishkan outside the camp, made from the extra half-shekels of the Jews who fell outside the camp, and that Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him. He links them to the last eight pesukim of the Torah and the forgotten halachos, and brings Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen on why the hillula is Rashbi's and not Rabbi Akiva's.

title.en: Lag Ba'omer, a secret every Jew feels

summary.en: Bringing the Ba'al HaTanya's siddur that tikkun chatzos mourns Yerushalayim, meaning yiras shamayim, the Rav says there is a hidden point in Yerushalayim and in the Jewish heart that the churban does not touch. Rashbi's day gives chizuk to the distant ones: their hidden love is untouched, and Jews feel the joy of Lag Ba'omer without understanding it. The talk ends with the crowd breaking into song.

title.en: The Torah and the Jews in exile

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara of Kerem B'Yavneh, where Rashbi rejects the fear that the Torah will be forgotten, and explains that the Torah, like the Jews, is scattered in galus, its halachos not in their place. He connects Lag Ba'omer, Purim and the nidachim outside the camp, where forgetting took hold.

title.en: No forgetting on Lag Ba'omer

summary.en: The Rav asks how Moshe, who received the Torah like a kallah and never forgot, could forget the vavim, and answers that the Jews are Hashem's kallah, who is never forgotten. Rashbi, the continuation of Rabbi Akiva, reveals on Lag Ba'omer that there is no forgetting, and the Rav ends with the pull of all Jews to Meron.

title.en: Seizing Yishmael's bow

summary.en: The Rav explains that the greatest victory is seizing the enemy's weapon, as David took Goliath's sword. Yishmael's power is the bow, the middah of yesod through milah; sefiras ha'omer repairs yesod, and on Lag Ba'omer, after hod shebehod, Klal Yisrael seizes the bow. He connects "vayehi roveh kashes" to the 70 tikkunim of Rashbi, who repairs all seventy faces of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Tefillah for the breaking of the bow

summary.en: After a long untranscribed stretch, the Rav closes with a tefillah that Hashem's kingship be revealed, that the kelipah of Yishmael be broken, and that there be a great kiddush Hashem in the world.

catalogTitle: רצה ר' שמעון שישמחו בהילולא שלו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wanted his hillula to be a day of joy: Lag Ba'omer reveals the inner core of every Jew, like Yom Kippur and Purim, and is a day of seeking Zion, and he calls on his listeners to thank Hashem for the open miracles He does for the Jews.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Eliyahu's words to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that through the Zohar the Jews will leave exile, and explains that this includes the chassidic sefarim built on it, since the Ba'al Shem Tov carried Rabbi Shimon's soul. The joy of his hillula is above nature, a joy of the days of Moshiach. Lag Ba'omer is like Yom Kippur and like Purim: all three reveal the inner point of a Jew, the 'rotzeh ani' the Rambam finds in every Jew, and Rabbi Shimon himself taught that the sin in Haman's time was only outward. Counting the omer today is a remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash, a way of seeking Zion, and Lag Ba'omer is a special day of it. Finally the Rav describes the crowds at Meron and the constant miracles in Eretz Yisrael, and says one must thank Hashem.

en: Eliyahu told Rabbi Shimon that through the Zohar the Jews will leave exile, and the Rav explains this includes all the holy sefarim built on it, especially those of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples.
The joy of Rabbi Shimon's hillula is above nature, a joy of the days of Moshiach that Jews feel and that cannot be held back.
Lag Ba'omer is both like Yom Kippur and like Purim, and all three reveal the inner core of a Jew.
Counting the omer today is a remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash and a way of seeking Zion, and Lag Ba'omer, which comes from the Holy of Holies, is a special day of seeking Zion.
