oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Adar, the lowest and most hidden month, carries the Megillah's personal message that Hashem is near even to the lowest Jew, and that in a year of a second Adar Hashem Himself completes what is missing.

abstract.en: The Rav opens the month of Adar by saying that Purim is widely misunderstood: its clowning and wine are an anesthetic for a remedy too strong to take awake. Purim has its own masechta, and Rav Masna opens the Megillah with the passuk that Hashem is near to us. Rashi calls the Megillah a letter, and the Rav explains that a letter is addressed to one person: the Megillah speaks to each reader privately. He then describes the ladder of souls, places and times. Our generation is the heel, yet still bound to the head, as the fingernail was once in the embryo. Nisan, from nes, is the month of open miracles; Adar, from aderes, a cloak, is the month of hidden ones. Adar matches the tribe of Dan at the rear of the camp, whom Amalek attacked as rejected. The Megillah answers that Hashem forsakes no Jew. In a leap year Adar Sheni has no permutation of the Divine Name, and Hashem Himself is the added one, so Purim belongs to the lowest.

en: The Rav says Purim's clowning and wine serve as an anesthetic for a spiritual remedy too strong to take with open eyes, and Purim works whether or not one feels it.
The key to the Megillah, from Rav Masna's opening passuk, is that Hashem is near to us even when events make Him seem far.
Because the Megillah is called a letter, its message is addressed privately to each Jew who reads it.
Nisan is the month of revealed miracles and Adar the month of hidden ones, yet Adar holds as many miracles as Nisan.
Amalek attacked Dan, the rejected tribe at the rear, and Parshas Zachor teaches that Hashem never forsakes even the lowest Jew.
In a year with a second Adar, the thirteenth month has no permutation of the Divine Name, and Hashem Himself is the 'kolel', the added one who completes Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Adar transformed; Purim misunderstood

summary.en: The Rav says the whole month of Adar was turned to joy, and that Purim is misunderstood as a kind of Jewish Halloween when it may be the greatest day of the year. Its clowning and wine are like an anesthetic for a remedy too strong to take awake.

title.en: A whole masechta for a small Yom Tov

summary.en: The Rav notes that Purim, a weekday Yom Tov with few halachos, earned its own masechta, unlike Chanukah or Shavuos. The Gemara explains the whole Megillah and opens it with about fifteen Sages, each bringing a passuk as a key to it.

title.en: Rav Masna's key: Hashem is near

summary.en: Rav Masna opens the Megillah with the passuk about a great nation to whom Hashem is near; the Rav explains that the events of the Megillah could have made Jews think Hashem was far, and the Megillah teaches the opposite. He then asks why Rashi, usually so terse, poetically calls the Megillah 'the letter of Purim'.

title.en: A book and a letter

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a book, written for whoever picks it up, with a letter, addressed privately to one person and read with closer attention. The Megillah is both, and its message is meant personally for every reader, even one who thinks Hashem's blessings are for others.

title.en: The ladder of souls and generations

summary.en: Recalling the three dimensions of creation, space, time and soul, the Rav describes souls arranged on a ladder in each generation and across history, from the Avos and the dor hamidbar at the head down to our generation, 'ikvesa d'Meshicha', the insensitive heel.

title.en: The embryo, the fingernail and Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the heel is no less part of the person: in the embryo every limb, even the last-formed fingernail, was included. So the last generation is still bound to the beginning, just as every place in the world is nourished from Yerushalayim, as shown by Shlomo HaMelech's planting.

title.en: Nisan the flag, Adar the cloak

summary.en: In time, Nisan, when the world was created, is the head of the months; its name comes from 'nes', a flag on a high pole, because Hashem shows Himself openly with miracles then. Adar, furthest away, comes from 'aderes', a cloak, the time when a person is in the dark and Hashem hides.

title.en: Hidden miracles: uncovering the hidden

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the supernatural miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim with the Megillah, where every event is natural and could appear in a newspaper. Yet taken together the plot shows a guiding hand, so the Megillah is full of miracles; following the Avodas Yisrael, 'Megillas Esther' means revealing the hidden, recognizing Hashem behind the mask.

title.en: Dan at the rear and Amalek

summary.en: Adar draws from Nisan as the toe from the head. The Rav describes Dan, the tribe at the rear of the camp, gathering what others lost, and its failings; Amalek attacked those expelled from the clouds, thinking Hashem had rejected them. Adar, like Dan, is at the bottom, and Parshas Zachor teaches that Hashem never forsakes any Jewish soul.

title.en: The Megillah's hope for the last generation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the Jews joined Achashverosh's feast, celebrating the apparent end of the seventy years, and lost hope; that generation at the end of the first galus corresponds to ours. The Megillah's personal letter tells every Jew that Hashem is near and has not forsaken him, and it ends with the Jews' teshuvah and with gentiles becoming Jews.

title.en: A second Adar: the moon falls behind

summary.en: The Rav leaves the halachos of drinking for later weeks and turns to this year's second Adar. Hashem is the sun and Jews the moon, so they count by the moon; when the moon lags, a thirteenth month is added, taking the Jews even further from Nisan. The Yerushalmi says the original Purim miracle happened in Adar Sheni.

title.en: The thirteenth month and the kolel

summary.en: The twelve months and twelve tribes match the twelve permutations of the Divine Name; the thirteenth month, like outcasts belonging to no tribe, has none, and is counted as the 'kolel', the added one. The Rav asks where the right to add one comes from and answers that the One is Hashem, as in the Midrash that Hashem completed the seventy souls and the six hundred thousand.

title.en: Purim Gadol: the Yom Tov of the lowest

summary.en: The Rav concludes that in a leap year the second Purim is a 'great Purim', when Hashem joins those left out and completes Klal Yisrael, so no Jew is rejected. Unlike Shabbos, felt most by tzaddikim, Purim is made for the lowest, and the lower one is, the more Purim can lift him.

catalogTitle: ביאור "כשם שהקב"ה לכל כך רשב"י לכל" (בית אהרן)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Beis Aharon's words that just as Hashem is good to all, so Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is for all, even the lowest: Lag Baomer, hod sheb'hod, is the day of the hidden 'sod' in which every Jew carries a secret worth that only the masters of sod perceive.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Beis Aharon: whoever has emunah in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai has chizuk from him, for he is for all, even the lowest. He sets alongside it the Maggid of Koznitz, who applied 'when will I come and see the face of G-d' to the longing for Lag Baomer. Following the Siddur Baal HaTanya, the week of hod is a second, finishing tikkun of the middos, and since the end is bound to the beginning, the lowest point reveals the highest. Like the Torah, the world has pshat and sod in place, time and soul: the Kodesh haKodashim, the fiftieth day, and Aharon, the soul of sod, for whom there is no aveilus. Rashbi, who revealed the secrets, is the aspect of the Kohen Gadol, so in Meron there is no mourning. In pshat one Jew is greater than another; in sod each is an indispensable letter of the Torah. Rashbi's day therefore gives chizuk even to the lowest.

en: The Beis Aharon teaches that whoever has emunah in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai draws chizuk from him, for like Hashem he is good to all, even the lowest.
The week of hod in sefirah is a second, overall tikkun of the middos, and at its lowest point, hod sheb'hod, the highest light is revealed, because every end is bound to its beginning.
The world, like the Torah, has levels from pshat to sod in place, time and soul: the Kodesh haKodashim, the fiftieth day, and the soul of Aharon the Kohen Gadol.
In the realm of sod there is no aveilus, since in truth everything from Hashem is chesed; therefore the Kohen Gadol was not bound by mourning, and at Rashbi's place in Meron one does not mourn.
Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah with a virtue no other Jew has, so in sod all Jews are equal and each must be honored, a lesson the students of Rabbi Akiva lacked.
Lag Baomer, like Purim, is a day for the lowly: every Jew carries a secret that only masters of sod like Rashbi understand, and this gives even the lowest chizuk that he is needed.

title.en: The end bound to the beginning

summary.en: The Rav explains that every end is bound to its beginning: the Torah's last parsha, tied to the lowest souls, is joined to Bereishis, the aspect of Moshe and Moshiach. So at hod sheb'hod, the lowest point of the tikkun, the highest light of Moshe, Moshiach and Rashbi is revealed, with joy and the sweetening of judgments.

title.en: Pardes in the world: place and time

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, and since the world was created from the Torah in place, time and soul, the world too has these levels. In place, Eretz Yisrael is drush and the Kodesh haKodashim is sod, beyond nature; in time, the fiftieth day after seven times seven is above time, which is why Moshe could add a day before Matan Torah.

title.en: Aharon, the soul of sod

summary.en: In the soul, the Rav explains, Aharon is the sod: he alone enters the Kodesh haKodashim, where even angels may not go. Aharon is hod, and the Gemara calls the Beis Hamikdash hod, so he is hod sheb'hod. Therefore the Kohen Gadol does not leave the Mikdash and may serve as an onen: in the world of sod there is no aveilus, for there everything is chesed.

title.en: Rashbi as the Kohen Gadol: no mourning in Meron

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rashbi, who revealed the secrets of the Torah on Lag Baomer, is the aspect of the Kohen Gadol, as sung in 'Bar Yochai'. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the joy of Lag Baomer is above the natural order, and tells of the Arizal stopping a tzaddik from saying Nachem in Meron and of the Satmar Rav having 'Bar Yochai' sung there in the Nine Days. Lag Baomer reveals geulah, and Shavuos brings one to the yovel and the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: The Maggid's words explained

summary.en: The Rav explains the Maggid: through sefirah Jews long for hod sheb'hod, the Beis Hamikdash, and 'pnei Elokim' means the innermost part of the name Elokim, which is all mercy. Then the aspect of Moshiach, Rashbi's aspect, is revealed and mourning ceases. He adds that every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, so that a single missing letter would make it invalid.

title.en: Honoring every Jew: pshat and sod

summary.en: The Rav explains that the students of Rabbi Akiva did not honor one another, which became grave in the days of sefirah. In pshat one Jew is greater than another, like the large beis of Bereishis; in sod all are equal, like the circle dance of the tzaddikim around Hashem, and each has a mission only he can fulfil. Rashbi, a student of Rabbi Akiva, revealed the sod, and with it the duty to honor every Jew.

title.en: Rashbi is for all, even the lowest

summary.en: Returning to the Beis Aharon, the Rav explains that even one who knows nothing of Rashbi's Torah but has emunah in him draws chizuk: every Jew carries a secret, and Rashbi understands every Jew. Like Purim, a day for the lowly, Lag Baomer falls on Purim's weekday, and 'gal' hints to it. He closes on the week of hod as a time when every Jew may enter the gates of tzedek, and returns to the Maggid's longing.

catalogTitle: רשב"י ממתיק דין הקשה של הוד

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, on Lag Ba'Omer, sweetens the harsh judgment of hod, turning the 'blood' of din into the 'milk' of chesed that is completed on Shavuos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the great crowds of Jews drawn to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the miracles and protection seen in his merit. He then explains that the work of the days of sefirah is to sweeten the gevuros, the harsh judgments, through teshuvah, which rises to binah. The hardest of them is hod, the fifth middah, furthest from binah: the Beis Hamikdash, called hod, was destroyed in the fifth millennium, and hod reversed spells the impurity of blood. Lag Ba'Omer, hod shebehod, begins the third part of the count, the dawn watch, when the blood of din starts turning into the milk of chesed, completed on Shavuos; hence dairy on Shavuos. He shows the same pattern in Av, the fifth month, with the passing of Aharon and of the Arizal, and links Rabbi Shimon to the passuk 'al tishkechi kol gemulav'. He closes with the greatness of the day and a story joining nigleh with nistar.

en: The purpose of counting sefirah is to sweeten the gevuros, the attributes of judgment, and teshuvah does this because it reaches binah, above the seven middos.
Hod, the fifth middah, is the harshest judgment because it is the furthest from binah.
The Beis Hamikdash is called hod and was destroyed in the fifth millennium, the time of hod, when hod was overturned.
From Lag Ba'Omer the blood of judgment begins turning into the milk of chesed, and on Shavuos the process is complete, which is why dairy is eaten on Shavuos.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who revealed the inner Torah on the day of his passing, holds the sweetening hidden inside hod.
